video.title: Build It and See If It Sells? That's How You Go Broke

summary: A short promo clip from Dark Horse Entrepreneur (episode 564) arguing that building a digital product quickly with AI is not evidence of demand. The host sets out three levels of evidence (existing spend, pain in buyers' own words, and commitment such as sign-ups, booked calls or pre-orders), says friends' opinions are worth nothing, and advises writing a go/no-go criterion before testing. The action is to write one sentence stating the buyer, price and result, plus the evidence that would prove you wrong. It is a validation framework, not a specific business, and ends by pointing to the full episode and a freebie.

tactics.name: Three-level evidence ladder for demand validation
steps: Level one: check for existing spend, meaning people already paying for something close to your idea; competition shows the market exists.
Level two: collect pain in buyers' own words from forums, reviews and comments, without prompting them.
Read the three-star reviews of competing products to see what buyers wanted but did not get.
Level three: get commitment, such as a specific sign-up, a booked call, or a pre-order (the gold standard).
Treat opinions, such as a friend saying they would buy, as level zero that does not count.

quote.text: Real evidence comes in three levels. Level one, there's existing spend.

video.title: How to Start an AI Automation Agency in 2026 (Step by Step)

summary: A tutorial from Mikey No Code on starting an AI automation agency in 2026 using real estate as the niche. He builds three Base44 Super Agents (speed-to-lead follow-up, inquiry triage/scoring, weekly executive reporting), then packages them as a 'Real Estate Growth Suite' with a setup fee plus monthly retainer. He covers cold outreach with a Loom demo and a free 15-minute audit, discovery calls, contracts, a 48-hour onboarding, case studies, raising prices, and hiring an operator after $5-10k MRR. The video is promotional for his Base44 master class and contains no first-hand revenue evidence; prices are recommendations.

video.title: The Most Profitable Business You Can Run From a Phone

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Eli, a former Connecticut real estate agent and truck dispatcher who built a trailer-subleasing business. He leased 53ft semi-trailers from a big lessor for about $350/month, rented them to truckers for about $180/week, and found customers through Facebook Marketplace and then Facebook ads. He claims about 300 trailers, $250k/month in billings and $40-50k/month net profit with two virtual employees, run from his phone. Key takeaways: net-30 supplier terms plus upfront deposits and weekly billing give immediate positive cash flow; GPS tracking and insurance structure matter; paid ads were the scaling lever.

video.title: Building a BORING Business Empire Nobody Knows You Own, Level by Level

summary: A narrated, fictionalised 'level by level' story of building a quiet portfolio of boring cash-flowing businesses over about 12 years: a holding-company structure, a small snack vending route, laundromats bought with SBA 7(a) loans, then car washes. Each level is illustrated with US market-range numbers and an 'opponent' (rival vendor, seller's cash claims, landlord, new competitor, key-staff departure, private equity). Key takeaways are to verify revenue with utility bills, make the lease outlast the loan, and use paperwork and checklists rather than fighting competitors. The numbers are market ranges in a hypothetical story, not an operator's own results.

video.title: I Make $13K/Month From (Yet Another) Fitness App

summary: Max describes building Max AI, a mobile lifting and fitness app, after noticing that lifters used several separate apps without one unified platform. He had little coding experience and used AI coding tools, then charged an upfront annual fee and grew through founder-led social content and paid ads. He says the app brought in nearly $14,000 over the prior 28 days, with growth from X, app downloads, and subscribers. His main advice is to launch around a problem you care about, learn which features and videos work, and share the building process publicly.

video.title: Don't Build Anything Until You Do This | Digital Product Validation

summary: Dark Horse Entrepreneur host explains a weekend plan to validate a small digital product (ebook, template pack, prompt library, mini course) before building it. Evidence must cost the buyer something: existing spend, specific pain in their own words, or commitment (email, call, pre-order, payment). The plan sets go/fix/kill thresholds on Friday, researches buyers on Saturday, then writes a one-paragraph offer, builds a mock-up and landing page, and asks for a real commitment on Sunday. Key takeaway: opinions are worthless, pre-sales are the strongest evidence, and a killed idea is a cheap win.

acquisition.how: Research and quote grouping can be agent-assisted, but community outreach and conversations are manual and cold DMs to individuals face PECR limits; inbound listings and SEO are more automatable.

onboarding.how: Landing page, payment and automated delivery email are standard software.

delivery.how: Digital files can be drafted by AI with human review and delivered automatically.

billing.how: Payment platforms handle checkout, refunds and receipts.

support.how: Low-touch product; an agent can answer FAQs with occasional human refunds or edge cases.

uk_applicability.notes: Works in the UK; digital products sell globally. Pre-sales need clear delivery dates and refunds under UK consumer law, and VAT on digital sales applies. Avoid cold DMs to individuals under PECR; ask questions in communities where allowed.

video.title: How to Use ChatGPT Dots to Build Apps in Minutes (AI + No Code)

summary: Mikey No Code demonstrates a workflow where an AI assistant called 'Dots' (ChatGPT Dots, as titled) researches app ideas and writes three phased build prompts, which are then pasted into the no-code builder Base 44 to build a 'branded carousel maker' web app. The app is built in three phases: manual editor, brand kit/presets/projects, and PDF/PNG export plus JSON backup. The key takeaway is that better upfront decisions (narrow idea, phased prompts with clear limits) matter more than the build speed. The video is also a promotion for the presenter's paid Base 44 master class (offered free via link). No revenue or market validation data is given.

video.title: Every successful startup starts with this one advantage

summary: Jeff Harmon (Harmon Brothers ad agency, co-founder of Angel Studios) tells My First Million hosts how he built marketing campaigns for Orbrush, Poopourri, Squatty Potty and Purple Mattress, and how Angel Studios funds and markets films through a member 'guild'. The central framework is 'find your glitch': spot a channel or market gap others ignore, such as early YouTube ads costing under a penny a view, and use it as a beachhead. He also covers a comedian-led ad creation retreat, celebrity face-warming for algorithms, vibe-coding with agents overnight, and mindset lessons about letting go of disputes. Most figures are self-reported and the transcript is auto-generated with some errors.

video.title: EP 564 Validate Digital Products Before You Build | AI Entrepreneur Plan

summary: Dark Horse Entrepreneur host explains a weekend plan to validate a low-priced digital product (ebook, template pack, kit) before building it. Evidence is ranked by what it costs the buyer: existing spend, pain in buyers' own words, and commitment (pre-order, payment, specific waitlist). The host recommends setting go/fix/kill thresholds on Friday, researching on Saturday, then building a one-paragraph offer and mock-up landing page and asking for commitment on Sunday. Key takeaway: speed of building with ChatGPT is not proof of demand, so test with real money or commitment from strangers first.

tactics.name: Set go/fix/kill thresholds before testing
steps: On Friday night spend about 10 minutes writing the pass mark before starting
Go: at least 3 strangers take a real commitment step, ideally payment or pre-order, or 1 paid pre-order plus several strong conversations
Fix: people have the pain and engage but nobody commits
Kill/park: no real people describing the pain and no spend nearby
Write on a sticky note as referee and adjust for audience size and price

steps: Check Gumroad, Etsy, Teachable, Stan Store, Amazon books for existing products with reviews, ratings and sales counts

Read 1-3 star competitor reviews to find the product gap

Have ChatGPT group and rank themes using only the real quotes

video.title: Do these 7 Things Immediately When Building Apps with AI

summary: Tutorial from Mikey No Code on seven habits to adopt immediately when building apps with AI, demonstrated by building a task manager in Base44. The steps are: prototype only the core function first, write structured prompts (what it does, looks like, what users can do, what to leave out), add authentication right after the prototype works, plan the data structure in Base44's discuss mode before adding features, run Base44's free security scan before publishing, test with realistic data across multiple accounts, and make scale-ready structural choices (workspace-based data model, back-end functions). The key takeaway is that most problems blamed on AI builders come from the process around them, and the order of decisions matters. The video repeatedly promotes the creator's Base44 masterclass ($499 'normally', offered free).

quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

tactics.name: Prototype the single core function first
steps: Identify the one most important user loop (for a task manager: type a task and see it in a list)
Prompt only that loop, explicitly excluding extras (no categories, priorities, due dates or auth yet)
Specify minimal design (e.g. white background, blue accent)
Test the loop manually (enter, add button, display, delete) before adding anything else

quote.text: it means building the single most important function and making sure it works correctly before adding anything around it
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

tactics.name: Four-part structured build prompt
steps: State what the app does and the data each item holds (title, priority low/medium/high, due date)
State what it should look like (layout, grouping, colours)
State what the user can do (checkbox to complete, delete, completed items move to bottom with strikethrough)
State what to leave out (no authentication, categories or team features yet)

quote.text: It should explain what the app does, what it should look like, what the user can do, and what should be left out
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

tactics.name: Add authentication straight after the prototype works
steps: Once the core loop works, prompt: add sign-up/login, each user sees only their own data, keep existing functionality and design unchanged
Create two test accounts, add different tasks in each
Switch accounts and confirm data is fully isolated

quote.text: Add user authentication with sign up and login. Each user should only be able to see and manage their own tasks
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

tactics.name: Plan the data model in discuss mode before adding features
steps: Open Base44 discuss mode (no code changes)
Describe all future features (categories, team assignment, projects) and ask how data should be structured to support them without rebuilds
Challenge weak suggestions (e.g. categories stored inside each task vs a separate category structure)
Return to build mode and add one feature at a time with 'Do not change anything else'

quote.text: Before I add any new features, I want to plan the full data structure for this task management app
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

tactics.name: Mandatory pre-publish security scan
steps: Run Base44's built-in security scan before every publish
Review flagged exposed API keys, broken access-control rules and dependency vulnerabilities
Apply recommended fixes one at a time
Re-run the scan until the app passes

quote.text: Making it a required step before every publish is one of the simplest ways to avoid shipping an app that works on the surface great, but is not secure underneath
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

tactics.name: Realistic-data testing
steps: Fill the app with realistic items: short and long titles, mixed priorities, overdue and future deadlines, active and completed states
Use more than one user account
Exercise every core flow as a real user would (create, complete, delete, switch priorities)
Fix layout and logic issues (e.g. long titles pushing buttons, overdue dates not flagged) before sharing

tactics.name: Scale-ready structural defaults
steps: Make records belong to a workspace rather than directly to a user, without changing visible functionality
Move important, consistency-critical logic into back-end functions instead of the browser
Avoid hard-coded values that should be configurable

quote.text: Update the data structure so that tasks belong to a workspace rather than directly to a user
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

video.title: How to Find a Side Hustle Where Customers Already Exist

summary: The Side Hustle Nation host revisits the idea of selling where customers already gather, covering online marketplaces, newer platforms, and offline locations. Examples include digital products, resale, teaching, rentals, physical services, and vending, with operators describing how they reached existing audiences. The strongest recurring advice is to research demand, choose a specific niche, and keep improving how products reach buyers. Many examples still require substantial human work, particularly for physical delivery and in-person selling.

video.title: This BORING Investing Strategy Beats the Market (99% Success Rate)

summary: David Heacock interviews investment manager Jonathan Boyar about valuing businesses by what an acquirer might pay, emphasizing cash flow, a margin of safety, and patience. Boyar describes his firm's public-equity management and paid research services, including how it finds ideas and sells reports. The conversation also covers sports-team investments, HVAC distribution, AI, and the host's air-filter business. The main takeaway is to understand the business and its cash flows, consider the price paid, and invest in a way the investor can stick with.

video.title: Give Me 25 Minutes and I Will Make You Rich

summary: George McConnell demonstrates a service that redesigns local businesses’ websites with an AI tool, then sends the finished demo to the owner as a sales pitch. His example uses a Miami fence company and a detailed brief covering the site’s design, copy, pages, lead form, and SEO. He claims the work earns his media team over $100,000 a month, but gives no service prices or sales-conversion evidence. The main takeaway is to show a prospect a tailored result before asking them to buy, while treating outreach as a numbers game.

speakers.name: George McConnell
speakers.description: Presents the tutorial, demonstrates the website build, and promotes YouMind.

ideas.name: AI-assisted website redesigns for local businesses
ideas.one_liner: Build a tailored website demo for a local business with an outdated or broken site, show it to the owner, and sell the rebuild with an optional maintenance retainer.
ideas.business_model: One-off website project sales, with an optional monthly retainer to keep the website running smoothly.
ideas.customer: Small or medium local businesses, especially family-owned contractors and service businesses such as fence repair, construction, pool services, and paving.
ideas.problem: Outdated, text-heavy, or malfunctioning websites may make it hard for prospective customers to find services, request a quote, or contact the business. The speaker says broken lead capture leaves money on the table.
ideas.offer: Build a complete, tailored website demo before contacting the owner. The demonstrated brief covers business details, existing images, brand positioning, design, page copy, navigation, a multi-step quote form, service areas, reviews, and technical SEO. Sell the site if the owner likes it; offer ongoing maintenance.

pricing.model: One-off project plus optional recurring maintenance retainer.
pricing.notes: The speaker does not state what he charges for a website or retainer. The requested $15,000–$25,000 agency-build appearance is a design benchmark in the prompt, not a stated sale price.

acquisition_channels.details: Search for local businesses, using a query such as “fence repair Miami.” Inspect their websites and social pages, then build a demo and send its link directly to the owner. The medium for sending the link is not stated.

quote.text: Now, you're not trying to convince someone that you can do it. Now, you're showing them exactly what you did.
quote.speaker: George McConnell

ideas.delivery: The operator gathers the business’s public details and images, assembles a long website brief, and asks YouMind to build the site. The demonstrated AI build creates pages, copy, navigation, and a quote-form design. The operator reviews the output, copies the link, and shows the demo to the owner. Hosting, domain transfer, live form integrations, and the ongoing maintenance workflow are not demonstrated.
unit_economics_claims: George says his media team’s service makes over $100,000 a month.
He suggests offering a monthly maintenance retainer, but gives no amount.
The service price, client acquisition cost, close rate, and delivery margin are not stated.
tools: A word-processing document for the website brief
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. YouMind subscription prices are mentioned, but the speaker does not identify a required startup budget.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. He says the demonstrated website build took about 1 hour and 24 minutes, but does not say how long it took to find a paying client.

acquisition.how: Software could help find and assess prospects, but selecting prospects and sending a tailored demo still needs review. UK rules restrict unsolicited electronic marketing to individuals and sole traders without consent; cold email to limited companies is allowed subject to the rules, and cold calls need TPS/CTPS screening.

onboarding.how: AI can process public site information and draft a brief, but a person must check the business details, image rights, service claims, and design requirements.

delivery.how: An agent can generate most pages and copy from a detailed brief. A person should verify facts, test forms and links, check mobile layouts, and handle deployment and integrations.

billing.how: The speaker describes selling the site and asking for a retainer but gives no automated quoting, contracting, invoicing, or payment process.

support.how: A retainer could cover routine monitoring, but fixing site problems, integrations, or inaccurate content needs human checks.

uk_applicability.notes: The website redesign offer can serve UK local businesses, but the demo is aimed at a Florida contractor. Adapt local service and weather claims, planning and building requirements, currency, and privacy wording. Outbound marketing must comply with UK PECR rules, including the stricter treatment of sole traders and individuals.

risks: The video does not show a paying customer accepting the demo, a sale price, or a conversion rate.
A generated site can contain invented or inaccurate reviews, ratings, service counts, locations, or other business claims; verify each one with the owner before publishing.
The demo form and SMS feature are described in the brief, but the video does not establish that a live form, CRM, or SMS integration works.
Using photos from a prospect’s current site in a sales demo does not establish permission to reuse them in a live site.
Unsolicited outreach to UK individuals and sole traders can breach PECR; an unspecified “send it to them” method needs a lawful channel.
A generated website may look finished while still needing accessibility, mobile, security, SEO, hosting, and functional testing.

video.title: 8 BORING Machines That Quietly Pay You for Years (No Employees Needed)

summary: The narrator presents seven unattended machine businesses, then gives a longer explanation of traditional cash ATM placement. The ideas rely on finding a busy location, making a host agreement, and using machines to serve customers without an employee on site. The transcript gives many revenue and cost figures, but most are narrator-reported estimates or examples, and the Harry story is presented without verifiable operator evidence. Its clearest practical advice is to confirm demand and the site agreement before buying equipment.

tactics.name: Lock the location before buying equipment
steps: Choose a machine that fits a site with existing demand.
Count traffic or check usage before purchasing.
Get the host agreement in writing and confirm site access, utilities, and permits.
Buy the machine only after the location is secured.

quote.text: Confirm the traffic first, sign the lease first, buy the machine last.
quote.speaker: Unnamed narrator

tactics.name: Use a simple ATM host pitch
steps: Scout cash-heavy businesses that are busy and have no ATM.
Offer the store a machine at no upfront cost.
Tell the owner that you handle the machine, cash, and paperwork.
Offer a monthly share of fees or another clear host payment.

quote.text: No upfront cost to you. That is it.
quote.speaker: Unnamed narrator

tactics.name: Scout, compare, pitch
steps: Count which businesses already have an ATM and which busy businesses do not.
Compare two processors' offers.
Pitch the best empty wall you found.
Start with one placement before building a route.

tactics.name: Use three filters for ATM sites
steps: Check for real cash traffic.
Make sure the host benefits from the placement.
Choose a site close enough to refill on an easy route.
Reject a location that misses any of the three filters.

video.title: This Food Truck Makes More in 10 Days Than Most Make All Year

summary: UpFlip profiles Ashley and Thaddeus, a New Orleans couple who started selling dessert and soul food plates out of their car trunk in Dallas with their last $40 in 2018 and now run the Bell Sweet Factory food truck in Miami. They claim over $4 million in sales since 2018, about $500k in the first truck's first year, $64-65k in June and about $52k in August, with average tickets of $50-70 and plates up to $173. Marketing is almost entirely TikTok and Instagram posts plus face-to-face guerrilla flyering; a customer built them a $50/month QR queue and text-notification system. They also earn from catering, an ebook on starting a food truck, and social media payouts, and describe a failed brick-and-mortar restaurant and a hostile influencer review they turned into publicity. Whisper transcript is noisy, so several numbers (especially the August P&L) are garbled.

video.title: 3 businesses we think are about to blow up

summary: Sam Parr and Shaan Puri of My First Million pitch businesses they think will grow. The first is oxytocin nasal sprays marketed to save marriages, inspired by Palmer Luckey's answer and biohacking subreddits. The second is affinity or fraternal memberships such as the Knights of Columbus, Good Sam, USCCA and AARP, which monetise loneliness and identity through insurance and financial products. They also discuss Angel Studios' member-voted, values-based streaming ($450M ARR), A24's model of buying overlooked films and guerrilla marketing, and the poor economics of film. The takeaway is to spot fringe trends early and monetise trusted communities with commodity financial products.

video.title: I Let Strangers Pitch Me Their Business Live

summary: The Koerner Office hosts a live pitch event in Utah. Ten strangers get 2 minutes to pitch and 10 minutes of critique from Chris Koerner, Nick and Brandon. The pitches range from an operating VA-funded massage business doing about $68k/month and a $1.5M ARR home-service marketing agency to pre-revenue ideas such as a seed cup, an NFC keychain, a containment diaper, a choose-your-path kids' letter subscription, an AI relationship app and mail-in cast iron cleaning. The hosts invested in or offered to help several, and the audience voted Go Seeds first, Pick a Path Letters second and Utah Veterans Massage third. The main takeaways are that distribution (especially paid ads and short-form video) is the recurring bottleneck, and that investors want proof of a repeatable process before funding. All numbers are unverified pitch claims.

ideas.name: Utah Veterans Massage
ideas.one_liner: Licensed therapists treat veterans in small leased rooms, paid about $90 per session by the VA via TriWest under a 12-free-session benefit.
ideas.business_model: Per-session insurance reimbursement (VA via TriWest); therapists paid per session.
ideas.customer: Veterans eligible for 12 VA-paid massage sessions; the VA refers by geographic proximity.
ideas.problem: Veterans in pain need access to medical massage that the VA funds, and new therapists struggle to find well-paid work.
ideas.offer: Medical and deep-tissue massage in one or two-room clinics, with billing, insurance back end and scheduling handled by the company.

pricing.model: VA reimbursement per session; therapist paid about $50
pricing.notes: Rates vary by state; the founder says they never go below about $89.

acquisition_channels.details: The VA (via TriWest) calls the company based on proximity to the veteran, so many small locations get referrals. No marketing spend. Getting into the network took about 8 months.

quote.text: we haven't spent a single dollar on marketing. The reason we have so many small office locations instead of one central is the VA will call us based on the geographic proximity to the veteran
quote.speaker: Aean Harden

ideas.delivery: Employed or contracted therapists treat clients in leased clinics (about $500-650/month rent each); therapists rebook clients at the end of each session; staff handle billing, insurance and scheduling.
unit_economics_claims: 750 sessions/month, $68k revenue, about $20k profit
$90 collected, $50 to therapist
Leases about $500-650/month per location
Credentialing automated with AI, about 25 minutes per person
tools: AI automation for credentialing and paperwork
ideas.startup_cost: not stated (rented a room one day a week to begin)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: about 8 months to get into the VA network; first rented room 18 months before the pitch

acquisition.how: VA referrals are inbound and need no marketing, but credentialing each new state is a gate.

onboarding.how: AI-automated credentialing is claimed to take 25 minutes per therapist; client booking comes via VA referral.

delivery.how: Hands-on massage by a licensed therapist in a physical clinic.

billing.how: Insurance back-end billing is claimed to be automated with AI and software; payer rules vary by state.

support.how: Schedulers (the founder's wife plus one) handle rebooking and queries with scheduling software.

uk_applicability.notes: Depends on the US VA/TriWest benefit and Medicaid-style rates. The UK has no equivalent per-session funded benefit, and NHS veterans' services are commissioned differently. Massage therapy would also need UK registration and insurance.

risks: Revenue depends on a single payer (VA/TriWest)
Each state differs in licensing, credentialing and pre-authorisation, so expansion may lag
Founder admits to a 'grow, expand and then figure it out' approach
Owner-operator bottleneck; needs a COO or operations manager
Valuation ask of $2M was seen as too high

video.title: This crazy simple app makes $50K/month

summary: Lino says he built App Max, an abs-focused fitness app, with no coding experience and grew it to about $55,000 in monthly revenue, with a stated pace of $60,000. He describes the app, its build tools, and how he moved from expensive influencer videos to an equity partnership and paid social ads. His playbook is to validate demand with social posts, ship quickly, test creator content cheaply, and scale ads only after finding content that works. The episode also includes the host’s promotion of Starter Story’s free app-ideas database.

speakers.description: Founder of App Max.

ideas.name: App Max abs fitness app
ideas.one_liner: A mobile fitness app that assesses users’ abs and gives them tailored plans and workout programs.
ideas.business_model: Paid fitness app; exact billing model not stated.
ideas.customer: People seeking visible abs or a summer shred; Lino says the target user is 15 to 30 years old.
ideas.problem: Lino says people seeking abs had no dedicated place to go for guidance.
ideas.offer: Users enter basic information about their fitness journey, receive a tailored abs plan and pre-made training programs, and can scan their abs for a breakdown including an abs score and body-fat percentage.

pricing.model: Paid app; customer price and billing cadence not stated.
pricing.notes: The transcript reports active paying customers but gives no subscription price.

acquisition_channels.details: Ran Meta ads using creator content, then moved the same creatives to TikTok ads. Lino says TikTok performed better for the app’s younger target users.

quote.text: And we would just run paid ads behind it, strictly through meta.
quote.speaker: Lino

acquisition_channels.details: Manually posted faceless TikTok slideshows. His recommended validation approach is to post three to four times a day and ask viewers to comment for the app.

quote.text: I would make a faceless TikTok page and start promoting your app through organic TikTok slideshows and start posting three to four times a day.
quote.speaker: Lino

acquisition_channels.details: Started with paid UGC from fitness influencers, later partnered with one large fitness creator in return for equity, and used that creator’s content in paid ads.

quote.text: And we partnered up with a big fitness influencer on social media in return for some equity, which helped us get the ground running off to start
quote.speaker: Lino

ideas.delivery: The app collects fitness-journey information, provides a tailored plan and pre-made workout programs, and offers a scan breakdown with an abs score and body-fat percentage. Lino says he built the app; the transcript does not describe who maintains it or handles customer support.
unit_economics_claims: Lino reports about $55,000 in monthly revenue, with a stated pace of $60,000 for the month.

video.title: The Hidden Cost of Building an Empire

summary: Short interview clip in which Nick Huber talks about the hidden pressure of running a holding company. He says he has raised over $50 million from 300+ investors and has about 325 employees depending on his companies, so big problems always reach him because his name is on it. He copes by doing the hard work when needed while keeping balance (fitness, date nights, friends, time outdoors with his kids). Owning three large companies smooths emotional swings because rarely do all three go badly at once. He weighs feedback by who it comes from and keeps about 15 trusted people who will challenge him if he becomes arrogant.

For each it gives rental rates, purchase costs, payback periods, who books, handover and reset routines, and a 'moat' (insurance, paperwork, deposits). It includes a failure story about skipping deposit and photos, a three-filter selection framework and a composite 'Harry' narrative. Figures are mostly generic, second-hand or illustrative, and the story is a narrated composite, so treat numbers as claims. video.title: 20 BORING Businesses Almost Nobody Has Started (Every One Still Wide Open)

summary: The video presents 20 under-served, mostly asset-based business ideas, from leasing land and placing coin-operated machines to renting warehouse space and operating digital billboards. For each, the narrator gives a price or other hard number, why the opportunity may be overlooked, and a first question to ask a relevant person. The examples are largely US-focused and presented as researched opportunities rather than the narrator’s operating businesses. The central lesson is to check local demand and terms by asking the people who own, manage, or use the relevant assets.

speakers.description: Narrator for Harry's Stealth Wealth; the transcript says Harry called a local airfield manager.

unit_economics_claims: National ground lease range: $500–$2,500 per month.
Industry database average: $900–$1,300 per month.
Mature multicarrier sites: $7,000–$8,000 per month.
tools: Tower lease consultancy landowner intake form

video.title: I Tested How Passive This AI Side Hustle Really Is

summary: Chris Koerner connects Claude to Omnisend and uses AI agents to send a paid consulting offer to people on his email list. The one week experiment reports $80 from 1,013 emails, with 16 calls estimated to take 80 minutes. Koerner says the $5 price, an unclear free email reply path, and the lack of follow-up weakened the campaign, and he considers testing a much higher hourly price. The tools automate campaign setup and analysis, but the consulting itself still depends on his time; Omnisend is also a promotional partner.

pricing.notes: The email also offered replies as a way to ask questions, which some recipients understood as free. Coaching, recurring services, and AI audits were mentioned as possible upsells without prices.

quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Koerner personally delivers the five-minute live consultations and may answer questions by email. TidyCal takes bookings, Stripe handles payment, and the booking calendar syncs with his calendar.
unit_economics_claims: Koerner reports $80 in campaign revenue from 16 calls, and estimates 80 minutes of consultation time.
He calculates campaign revenue per recipient at about $0.08.
He claims he has no costs, but does not quantify payment processing or software fees.
His $120,000-per-year illustration assumes 40 paid hours per week at $60 per hour; it is hypothetical, not observed profit.
He says a $1,000-per-hour consultation could yield 12 times the revenue from the same email send, but this was only a proposed test.
ideas.startup_cost: Koerner says he has no costs for selling his time. Actual payment-processing and software costs are not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Koerner reviewed campaign results one week after sending the email.

acquisition.how: Claude and Omnisend can segment contacts, draft, and send campaigns. Building a permission-based audience and choosing the offer still need human direction and review.

onboarding.how: TidyCal, Stripe, and calendar syncing can take payment and book an available slot automatically, subject to occasional checks.

delivery.how: Koerner must personally conduct each live consultation or write each substantive email answer.

billing.how: Stripe is integrated into the booking flow and can collect the stated booking price automatically; exceptions and accounting still need review.

support.how: Questions and consulting answers require Koerner's judgement and time. Agents could draft routine replies, but the paid advice remains human-led.

uk_applicability.notes: The consulting and booking model can work in the UK, but email acquisition needs UK PECR compliance: obtain consent for marketing to individuals and sole traders unless an exception applies; marketing to corporate subscribers has different rules. Cold calls must be screened against TPS/CTPS. Adapt the currency and payment terms for UK customers.

risks: The $5 price may signal low quality and earns little for each human-delivered session.
Offering a reply-by-email path alongside a paid booking confused some recipients about whether advice was free.
The reported campaign revenue does not establish that the same response rates will hold across the full list or at a much higher price.
The business sells Koerner's time, so it does not run almost entirely on agents.
In the UK, sending marketing emails to individuals or sole traders without the required consent can breach PECR.
Koerner granted the AI connector read and write access to Omnisend, creating account and data risks if access is misconfigured.

video.title: It Took Me 20 Years to Master Business. You Get It In 25 Minutes

summary: David Heacock, founder of Filterbuy (US air filter manufacturer, claimed ~150,000 filters/day and ~$25M/month revenue), shares five stages of building a boring business: commit long enough to learn, fund the constraint, build systems that preserve judgment, don't diversify before the core is ready, and build resilience and legacy. He recounts leaving Goldman, buying a declining $300k/yr business with debt, taking $50k salary for 7.5 years, and losing millions in 2021 by launching a freight company and buying an HVAC business while the core was doubling. Key takeaway: do the work yourself first, turn judgment into systems, and put capital into the core constraint rather than diversifying early.

video.title: You Can't Fake This Online

summary: Short clip from an interview with Nick Huber (Sweaty Startup) about building a social media audience as an operator. He says audience growth requires first doing something interesting in business and then writing good copy without caring what others think. He estimates he spent about two hours a day on Twitter/X in 2021 and calls it the highest-ROI work he has done, but says the same posts that gained 3,000-4,000 followers in 2021 now gain about 50. The key takeaway is that radical transparency builds trust and a network that sells your companies and products, but timing on the platform mattered a lot and it is much harder today.

video.title: 3 BORING Operator Rules Costco, Walton, and Gates Used to Win

summary: A compilation video of three operator-playbook essays using Costco's Jim Sinegal, Sam Walton, Bill Gates, Charlie Munger and others as case studies. Part one covers four hiring/retention rules and a 'rehire score' exercise; part two argues small businesses beat bigger rivals by copying proven ideas and shipping them better (the 'steal and ship loop'); part three sets out three trust rules (one unbreakable promise, refuse excess margin, spend on existing customers) illustrated with a fictional auto-repair owner. There is no real business idea or first-hand operator data; it is generic small-business advice built on a fictional character 'Harry' and secondhand statistics.

summary: Nick Huber (Sweaty Startup) answers two questions in a short excerpt: how to find and manage business partners, and whether to focus on one business or branch out. He says partners are hard to find and fail for moral reasons or because the value equation is off, and that splitting equity too many ways in small businesses leaves nobody making money. He notes that only 3 of his 11 companies matter financially (power law), four are unprofitable, and that 8 of 10 wealthy people he knows focused on one business. He pivoted out of a brutal student moving and storage business into self-storage. Key takeaway: focus on a good business, pick partners carefully, and stay open to better opportunities as momentum builds.

video.title: I Went Shopping for $675/Month Cash Flow Businesses (Live Walkthrough)

summary: Nick and online business broker Joe walk through listings on Flippa, including a pest control content site, a water sports ecommerce store and an AI homework SaaS. They discuss checking traffic and financial records, valuing businesses, seller financing, and risks such as falling traffic, customer concentration and weak transition plans. Joe says buyers should have a plan to improve a business and verify seller claims before closing. The video also touches on faceless YouTube channels, pest control directories, vending machines and buying a portfolio of online businesses.

video.title: We tested Instinct, Muse and Grokbot. They’re ridiculous.

summary: Sam Parr and Shaan Puri of My First Million discuss the new wave of consumer AI personal assistants (Instinct, Meta's Muse and Grok Bot), comparing it to the Uber vs Lyft race. Shaan shares uses (chasing a repair company's executives, booking a massage, winning a ticket refund) and Instinct's claims: $10B valuation within months, 10% daily growth, over $1B in agent transactions, 40% of users adding a card in three weeks with 80% retention, and a plan to monetise via transaction cuts, disintermediating Amazon and travel sites. They argue EQ (supportive check-ins) matters as much as IQ. Sam reports small creators earning $1M-10M a year from AI company sponsors and a data company (micro1) offering $800k for Hampton's private data. They also cover an OpenAI agent 'exploit gym' incident, regulation motives, OpenRouter and the 'frontier of knowledge' idea for spotting startup gaps.

video.title: He Makes $27K/Month Sending Text Messages

summary: Aaron Fuks of Hyros (Denver) explains how he built a B2B referral-pipeline business for home service trades (siding, painting, electrical, landscaping). He cold calls and mass-texts businesses in adjacent trades, gets a real bid or project first, then uses it as proof to sell partner introductions to a client. Pricing moved from $150 per appointment to $6,000 for 10 intros plus a $250-500/month nurturing fee, with claimed revenue around $27K last month. Key takeaway: bring value first (a real bid), sell relationships rather than leads, and run it on GoHighLevel with minimal cost.

ideas.customer: Home service business owners (siding, painting, electrical, landscaping, interior design, general contractors) wanting referral partners in adjacent trades
ideas.problem: Trades want steady high-value jobs from upstream partners (roofers, builders, designers) but lead marketplaces are shared and poor quality, and cold outreach is hard and time-consuming.

pricing.notes: Pricing 4x'd after pivot to packages with guarantees. Close is a menu: 20, 40 or 120 appointments. Commission of ~30% paid to the caller per appointment.

summary: Host Dark Horse Entrepreneur ranks seven AI side hustles by a five-factor rubric (startup cost, skill barrier, weekly hours, time to first credible sale, risk), scored 1-5 with lower being better. Ranking from fastest to slowest: content clipping (7/25), AI-assisted freelance gigs (10), done-for-you AI social media for local businesses (12), AI art/print-on-demand (13), AI consulting (14), AI content/YouTube automation (17), AI micro SaaS (22). The ranking relies on the host's own subjective scores and on other creators' videos, not first-hand results. Key takeaway: pick one hustle and commit to a 30-60 day proof-of-concept deadline rather than shopping for new ideas.

video.title: The Reason You're Not Making More Money

summary: The interviewer and Nick Huber discuss how to compare business opportunities by estimating revenue per worker-hour, using provider quotes, crew size and job duration. Huber describes pest control and door-to-door sales as examples, then argues that sales is central to entrepreneurship and should not be the first function a founder outsources. The conversation offers examples and rules of thumb rather than a full operating plan for any one business.

video.title: He Re-Invented this Oversaturated Business (And Makes $3M/Year)

summary: Stanley Henry describes how he built The Attention Seeker from a LinkedIn personal-brand service into an organic social agency for large brands and solo operators. He explains how the agency tests repeatable content formats, why it gives new series time to find an audience, and how it uses AI to reduce coordination work while keeping creative production human-led. He also describes a newer education business selling webinars and digital products to the audience he built. The main takeaway is to earn attention with a simple, entertaining story, test consistently, and add sales messaging only after the content has proved itself.

ideas.offer: Develop a social content strategy and repeatable series, then produce and manage organic content across platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and podcasts. The agency may later add paid distribution or calls to action.

tactics.name: Build proof on your own channels before selling the service
steps: Choose a platform and post consistently about the work and your journey.
Use your own account to test formats and show prospective clients what you can do.
Let prospects see the work and do their own due diligence before approaching you.

quote.text: our whole like I guess philosophy is first we do it for ourselves and then we prove it and then we do it for clients.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Build an initial professional network through frequent in-person meetings
steps: After returning to a market where you lack a network, post about the journey and meet as many relevant people as possible.
Stanley held five to six coffee meetings a day and attended networking events for six months.
Keep in touch and respond when people ask for help with the skill you have been demonstrating.

quote.text: So for 6 months straight, I just like had five to six coffee meetings with people every day.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Test a new platform by hiring platform-native talent
steps: When TikTok looked promising, Stanley hired a creator with a large TikTok following.
Ask the creator to make content for the company account while learning what works on the platform.
Use the results and platform knowledge to decide whether to expand.

quote.text: Let's learn how this works. Try make us content as our brand and then we'll try to learn what's working on the platform
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Give a new internal content creator a measurable production target
steps: Hire an internal creator whose full-time job is making content.
Set a target of five videos a day and give the person six months to learn.
Ask for a weekly report covering what they did, learned, and will start, stop, and continue.
Review progress and add specialist guidance only after the creator has tested enough content.

quote.text: every week you need to tell me what you did, what you learned, what you going to start, stop, continue.
quote.speaker: Stanley Henry

tactics.name: Make a local business recognisable to its target area
steps: Make the location clear in the content, including naming the town or area served.
Publish consistently so platforms can test the content with a local audience.
Judge results by local reach and the credibility or calls it creates, not just viral view counts.

quote.text: if you mention I'm the number one, you know, plumbing business in West Palm Beach, then like it's going to show to people in West Palm Beach.

tactics.name: Let an organic series establish audience interest before adding sales calls to action
steps: Start with one repeatable series designed to entertain or create a feeling associated with the brand.
Keep the early format consistent and allow it time to find an audience.
After the characters and format have established interest, add service or product content and calls to action.
Put paid distribution behind content that already shows audience interest.

tactics.name: Keep early creative tests simple
steps: Start with the core story and use the simplest edit that communicates it.

Use early results to decide which extra elements are worth adding.

video.title: I Thought I Understood Credit Cards Until I Talked to This Guy

summary: Host Chris Koerner interviews Brandon Elliot about using credit cards, bank relationships, and other bank products to obtain business funding, often at promotional interest rates. Elliot describes funding real estate, cleaning up credit profiles, and selling authorized-user access on credit cards. He also shares examples involving business auto loans, property investment, and construction. The main takeaway is that credit access can support business and property investments, but the process involves fees, careful timing, and substantial debt and compliance risks.

Application sequencing and credit utilization can affect access to future credit and personal credit scores.

video.title: Forget Storage Units. He Rents Out Empty Dirt Instead?!

summary: UpFlip host walks through Chris Conrad's 'Long Yards' business, which rents fenced, gated dirt lots (storage yards) to contractors and other tenants on month-to-month terms. Chris explains how he found tenants early on (approaching vehicles, flyers at Home Depot, online marketplaces), how land is evaluated (net rentable square footage, NOI, cap rate) and how deals can be done via purchase, lease or profit share with landowners using investor money. He claims one Canadian flagship nets $25k/month at a 62% margin and that he works about five hours a week with on-the-ground staff. The key takeaway is that the model is simple operationally but is really a land and real estate business that needs capital, partners and underwriting skill.

support.how: Phone enquiries (5 to 8 a day per site) and site issues are mostly handled by staff; some triage could be AI-assisted.

tactics.name: Underwrite land with net rentable sq ft

video.title: The Most Profitable AI Business You've Never Heard Of

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates using Claude with Beehiiv’s MCP to connect a newsletter list to a community and find engaged subscribers. He then pitches an AI-assisted service that helps business owners reactivate their email lists and generate sales, using a landscaping example to model potential returns. The video also explains community launch tactics, suggests starting a local newsletter from an existing customer list, and shows Beehiiv community features. Its central business case relies on hypothetical conversion and revenue assumptions, and Koerner discloses an affiliate link and discount for Beehiiv.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; demonstrates Beehiiv and Claude and pitches AI-assisted newsletter monetization.

ideas.name: AI-assisted email list reactivation and monetization service
ideas.one_liner: Help businesses use their existing email lists to identify engaged past customers and generate repeat sales, using AI and email-platform tools.
ideas.business_model: Monthly retainer, potentially with payment contingent on revenue generated.
ideas.customer: Business owners with existing email lists, including home-service businesses such as landscapers and plumbers.
ideas.problem: Their lists may be large but disconnected from other products, poorly segmented, or not used to generate repeat business.
ideas.offer: Connect or import a client's list into Beehiiv, inspect engagement and subscriber data, create useful segments, and prepare or send campaigns to invite engaged past customers to buy again.

pricing.model: Suggested monthly retainer; Koerner also suggests a no-risk arrangement where the client pays only if revenue is generated.
pricing.notes: The $1,000 monthly retainer and no-risk arrangement are suggestions, not results from a demonstrated client engagement.

acquisition_channels.details: Start with business owners the founder already knows, offer to manage their list, and ask satisfied clients to refer peers.

quote.text: But most importantly, you need to manage the email list of people you know and help them make more money with it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Koerner suggests posting in Facebook groups for local communities to reach business owners; he gives no specific post or response data.

quote.text: You can use ads. You can post in Facebook groups to local communities. Post on Reddit, yada yada yada.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Koerner also suggests ads and Reddit posts to reach business owners who are not already known to the founder; no specific campaign process is provided.

quote.text: You can use ads. You can post in Facebook groups to local communities. Post on Reddit, yada yada yada.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Use Claude connected to Beehiiv through its MCP to inspect list data, rank subscribers, create segments, and prepare or send email invitations. The operator or client still needs to decide what to offer, approve consequential messages, and may call highly engaged subscribers personally.
unit_economics_claims: Koerner models a landscaping list of 20,000 subscribers, with half treated as inactive and 40% of the remainder opening emails, yielding 4,000 active subscribers.
His hypothetical assumes a 0.1% monthly conversion rate, four projects per month at $3,000 each, or $12,000 monthly revenue before costs.
He suggests charging $1,000 per month and describes the hypothetical return as 12x, without substantiating the conversion or revenue assumptions.

acquisition.how: Client acquisition is described as relying on relationships, referrals, groups, ads, and posts. In the UK, software-led unsolicited marketing to individuals and sole traders is constrained by PECR; cold email to limited companies and screened cold calls require care.

onboarding.how: AI can guide a client through exporting a CSV, importing a list, and connecting the platform, with routine human review of access and data permissions.

delivery.how: Agents can inspect engagement, create segments, and draft campaigns, but a person should verify data, claims, consent, and campaign content before sending.

billing.how: A recurring retainer can be invoiced automatically; the suggested pay-only-on-results arrangement would need human review of attribution and revenue.

support.how: AI can answer routine platform questions, but client coordination, offer decisions, and interpretation of results need regular human input.

uk_applicability.notes: The email-list service concept transfers, but UK GDPR and PECR affect list permissions and marketing. Existing consent and the distinction between corporate subscribers and individuals or sole traders matter; the video does not discuss UK rules.

risks: The example's list size, open rate, conversion rate, project value, and resulting revenue are hypothetical assumptions, not demonstrated client results.
A client may not have valid permission to use its list for the proposed campaign; check lawful basis, privacy information, and opt-outs before processing or sending.
The video's AI demonstrations do not establish that an agent will reliably interpret list data or send the right campaign without human review.
The proposed no-risk, pay-only-on-results arrangement could create disputes about attribution and what counts as revenue generated.

video.title: I built this website in 8 hours with Claude. Now it makes $40K/month

summary: Starter Story host Gus interviews Frank Michael Smith, a non-technical sports creator who built Geogames (Geosports, Geohistory and others), a daily five-question map-tap trivia web game, in about eight hours with Claude. He claims about $40K/month (roughly $30-35K programmatic ads plus about 1,800 Pro subs via Stripe) and 700K monthly active users. Growth came from word-of-mouth sharing (53% share rate), playability inside X, and a 'host' programme where sports personalities write the daily questions and retweet. Key takeaways: build for web, build in shareability, start now, and stay in the game long-term.

video.title: The Psychology of Sales (How We Sell $100M)

summary: Codie Sanchez presents a sales tutorial organized around five parts of the brain, covering authority, social proof, scarcity, visual framing, price anchoring, language, delivery, and trust. She gives example scripts and cites studies and anecdotes to support the techniques, but does not explain a specific operating business in depth. The video ends by inviting business owners to book a call with her advisors, and it also refers to her book Owner Beyond. The central takeaway is to make sales claims concrete, frame offers around the customer's outcomes, and build trust without forcing a sale.

tactics.name: Borrow authority from a credible third party
steps: Have someone other than the seller introduce relevant expertise.
State the person's role and specific experience before transferring or introducing them.
Use authority where the buyer is alone or unfamiliar with the seller; do not simply claim expertise about yourself.

quote.text: Let me put you through to Peter, our head of sales. He was over 20 years selling properties in this area.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Use specific, truthful social proof
steps: Explain what most customers choose or do.
Use a number when you have evidence for it.
Use the information to help customers compare options, rather than presenting an unsupported figure as fact.

quote.text: Not just most people, but 75% of people need this offer.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Make scarcity concrete
steps: If capacity is genuinely limited, state the actual number of places and how many remain.
Avoid the generic phrase “Limited spots available.”
Do not imply a capacity limit that is not real.

quote.text: Remember, we want to use a number, so I have four slots in this cohort. Two are gone.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Frame price against a larger comparison
steps: Present a relevant comparison before stating the offer price.
Quantify what the customer may gain, lose, or save if the transcript's example can be supported.
State the price and then pause instead of adding more arguments.

quote.text: Your offer should sound like, and the price is $20K. Are you in?
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Make sales language concrete and listen closely
steps: Replace vague promises such as fast delivery with a specific date or measurable outcome.
Remove softeners, filler words, and unnecessary apologies; pause when you need time to think.
Reflect the customer's own words accurately before explaining why the offer fits.

quote.text: Make everything you say concrete. This is a good rule, because if you can't visualize it, they won't value it.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Build trust before asking for a sale
steps: Tell a prospect when the offer is not a fit and do not force it.
Get to the stated purpose of the call without wasting time on small talk.
Look for genuine shared interests before a meeting; do not manufacture similarities.
Give something useful and tailored before asking for a commitment.

quote.text: The more you can give, the more trust you build and the higher the chance the person will buy from you.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

quote.text: The setup before the sale actually matters more than the sale itself.

lessons.lesson: A price is judged in relation to an anchor; make comparisons relevant to the customer's likely gain, loss, or savings.

video.title: Claude Opus 5.5 + Higgsfield AI: 7 CRAZY Use Cases

summary: George McConnell demonstrates seven ways to use Claude Opus 5.5 connected to Higgsfield AI to build an online brand's visual assets for a fictional water-bottle brand, Von. Claude acts as creative director while Higgsfield renders: inventing a product line and palette, locking a consistent named AI model, self-auditing renders for logo and face accuracy, copying a filmed motion, re-rendering in new locations, one-take videos and a 30-second ad with voice-over. He says he sells this as a media-company service but gives no prices or revenue. Takeaway: agentic image/video pipelines with automatic QA make brand content production largely automatable, though human prompt checks still matter.

video.title: 10 Boring Businesses You Can Start Without Quitting Your Job

summary: Johnny ranks ten businesses he says can be started around a full-time job, from seasonal services to recurring commercial contracts. The list focuses on starting costs, after-work fit, customer acquisition and whether the owner can hire others to deliver the service. Remote cleaning gets the most personal detail: Johnny describes a model where independent cleaners do the work while the owner manages bookings, recruiting and customer service. He also promotes Home Service Academy training for that business, so the video combines business education with a sales pitch.

video.title: The Most Overlooked $1K/Hour Business Anyone Can Start

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Mike Herod about Voskills, a Florida trade school that runs woodworking and shop skills classes for children. Herod says the business began with a Facebook post and a few free classes, then grew through repeat students, homeschool groups, camps, school contracts, and state scholarship payments. The classes can be mobile and use simple projects and reusable tools; the transcript gives examples of pricing, costs, and revenue, though several figures are estimates or rough recollections. The core takeaway is to test demand with a simple offer, collect payment up front, keep projects safe and manageable, and use photos and word of mouth to build trust.

speakers.name: Mike Herod
speakers.description: Owner of Voskills, a trade school and shop class provider in West Palm Beach, Florida.

ideas.name: Children's woodworking and shop skills classes
ideas.one_liner: Run hands-on woodworking workshops, camps, and group classes for children, delivered at a shop or at the customer's venue.
ideas.business_model: Per-child hourly fees for small classes and events; camp fees; group contracts; some Florida families pay through the Step Up scholarship program.
ideas.customer: Parents of children, especially homeschool families and co-ops, private schools, and local groups. Herod describes age groups of 7–9 and 10+ and says the wider business serves ages 7–18.
ideas.problem: Parents have few places for children to learn practical shop skills, use tools safely, and build confidence through making things.
ideas.offer: Supervised woodworking and shop skills sessions using simple projects such as robots, flags, bird feeders, cornhole boards, and other kits. Formats include birthday and family events, recurring classes, foster community classes, school programs, and three- or five-day camps.

pricing.model: Per child per hour for many classes; fixed per-child camp fees; negotiated group contract pricing.
pricing.notes: Herod says he sometimes reduces per-head pricing for larger groups, but describes the 30,000 USD contract as having a different price structure. The transcript also mentions a 500 USD per-student skateboard class as a special project.

acquisition_channels.details: Started with a post on Herod's personal Facebook profile, then posted photos and updates consistently, reportedly every day.

quote.text: I just post. I just post pictures all the time.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

acquisition_channels.details: Posted in homeschool and local mothers' groups; Herod says the business participates in three homeschool groups and describes them as tightly connected communities.

quote.text: And we're in three homeschool groups. One's got 9,000, one's got 5,000.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

acquisition_channels.details: Free trial classes generated inquiries and referrals; Herod says homeschool families talk to one another and the business gained repeat students.

quote.text: It just becomes a word of mouth. It become word of mouth.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

acquisition_channels.details: Created a Google profile and collected Google reviews; Herod says the profile was also needed for the trade school.

quote.text: We did a Facebook page and then then we did a Google profile
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

ideas.delivery: Herod, his wife, his son, and occasional helpers supervise children using hand tools and age-appropriate power tools. Classes take place at their commercial shop or at homes, parks, schools, and other venues. They bring tables, tools, and prepared project kits; sessions may be one-off events, recurring classes, or camps.
unit_economics_claims: Herod says a one-hour class for 10 younger children brings in 750 USD, with about 150 USD in costs and 600 USD profit.
Herod says the 30,000 USD, 14-week contract should leave about 10,000 USD after extra tools, materials, and staffing.
Herod says he made 50,600 USD from March through July, when classes were held at the commercial site.
Herod says spring break brought in 12,000 USD in one week, teaching only morning classes.
Herod says the hand-tool setup can cost about 425 USD and can be paid back by the first class.
ideas.startup_cost: Herod estimates about 425 USD for a basic hand-tool setup for six workstations. He says a very lean first class could cost less than 300 USD if the founder borrows a table and uses tools already available. A power-tool setup for six is estimated at about 4,100 USD.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Herod says he posted around November 20, held two free classes, then booked paid events and classes in the weeks before Christmas.

acquisition.how: Posts and event listings can be scheduled, but the described acquisition depends on local community participation, photos, and human replies to parents. UK marketing rules also limit unsolicited electronic messages.

onboarding.how: A booking page and payment link can collect registrations and payment, but age suitability, venue details, consent, and safety questions need human review.

delivery.how: A qualified adult must supervise children using tools, teach the projects, and enforce safety rules throughout every session.

billing.how: Online checkout can take payment up front and reduce routine billing work; scholarship or group contracts still need reconciliation and human administration.

support.how: Parents ask about ages, dates, locations, and project suitability; an agent could draft replies, but staff need to handle safeguarding and individual needs.

uk_applicability.notes: The workshop format and parent-funded classes can transfer to the UK, with changes for safeguarding, insurance, venues, pricing, and local school or homeschool arrangements. Florida's Step Up scholarship vendor payments are specific to that state and do not transfer directly.

risks: A tool injury could seriously damage the business; Herod says to set firm safety rules and not relax them.
Children need close supervision, age-appropriate tools, eye protection, and projects sized to finish in the available time.
Parents may not consent to photos or videos being posted; Herod describes using waivers and excluding or obscuring children when requested.
The work is physical and locally delivered, so it cannot be run almost entirely by software agents.
A commercial venue may reassure parents but adds rent and operating costs; mobile delivery avoids some fixed overhead.
Florida scholarship funding and payment timing are not evidence of equivalent UK public funding.

warnings.warning: Safety is a non-negotiable: Herod says one injury could wreck the business. He requires eye protection and starts classes with safety rules.
Avoid projects that are too complex for the session. Herod says early classes ran long when he added paint and glue, then he simplified the projects.
Herod advises against using nails with children because he considers them an injury risk; he uses screws instead.
Parents may decline permission for photos. Use clear waivers and respect requests to leave a child out of posted images.
Herod says he initially overbought tools because he did not know what the classes needed; he recommends starting with a basic kit and borrowing where possible.
Herod says cheap lumber made the experience worse and later switched to higher-grade pine.
Florida's Step Up scholarship payments are location-specific; the episode's 24-hour payment claim should not be assumed to apply to UK funding.
The host and guest discuss the business in a promotional setting: the host solicits podcast applicants and paid community memberships, while Herod says Milwaukee supplied free tools.

video.title: The Most Overlooked $1M Business Every Town Needs

summary: Chris Koerner tours Laundry Spot's flagship store in Hamilton, Ohio with co-owner Tyler. The family business builds large, modern laundromats with cloud-controlled washers, direct soap injection and any-payment options, priced at parity with old competitors; the Hamilton store did about $1.025M revenue and $420k profit last year. Tyler shares startup costs ($1.2M-$2.2M excluding real estate), site selection, a grand-opening playbook with two free-laundry weekends, commercial laundry at $1-$3/lb, and the new franchise (36 units in 8 months). Key takeaway: build new, better stores rather than buying old ones, and remove every bit of friction for customers.

video.title: Everyone Ignores this Business, But It Makes $6M/Year

summary: Jay describes building a vending business, then adding coffee service and five-gallon water delivery before focusing on Mountain Glacier, a bottled-water production business. Today he says the business is constrained by production, freight costs, and financing after a difficult robotics installation. David Heacock advises him to understand customer-level profitability and cash flow, simplify freight, and verify what growth would actually earn before expanding. The businesses depend on physical production and delivery, so they offer limited scope for agents to run unattended.

summary: The host describes criminal uses of AI, high-profile fraud cases, and growing law-enforcement attention, then argues that legitimate founders should look for problems AI creates. The main opportunity he identifies is protecting and verifying human-made voices and content. He also briefly recommends using AI for content, workflow automation, and freelance services. The episode promotes the host’s AI Escape Plan newsletter and does not present a tested business with operating results.

summary: The video profiles Seminole Bee Farms, a Florida beekeeping business that sells honey and earns additional revenue from bee removals and educational tours. Slobo and Alejandra describe starting with under $500, growing to more than 150 hives, and adding a retail store, farm stand, markets, and online sales. The business requires regular, hands-on care of bees and physical work, so its core operations are difficult to automate. Its most transferable lessons are to diversify revenue, build local discovery through a visible location and word of mouth, and avoid harvesting honey before it is ready.

tactics.name: Start with a nucleus colony or attract a swarm
steps: Hang a swarm trap to invite a colony, or buy a nucleus colony from a local beekeeper.
Slobo recommends buying a nucleus colony because the beekeeper checks that it is established and ready to grow.
Begin with two or three hives so colonies can be balanced if one is struggling.

quote.text: You can do a beer removal. You can hang a swarm trap, swarm traps look like this. So you can simply hang one on a tree and it can invite a new colony straight to the swarm trap.
quote.speaker: Slobo

tactics.name: Use a self-serve roadside stand to make local honey easy to discover
steps: Place honey by the street where passing drivers can see it.
Let customers choose products and pay through a cash drop or the named peer-to-peer payment services.
Use local visibility and customer referrals to build awareness.

quote.text: people can drive by, and they see the farm stand, and they pick out whatever honey they like, and they can drop their cash in there.
quote.speaker: Slobo

tactics.name: Add seasonal revenue alongside honey
steps: Notice when honey sales slow and removals pick up.
Add bee removals and education tours as complementary services.
Treat the different revenue streams as a way to reduce dependence on honey sales alone.

quote.text: we're always trying to find different ways to make money because honey sales can slow down on the summer and the beer moveals pick up in the summer.
quote.speaker: Slobo

tactics.name: Build a local service reputation from honey customers
steps: Let honey customers know the business also rescues bees.
Respond to property owners who find colonies on their land.
Use referrals generated by the existing honey business to bring in removal jobs.

quote.text: People know that you do honey so they're like, okay, I have bees, this guy, he can maybe rescue these bees from my properties.
quote.speaker: Slobo

tactics.name: Stabilize rescued colonies before moving them
steps: Bring rescued colonies to a holding apiary.
Check that the colony has a queen and that she is laying.
Feed colonies, treat for mites, and let them establish for one or two weeks before moving them to other apiaries.

quote.text: So we bring them here so we can make sure they're okay, make sure they have a queen, make sure they have enough food, and once they're well established, then we can move them out to our other apiaries.
quote.speaker: Slobo

tactics.name: Choose a retail location for existing foot traffic
steps: The founders moved to a shopping plaza near a popular restaurant after the previous building's new owners planned to triple the rent.
They say restaurant visitors began coming into the new shop and formed a new customer base.
Evaluate nearby customer traffic before committing to a retail location.

quote.speaker: Slobo

steps: Stock honey from other beekeepers as well as the founders' own local honey.
Add infused and monofloral varieties, books, children's products, candles, and beauty products to give different shoppers options.
The founders say they wanted the store to feel exciting for families and children.

Do not rush to extract open cells containing nectar.

video.title: People are doing $100M+ in sales on this app (ft. Whatnot founder)

summary: Grant LaFontaine, founder of Whatnot (live-shopping marketplace, claimed ~$20B valuation), tells the story of starting it with Logan Head after abandoning a full-service Craigslist idea because delivery economics failed. They chose Funko Pops from eBay sales data, solved the marketplace chicken-and-egg problem by being the first seller, and grew buyers through YouTube influencers and a viral share-to-enter giveaway. Live selling launched in July 2020 and drove growth to roughly $1B in sales within about two years. The key takeaways are to start in a tiny niche, seed one side of a marketplace yourself, be customer-driven rather than vision-driven, and use unscalable growth hacks early. The host also lists ecosystem opportunities around Whatnot: wholesale supply marketplaces, multi-channel networks and tools.

video.title: I Built a Luxury Brand in 30 Minutes with GPT-6 Astra

summary: George McConnell demonstrates a workflow for positioning a $12 water bottle as a proposed $68 lifestyle accessory using ChatGPT-6 Astra and Higgsfield. He builds a fictional customer profile and brand direction, then generates product images, lifestyle scenes, and video ads. He also asks Astra for a hypothetical 30-day launch plan and a $10,000 budget allocation. The video shows a creative prototype, not a launched product or verified sales.

ideas.name: Premium lifestyle water bottle brand
ideas.one_liner: Position a sourced 40 oz bottle as a studio-to-street accessory for wellness and athleisure customers, using AI-generated brand strategy and advertising creative.
ideas.business_model: Proposed one-off retail sales of a physical product; the intended sales platform and checkout are not stated.
ideas.customer: An aspirational wellness and athleisure consumer, illustrated as a woman aged 25 to 40 who attends Pilates, buys premium activewear, skincare, matcha, and other lifestyle goods.
ideas.problem: The target customer wants an attractive, convenient bottle that fits her personal style and daily routine. The video also discusses concerns such as tipping, spills, sustainability, and visibility, but does not validate these needs with real customers.
ideas.offer: A translucent smoke-gray 40 oz bottle with a brushed steel cap, black collar, and silicone carry strap, branded as Von and presented as a studio-to-street fashion accessory. The proposed brand includes premium packaging, lifestyle imagery, and UGC-style advertising.
