acquisition.how: Paid ads and storefront acquisition can be managed with software, but creator outreach and retail selling involved research and human follow-up. In the UK, unsolicited marketing DMs to individuals and sole traders require consent under PECR; cold calls must screen TPS/CTPS.

onboarding.how: Shopify captures orders and email sign-ups, and the subscription tool can handle recurring enrollment. Human review is still useful for product questions and exceptions.

delivery.how: A manufacturer and distributors handle much of production and shipping, but the product is physical and the founder still manages supply, packaging and stock issues.

billing.how: Shopify and the subscription app can process one-off and recurring payments, with routine human checks for failures and cancellations.

support.how: Email and tracking updates are automated, but Eli described personally answering customer questions and handling subscription changes.

uk_applicability.notes: A premium functional coffee brand and subscription store can operate in the UK, but the founder would need UK-compliant food labelling, ingredient and health-claim choices, organic certification arrangements, and local manufacturing or import logistics.

risks: The founders initially bought ads before establishing social proof, influencer coverage or a credible brand presence and said they wasted money.
A premium price narrows the potential customer pool, while high acquisition and shipping costs make repeat orders important.
Some customers do not subscribe or return, so revenue and payback depend on retention.
The coffee brewed more slowly than regular coffee and caused problems with some machines; the team spent time testing and improving this.
The manufacturer expected continued growth and could put pressure on the founders to increase volume.
Retail purchase orders can arrive on short notice and create bag and packaging supply problems.
Customer questions can require manual support even when answers and account links are available online.
The founders said the first high-follower affiliate partnership sold fewer bags than a smaller, more niche account, so follower count alone was a poor predictor.
Unsolicited Instagram outreach to individual creators may require prior consent under UK PECR; the described outreach should be adapted for UK law.

tactics.name: Use personal experience to shape the product
steps: Start from an ingredient or routine you know personally.
Test combinations with potential customers instead of assuming they want the first version.
Look for a product format that fits an existing daily habit.

quote.text: And then when I started testing now with people, they actually don't want just turmeric in their coffee.
quote.speaker: Eli

tactics.name: Negotiate a low-cash manufacturing arrangement
steps: Find a manufacturer whose existing equipment and certifications cover most of the process.
Offer to fund a small equipment addition the manufacturer needs for the new ingredients.
Explain how the new product category could help the manufacturer serve other brands.
Negotiate payment terms so the founder can sell product before paying the production invoice.
Agree a small initial order and understand what growth the manufacturer expects in return.

quote.text: So every time we produce the bag of coffee, we sold that bag of coffee, and then we got invoice a month later from the manufacturer.
quote.speaker: Eli

tactics.name: Collect early reviews before sending paid traffic
steps: Send product to friends and family as early testers.
Have testers place orders through the store using a discount code so purchases can be verified.
Ask satisfied testers for reviews without pressuring people who do not like the product.
Use the feedback to check the order and manufacturing process before a larger launch.

quote.text: And we basically said, if you like our coffee, please go online and review this, right? That's the way we got reviews early on.
quote.speaker: Eli

tactics.name: Build social proof before scaling ads
steps: Establish a credible social presence and collect creator content before making a large ad commitment.
Seed the product with relevant creators and give the brand time to build a visible track record.
Only increase paid acquisition after the store no longer looks unknown to first-time visitors.

quote.text: we should have absolutely taken the time to find influencers first, reach out to whatever was longer to get a real brand on that screen before we did it.
quote.speaker: Eli

tactics.name: Approach small, relevant creators with a low-pressure offer
steps: Identify creators in health, wellness and organic food, often with fewer than 10,000 followers.
Research each account and explain why its audience might fit.
Offer a free bag and ask them to post only if they genuinely like it.
Track which accounts lead to posts and sales; do not judge only by follower count.

quote.text: And I am, you know, I sell in technology. So my mantra is not just blast and pray. It'd be like looking at them, understanding them and giving them a reason why I picked them.
quote.speaker: Eli

tactics.name: Use performance-based creator partnerships where possible
steps: Offer affiliate codes or commissions when a large upfront fee is unaffordable.
Compare the commission cost with paid acquisition cost before agreeing to a higher rate.
Consider a paid creator test only when the creator already knows and likes the product and the spend is manageable.

quote.text: to keep it to keep it low risk, you know, the performance-based model is kind of leaves some upside for them and minimizes risk for you.
quote.speaker: Eli

tactics.name: Test price and bundle options against shipping economics
steps: Test different prices and observe both conversion and average cart value.
Offer one, two and three-bag options so customers can increase their order while shipping cost per bag falls.
Make subscription savings and free shipping clear, and tell customers when the next subscription order will happen.
Keep an easy cancellation path to protect customer trust.

quote.text: I probably chain up pricing 30 to 40 times. Just testing things to figure out what works, what sticks, how do you get the average cart value higher?
quote.speaker: Eli

tactics.name: Track the full value chain and retention
steps: Track customer acquisition cost, product cost, shipping, gross margin and repeat purchase behavior together.
Estimate customer lifetime value using observed subscription tenure, then revise the estimate as data accumulates.
Ask customers why they bought again or did not return.
Improve the product and customer experience before increasing ad spend.

quote.text: know your numbers and choose a product where the margins will allow you to stay in business.
quote.speaker: Eli

tactics.name: Use distributor introductions to approach retail buyers
steps: Work with distributors that already supply relevant stores.
Ask which buyer handles coffee, then contact that buyer with a sell sheet and tasting offer.
Run in-store tastings where practical and help the retailer sell through the product.
Prepare inventory and packaging for short-notice purchase orders.

quote.text: And then we do demos and tasting sometimes, too, that make sure people can taste our coffee and, you know, we try to help the store sell it
quote.speaker: Eli

tactics.name: Expand to Amazon cautiously
steps: Check whether customers are already searching for the brand on Amazon.
Use a marketplace specialist to help set up the listing if needed.
Start with a manageable amount of inventory and learn from the launch.
Wait to spend on marketplace ads until the listing has enough reviews to establish trust; no review threshold was stated.

quote.text: We'll do that. We'll, we'll, we'll, we'll learn from our mistakes before we will not pay for ads and Amazon until we get X number reviews
quote.speaker: Eli

warnings.warning: The founders spent heavily on ads before building social proof, a meaningful social presence or influencer coverage, and Eli said they wasted money.
The founders initially underestimated long-term customer value, acquisition cost, product cost, shipping and other expenses, leaving the business near break-even.
A high product price can limit the number of buyers and raise customer expectations; a single shipped bag was described as costing $36.
Some customers do not subscribe or return, so strong subscription tenure among loyal customers does not guarantee that every acquired customer will pay back acquisition cost.
The product brewed more slowly than regular coffee and could leave some brewing machines dirty, creating a product and customer experience challenge.
Retail growth creates inventory and packaging pressure when purchase orders require stock on short notice.
The manufacturer expected continued growth to justify its support, which can create pressure to increase ad spending or order volume.
Large creator audiences did not always translate into sales; a smaller, more relevant account reportedly sold more product.
The guest said some affiliate applicants did little after joining, so accepting every affiliate request may consume time without producing sales.
The described Instagram direct-message outreach to individual creators would need to comply with UK PECR consent requirements if used in the UK.
The transcript is a local Whisper transcript with likely recognition errors in several names, numbers and product terms; ambiguous claims should be treated cautiously.

lessons.lesson: Choose a product with enough margin to cover acquisition, production, shipping and customer service, and track those costs together.

quote.text: The number one thing I will say is know your numbers and choose a product where the margins will allow you to stay in business.
quote.speaker: Eli

lessons.lesson: A replenishable product can support subscriptions, but repeat buying and customer lifetime value must be measured rather than assumed.

quote.text: You have to have margins of your shipping things online that either people are repeating as customers will always think about the AOV of a cart in the long term value.
quote.speaker: Eli

lessons.lesson: Build trust and social proof before scaling paid acquisition, especially when the brand is new and unfamiliar.

quote.text: we should have absolutely taken the time to find influencers first, reach out to whatever was longer to get a real brand on that screen before we did it.
quote.speaker: Eli

lessons.lesson: Use customer feedback to understand why people buy, repeat, or leave, then adjust the product and offer.

quote.text: when you're starting a business, like focusing on what customers want and then asking them for feedback. Like, hey, why did you buy this?
quote.speaker: Eli

lessons.lesson: Creator fit and audience relevance can matter more than follower count.

quote.text: Like, numbers are important. And even if they're getting a lot of traction, it might not matter to their audience lesser specific on that niche
quote.speaker: Eli

lessons.lesson: A clear subscription benefit, transparent order reminders and easy cancellation can encourage repeat buying without damaging trust.

quote.text: We want people to buy our coffee because they want it.
quote.speaker: Eli

lessons.lesson: Outsource work that consumes too much founder time when the cost fits the business, while keeping oversight of the customer experience.

quote.text: I would say just focus on outsourcing as much as possible, much as you're willing to.
quote.speaker: Eli

lessons.lesson: A small first production run and negotiated payment terms can reduce the cash tied up in inventory.

quote.text: So we were able to do it from a cash flow away that it actually made sense for us.
quote.speaker: Eli

lessons.lesson: Move slowly enough to learn when the business is a side project and the founders have limited time or appetite for large spending.

quote.text: But sometimes slower is the right move to learn.
quote.speaker: Eli

lessons.lesson: Good fulfillment and customer service matter because acquisition spending is wasted if the product experience fails after the sale.

quote.text: if you don't have Rockstar fulfillment in like a great product, a great customer experience, like the other stuff matters because if you have a leaky bucket down at the end
quote.speaker: Nick

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest is an operator who describes the manufacturer relationship, acquisition methods, subscription setup, retail operations and several business figures. The numbers are self-reported and unaudited, some claims are approximate, and this local Whisper transcript contains likely recognition errors.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The episode contains sponsor reads for Shopify, Quo, Gusto and Indeed. The host also promotes a free list of replenishable product ideas, and the guest's coffee brand is promoted with a discount code and website.

video.title: Everyone Overlooks This Simple Side Hustle

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Don, who runs a family fresh-squeezed lemonade business at the Frisco and Dallas farmers markets in Texas. It made about $250k last year over about 8 months, selling 32oz cups at $7 that cost about $1.25 to make. Don explains the recipe, equipment (about $1,500 to start), warehouse prep, staffing with his kids, a $300 booth fee, and expansion into $1,000-3,000 caterings, $500 cart rentals via Facebook Marketplace, venue concessions and a $19k frozen-banana trade-show job. His advice is to stop overthinking and just post up with a quality fresh product.

summary: Side Hustle Nation host Nick Loper interviews Steve (App Masters, 17 years in app marketing, now acquiring and building vibe-coded apps). Steve's playbook: find keywords people search in the App Store (ASO), unbundle a feature from big apps, build a one-feature app named after the keyword, use a hard paywall with copied competitor pricing, and optionally run a lifetime-deal growth hack or Apple Search Ads. He claims apps earning from about $200/month to $35k MRR, and says roughly 40% of apps he launches make money. Key takeaway: distribution (ASO) matters more than features.

video.title: The Most Profitable Side Hustle to Start With No Money

summary: Brothers Jackson and Carson describe wholesaling vacant land by finding home builders first, learning their buying criteria, then contracting with landowners and assigning the contracts to those builders. They say the business can start with a phone and internet, while their scaled operation used direct mail, callers, software, and a small team. They explain how they price deals, screen land, manage contracts, and use referrals, and they compare land wholesaling with house wholesaling and property flipping. The key takeaway is to find a real buyer before making offers, price accurately, and build the skill by doing the work consistently.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office.

speakers.name: Jackson
speakers.description: Co-founder of the land wholesaling business with his brother Carson.

speakers.name: Carson
speakers.description: Co-founder of the land wholesaling business with his brother Jackson.

ideas.name: Builder-first vacant land wholesaling
ideas.one_liner: Find a builder's land buy box, contract suitable vacant land below that price, and assign the contract to the builder for a spread.
ideas.business_model: Assignment fee or margin between the seller's contract price and the builder's purchase price.
ideas.customer: Home builders buying scattered lots, plus landowners willing to sell vacant land.
ideas.problem: Builders need lots that fit their locations and specifications; some landowners want a quicker sale without agent fees and a long listing period.
ideas.offer: Source a suitable lot, agree a price with the owner, and assign the purchase contract to a builder already interested in that type of lot.

pricing.model: Keep the difference between the contracted seller price and the builder's price; the speakers also describe some deals as a percentage of the builder's price.

price_points.label: Average deal profit claimed by the guests
Typical transparent margin described by the guests
Typical offer range described by the guests

pricing.notes: Prices depend on location, lot characteristics, buyer criteria, and negotiation. The speakers describe 90–95% margins for their operation, but do not define the margin calculation.

acquisition_channels.details: Contact builders first, including builders identified from newly built homes listed for sale on Zillow, and ask for their buy box: location, lot size, and price.

quote.text: you go on Zillow and you filter it by houses built in 2025 or 2026, right? For sale.
quote.speaker: Jackson

quote.text: My favorite is actually direct mail. So, we'll send them a one-page introduction letter and then we'll send them a contract.
quote.speaker: Jackson

acquisition_channels.details: Call landowners to ask whether they would sell, explain the net cash offer and closing terms, and make a specific offer. The guests also used overseas callers at scale.

quote.text: Hey, Chris. Is this the owner of 123 Main Street? Awesome. I I was reaching out. Would any chance would you be open to selling this property
quote.speaker: Carson

acquisition_channels.details: The guests previously sent large volumes of text offers in selected US states, but say they stopped texting to limit liability and warn that rules vary. This channel cannot be copied into the UK without consent and legal review.

quote.text: So, to send 50,000 messages a month, it's about 1,200 bucks a month to send.
quote.speaker: Jackson

acquisition_channels.details: Monitor newly listed land in a target market and make an early offer before other buyers respond; the guests describe using listing alerts.

quote.text: if I just go and I have notifications on and first thing in the morning and as the new ones come in
quote.speaker: Jackson

acquisition_channels.details: After closing, send a handwritten thank-you letter and offer a referral payment if a referred owner completes a deal.

quote.text: if you refer a family member or a friend to sell their property with us and we get a deal done, we'll send you $1,000 in cash
quote.speaker: Jackson

ideas.delivery: The operators identify and qualify land virtually, agree an assignable purchase contract with the landowner, then assign it to a builder and send the contracts and deal details to a title company. They say their team checks title progress and keeps buyers and sellers updated; the builder decides whether to proceed after reviewing or driving by the lot.
unit_economics_claims: The guests claim an average gross profit of about $8,600 per deal.
They claim their operation has 90–95% margins, without defining the calculation.
They say one deal can take them 30 minutes to an hour of their own time.
They describe examples where a 10% spread on a $750,000 lot would yield $75,000.
ideas.startup_cost: The guests say it can be started with an iPhone and internet connection and describe a free-start workflow. No typical startup cost is stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: No typical timeline is stated. The guests describe one free-start participant earning an assignment fee within 14 days.

acquisition.how: Software can build lists, enrich owner records, prepare mail, and monitor listings. Finding a suitable builder, checking records, and negotiating with owners still need human judgement. In the UK, unsolicited marketing texts, WhatsApp messages, DMs, and emails to individuals and sole traders require consent; cold calls must be screened against TPS/CTPS.

onboarding.how: Forms, e-signatures, reminders, and data entry can be automated, but contract terms, authority to assign, title issues, and local legal requirements need human review.

delivery.how: Agents can assemble parcel data, compare buyer criteria, and coordinate documents. A person still needs to check suitability, resolve exceptions, and handle buyer and seller decisions; physical inspections may be needed.

billing.how: A title or escrow provider handles closing and disburses the assignment proceeds. Software can track milestones and reconcile the payment, with a human checking the closing statement.

support.how: Routine status updates and reminders can be automated, but negotiations, title problems, and trust-sensitive conversations need a person.

uk_applicability.notes: The buyer-first land sourcing model could be adapted to UK land and developers, but the speakers' US contracts, title-company workflow, datasets, and market examples do not transfer directly. UK property, planning, title, data-protection, and marketing rules need local review.

risks: A buyer may reject a lot after reviewing slope, wetlands, protected wildlife, utilities, access, or other site constraints.
The guests say overpricing a contract can make it difficult to assign; they warn against mass-sending offers above plausible value.
Land conditions and local rules vary by state and market; they recommend learning the local checks and doing due diligence before making offers.
The guests say their model is difficult to sell as an exit and that high profits created a large tax bill for them.
The guests say they no longer use mass texting because they wanted to limit their liability. UK unsolicited marketing texts to individuals and sole traders require consent.
The business depends on reliable buyers and on the seller understanding the assignment arrangement; the guests advocate being transparent about their role and margin.

acquisition.how: Mailing and owner research can be supported by software, but sourcing and evaluating a specific parcel still require human judgement.

ideas.name: House wholesaling

ideas.customer: House sellers and fix-and-flip investors.
ideas.problem: A seller wants to sell a house, while an investor wants an acquisition at a price that leaves room for a renovation and resale.

delivery.how: House condition, inspections, occupants, and buyer coordination require substantial human work.

support.how: Seller and investor conversations, inspections, and exceptions require a person.

tactics.name: Start with the builder's buy box
steps: Identify builders that sell newly built homes, using listings as a lead source.
Ask what locations, lot sizes, and prices the builder will accept.
Record the criteria and buying contact in a simple spreadsheet.
Only source parcels that match the stated requirements.

quote.text: So the first thing, the way we do it with the builder first method is you get the builder's buy box.
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Find owners and make offers below the buyer price
steps: Build a list of owners whose parcels match the builder's buy box.
Prioritise owners who have held the property for a long time and paid less, as the guests describe.
Use parcel records and owner lookup tools to find contact details.
Calculate an offer that leaves a spread while still making sense against current alternatives.

quote.text: And then we would reverse engineer it, go find sellers, go pull a list of owners that are offmarket properties
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Use consistent lot criteria for batch offers
steps: Choose a market with multiple builders and repeated, similar parcels.
Group parcels by location and lot characteristics.
Avoid mixing parcels with materially different sizes or conditions in one offer campaign.
The guests say similar parcels let them make many consistent offers.

quote.text: So I want to send a thousand offers at once. I can't do that if every lot's different.
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Use direct mail with an offer and contract
steps: Send a one-page introduction to the owner.
Include the offer and purchase contract in the mailing.
Give the owner a phone number and email to respond.
Track signed contracts and follow up on responses.

quote.text: we'll send them a one-page introduction letter and then we'll send them a contract. And on that contract, I'll put our offer on it.
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Explain the seller's net proceeds
steps: Compare the offer with the seller's likely net after agent fees and closing costs.
Explain the time difference between a direct close and a listing, using specific local comparisons only when known.
State the amount offered, the expected closing time, and who pays closing costs.
Do not claim a buyer is ready unless one has actually been lined up.

quote.text: And when you explain it like that, like they actually are benefiting from it. You already have somebody lined up and you're not really messing with them
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Keep seller outreach honest
steps: Tell the seller that you work with builders and intend to assign or pass the property to a builder.
Explain the intended margin where relevant, as the guests say they do.
Do not pretend to be the builder or misrepresent who will buy the property.
Make offers that can be completed and disclose material uncertainty.

quote.text: We have always taken an honest approach. anybody we've taught to do this, we tell them to be honest
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Use a contract feasibility period and buyer deposit
steps: The guests say their seller contract includes a feasibility study through the closing date.
They say earnest money is not due until closing under their contract.
They make sure the builder's assignment contract has a due date for its earnest money.
Confirm contract terms with qualified local counsel before using them.

quote.text: And we have a feasibility study. That means we can back out to the day of the closing date with no risk.
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Check land constraints before closing
steps: Check aerial imagery and local records for wetlands, slope, utilities, access, wildlife, and other constraints mentioned by builders.
Ask the city or county what reports are available when a local term is unfamiliar.
Confirm parcel-specific concerns with the builder before relying on a contract.
Use a termination right if the parcel fails the stated feasibility checks.

quote.text: you just basically just call the city and say, "What does this mean? How do I get a report for it?"
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Call neighbouring owners before a sale
steps: Look up the owners of neighbouring parcels after securing a deal.
Contact them as a courtesy and explain that a builder may buy the land.
Ask whether they would like to extend their yard or buy the lot.
Do not assume a neighbour will pay more; check whether they have interest and funds.

quote.text: the first thing I do is I call the neighboring houses, right? Because the most annoying thing is a homeowner.
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Ask for a meaningful referral
steps: After closing, send a handwritten thank-you letter.
Ask the seller to refer a friend or family member who may sell land.
Offer a stated cash payment only if the referral results in a completed deal.
Track referral source and closing so the reward is paid consistently.

quote.text: if you refer a family member or a friend to sell their property with us and we get a deal done, we'll send you $1,000 in cash
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Keep leads warm after an initial no
steps: If the owner rejects the offer, stay polite and invite them to save the caller's details.
Explain that the price may change and that the business continues to buy land.
Record the conversation and follow up only through a lawful channel.
Revisit the lead if the owner gets in touch later.

quote.text: save my name Jackson land guy and when if you need to sell for whatever reason if you need cash I will be able to close in two weeks
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Make a specific counteroffer rather than accepting immediately
steps: If a seller counters, pause briefly and confirm the counter with a partner.
Return with a clear answer and restate the agreement.
The guests say they sometimes counter slightly below the seller's requested amount to improve the chance the contract is signed.
Do not use a counteroffer to mislead the seller about the buyer or terms.

quote.text: If they text back and say, "I want 20 plus closing costs." We're not going to say yes again
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Screen and train callers for tone
steps: Interview several candidates together on Zoom.
Ask about experience and have each candidate tell a short story about themselves.
Prioritise friendliness and attitude, which the guests say affected lead volume.
Treat overseas assistants respectfully and train them on the actual process before delegating calls.

quote.text: the biggest thing is it hasn't been accident. It hasn't been how smart they are, it's how friendly they are and their attitude.
quote.speaker: Jackson

tactics.name: Monitor new land listings
steps: Set alerts for new listings in a market with active builders.
Review new parcels as they appear.
Make an offer early only after checking buyer demand and the parcel.
The guests say older listings may already have attracted many offers or have an undisclosed issue.

quote.text: if I just go and I have notifications on and first thing in the morning and as the new ones come in
quote.speaker: Jackson

evidence_quality.rationale: The guests present themselves as first-hand operators and give detailed workflows, deal examples, and operating figures. The claims are self-reported, some figures are approximate or lack definitions, and the transcript contains obvious transcription errors. The host and guests also promote paid or owned products and communities.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The guests promote Buyer Bridge, their own software, and Carson and Jackson communities. The host includes sponsor and promotional reads for Beehiiv, paid business plans, and Playmakers AI; these were not treated as business ideas.

video.title: 9 BORING Products I’d Sell If I Needed Money

summary: Tim Richard, an e-commerce founder, lists nine 'boring' product niches that he says have high Google search volume, low keyword difficulty and few dedicated brands. They are stainless steel litter boxes, hojicha latte, satin sheets, rice water shampoo, key fob covers, beef protein powder, men's crossbody bags, non-tarnish jewelry and floor couches. His method is to use social media and Ahrefs keyword data to find rising search trends, then build a branded site around one specific term. The picks are his own opinion, with no tested sales data for any of them. The video also promotes his paid 'idea book' database.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Derek, who turned a $250-300 Amazon inflatable movie screen bought as a Christmas gift into Backyard Movie Theater in North Dallas. After a windy first HOA booking flopped, he bought a 20 ft commercial screen from Alibaba (~$3,500 plus ~$1,000 shipping), plus a $1,100 projector and two $1,500 JBL speakers, and sells packages from $375 to $1,500. He also designed a custom indoor air-conditioned inflatable theater (about $3,500 all-in, $1,700 per booking) because Texas summer movies can't start before 9:30pm, and added a $20k LED dance floor rented at $3,000. He claims $10k of bookings in one week, about $40k last year and $90-100k expected this year at 70-80% margins, mostly from Facebook Marketplace and referrals.

summary: Chris Koerner pitches a low-effort AI side hustle: cloning a realtor's voice with Fish Audio S2 Pro and generating pre-written voicemails in the languages of multilingual buyers, sold for about $200-500 a month. He demos the workflow (clone voice from a 17-second sample, draft scripts with an LLM, translate, generate audio, save to Google Drive) and claims it costs cents per message. He then lists adjacent ideas (audiobook narration, YouTube dubbing, local-business voiceover, other multilingual professions) and a day-by-day plan to land the first clients. Key takeaway: cheap voice-cloning tools let a solo operator sell a productised service, but the claims are hypothetical and the video promotes an affiliate-style code for Fish Audio.

ideas.name: Multilingual cloned-voice voicemails for realtors

ideas.business_model: Monthly retainer/subscription plus optional setup fee; possible free or one-off package as a foot-in-the-door.
ideas.customer: Real estate agents and brokerages in markets with many non-English-speaking buyers.
ideas.problem: Realtors cannot leave voicemails in other languages, and generic translation does not sound like them, so they lose speed-to-lead and trust with multilingual buyers.
ideas.offer: Clone the realtor's voice from a 30-60 second clip (or existing social video), then deliver a library of pre-recorded translated voicemails (new listing, price drop, showing confirmation, missed appointment, etc.) in the same voice.

pricing.model: Monthly recurring fee, optional setup fee, or one-time package as loss leader
pricing.notes: Suggests a one-time free or cheap package first to get a foot in the door, then upsell AI services.

acquisition.how: Friend outreach, lunches and visiting offices are human. Cold outreach to individual realtors (often sole traders) by SMS/DM/email is restricted under UK PECR; only inbound or limited-company email is feasible by software.

delivery.how: LLM script writing, translation and TTS are scriptable via API, though the demo uses the UI one message at a time and a native speaker should check translations.

support.how: Revision requests, re-recordings and translation complaints can be handled by an agent with human review.

uk_applicability.notes: Technology works the same, but the demand rests on US demographics and a US-style voicemail-driven realtor workflow. UK agents mostly use email and WhatsApp, and sending voicemails or automated marketing calls to leads is regulated by PECR and UK GDPR, and voice cloning needs documented consent. A UK version would target London and other multilingual markets and possibly other languages.

video.title: 9 High-Ticket Services Nobody Is Offering (In Your Town)

summary: Tim Richard lists nine high-ticket local services he says few businesses target, using Ahrefs search volume, keyword difficulty and weak Google map packs as evidence: Venetian plaster, generator installation, accessible bathroom remodels, riding lawn mower repair, luxury restroom trailer rentals, attic fans, stucco repair, EPDM/TPO flat roofing and crawl space encapsulation. He gives job prices (e.g. 3,000-6,000 USD accent walls, 13,000 USD accessible bathrooms, 5,500 USD crawl spaces) and a few second-hand operator results (an Ohio mower repairer profiting 200,000 USD/yr; a restroom trailer operator netting ~60,000 USD in year one). He also pitches a hub model: rank nationally and route jobs to subcontractors. Takeaway: SEO gaps exist in specialist trades, but most require skilled physical work and US-specific demand.

video.title: He Made $60K His First Month With This Boring Business

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Mike from Iowa City, a tile installer who launched a garage-floor concrete coatings business (flake floors using polyurea base and polyaspartic top coat) around February-March 2026 with his brother and two experienced partners. He claims $60K revenue in April and $69K in May with over 50% profit, driven almost entirely by Meta ads, instant phone follow-up, upfront $8/sq ft pricing and a 10% deposit. Key takeaways: blue-collar service bars are low (answer the phone, show up, be transparent on price), AI (Claude) writes all ad copy and advises on ad budgets, and startup cost can be roughly $15-25K or under $1K by renting a grinder.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews John Cheney, who vibe-coded an AI services business in a weekend, did $180k in six weeks and about $1M in six months, and now has 27 employees. The episode focuses on free customer acquisition: pitching local TV news with a human-interest angle (one segment brought $200-$300k of deals), press releases around partnerships (BYU athletics, Replit), daily authentic social posting, and posting as a whole person. Chris adds his Buc-ee's story, where one cold email to a Texas Monthly reporter led to $180k in sales and a business now making $1M+ net profit a year. Key takeaway: earned media and consistent posting are cheap, asymmetric bets, and fear of others' judgement is the real blocker.

video.title: The Simplest AI Side Hustle for Beginners

summary: Chris Koerner shows a beginner AI side hustle for garage door repair owners: build an instant quote generator and a job profit tracker with Lovable (no code), plus an after-hours AI voice answering agent in GoHighLevel. He scrapes about 513 Google Maps listings with Outscraper for $111, filters to mobile numbers, cold-texts 50 owners via Straight Text, and gets roughly 40-50% replies and one 'yes' within an hour. He pitches $50 per closed lead with no upfront cost and extrapolates to $100k/month, which is hypothetical. Key takeaway: lead with a low-risk offer, validate with real outreach before building, and use no-code/AI tools to ship fast. Lovable is a channel sponsor and the cold SMS method is illegal in the UK for sole traders.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; demonstrates the build and outreach live.

ideas.name: AI after-hours voice answering agent for garage door repair companies
ideas.one_liner: Set up a GoHighLevel AI voice agent that answers missed after-hours calls for garage door repairers, captures name and address, and charges per closed lead or a monthly fee.
ideas.business_model: Per-lead fee (pitched $50 per closed lead) with possible later monthly retainer; Chris also mentions $20-$200 per lead or hundreds per month.
ideas.customer: Owners of small garage door repair businesses (Dallas-Fort Worth in the demo) who miss after-hours calls.
ideas.problem: Owners are on job sites or off duty with phones on silent, so after-hours leads go to voicemail and are lost to competitors; 78% of customers hire the first company to quote.
ideas.offer: A 24/7 AI voice agent that answers calls, collects name and address, emails a call summary and transcript, and can forward urgent callers to the owner. Free setup, no contract, pay only when a lead closes.

pricing.model: Pay per closed lead (test offer), possibly monthly retainer later
pricing.notes: Chris says he may add contracts, upfront money or a retainer later; the first offer is deliberately low-risk.

acquisition_channels.details: Scraped Google Maps with Outscraper, kept mobile numbers only, and bulk-texted 50 owners from Straight Text with a short message ('Hey, I'm here in Dallas. Do you still fix garage doors? I found you on Google Maps'), then sent the pitch to those who replied.

quote.text: Do you answer your phone after hours? The reason I ask is because I created an AI voice agent that will
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Google Maps listings used as the lead source, not as an inbound channel.

ideas.delivery: Agent built in GoHighLevel's Voice AI with a custom prompt/knowledge base generated by ChatGPT. Each client gets a dedicated or ported phone number, a workflow forwards urgent callers to the owner (with secondary and tertiary fallbacks), and emails with transcripts go to agency and owner.
unit_economics_claims: Setup took a couple of minutes; GoHighLevel AI employee has a 30-day free trial
Total validation spend under $100 (scrape plus texting software)
Extrapolation: 200 customers x $500/month = $100k/month (hypothetical)
ideas.startup_cost: Under $100 to validate (scrape cost $111 in the demo, GoHighLevel 30-day free trial for the AI employee)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: not stated; first 'yes' reply came in under an hour but no money was collected

acquisition.how: Lead scraping and list cleaning can be scripted, but the demonstrated channel is unsolicited SMS, which is unlawful in the UK for sole traders and individuals under PECR. A legal UK version would use cold email to limited companies or inbound ads/SEO, and replies would still need a human or agent to handle.

onboarding.how: Agent creation, number provisioning and prompt generation are largely templated; a human checks the knowledge base and ports numbers.

delivery.how: Once configured, the voice agent answers calls, logs transcripts and forwards urgent calls with no human involvement; occasional prompt tuning is needed.

billing.how: Per-closed-lead billing needs the owner to report which leads closed, which is hard to automate; a flat monthly fee via Stripe would be near-unattended.

support.how: Owners will need help with call handling and disputes over lead attribution; AI can handle first-line questions.

uk_applicability.notes: Voice agents work in the UK, but the cold SMS method breaches PECR for sole traders; UK suppliers would use limited-company cold email or TPS-screened calls. Call-recording and AI disclosure rules (UK GDPR) apply. Market is smaller and Google Maps categories differ.

lessons.lesson: A risk-free launch offer (no upfront, no contract, pay per closed lead) removes price as the reason a test fails; raise prices later.
Pick niches with high ticket sizes and urgent, after-hours demand that big players have not yet consolidated.
Voice AI that took venture-funded startups to build can now be approximated in minutes with templated platforms, so the moat is distribution, not the tech.

video.title: I Found 5 Stupid Products Doing $1M+ on Shopify

summary: The Casper Capital narrator reviews five unusual physical products and the marketing choices behind their reported sales: Squatty Potty, Hostage Tape, Plunge, the Oodie and Loop earplugs. The examples center on humor, giftability, visible identity and influencer exposure as ways to make products stand out. The narrator also describes Plunge’s premium pricing and Loop’s pivot toward the ADHD community. Sales figures are presented without cited sources, and the video includes a promotional pitch for Team Drop.

video.title: How a Regular Guy Started a 1-Person Business with AI

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Phil, a semi-retiree with no coding background who started an AI agency after listening to the podcast. Phil landed a $50,000 six-month retainer with a $1.4B investment firm, a success-based grant-writing app (Grant Craft) for a nonprofit, and a $3,500 + $1,500/month product-launch automation deal for a chiropractor, all from friends and friends of friends. He records discovery meetings and uses Claude for solutions, pricing and contracts, building in Go High Level and Claude Code. Key takeaways: sell to your warm network, listen more than talk, ask for referrals, and productise custom builds.

video.title: 7 Side Hustles For Beginners

summary: Tim Richard lists seven beginner-friendly side hustles he says he has tried or knows about: ShareTown furniture-return resale, Amazon retail arbitrage, Craigslist flipping, finding contract gigs on Indeed, Etsy print-on-demand with Printful and Canva, building a niche content following, and home services. The home services business (starting with junk removal, later outsourced to contractors) is his own and the one he favours, with claimed earnings of $3,000+ a day and seven-figure annual profit. Most other ideas are described in general terms with clips of other people's earnings. The key takeaway is that low-barrier, local, hands-on work like flyering for home services is the easiest start, though it is the least automatable.

video.title: I Told an AI Agent to Make Me Money. It Did.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Brandon Doyle (David AI), who used his OpenClaw AI agent ("Zach Morris", reached via iMessage) to launch three experiments over a month. A custom bedtime-story email subscription (Dreamtales) reached about $300 MRR from ~33 customers on roughly $400 of ads. An agent-built website plus postcard plus cold-call funnel for 350 Utah home-service businesses produced a claimed ~$8K MRR from about 17-20 marketing clients. A Facebook Marketplace/eBay flipping idea was dropped. The key takeaway is that agents did the build and outreach prep, while hard-to-ignore physical postcards and human closing calls drove the results.

summary: Chris Koerner reviews seven businesses built around white-labeled or add-on software, mostly using GoHighLevel, and explains how they target specific niches. He highlights recurring pricing, starting with a narrow feature, and building from knowledge of an industry’s problems. He also covers localized software opportunities, research tools, and a plugin model. His central caution is that one-time pricing can fail when ongoing platform, support, and acquisition costs outlast the customer payment.

video.title: AI Agents Are Finally Easy to Set Up

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates setting up an OpenClaw agent on Hostinger to search for trending business stories and return summaries and content angles through Telegram. He adjusts the agent’s skills after web search fails, then suggests adding past episode transcripts and connecting tools for ongoing alerts. The video also mentions using timely trend coverage to attract views and starting an AI implementation agency for small businesses. The main takeaway is that a hosted agent can reduce setup friction, but its research still needs refinement and human review.

video.title: The Best Side Hustle for Beginners (Any Age)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews two college-age resellers, Lucas and John, from rural North Carolina/Virginia, who started on eBay selling childhood Legos and thrift-store finds, then moved into bulk consumer electronics. They describe buying 500-unit lots from a European supplier, a bad batch that lost about $4-5k, and diversifying into US suppliers via about 1,000 cold calls and 12,000 emails. They claim six figures of revenue last year and say anyone can make $1,000-5,000 a month with 2-5 hours a week. Key takeaway: reselling starts with low risk (sell your own stuff, thrift, Facebook Marketplace to eBay), but sourcing is the bottleneck and supplier concentration is dangerous.

video.title: The Laziest AI Side Hustle Just Got Even Easier

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates a workflow for making faceless YouTube videos with Claude and Higgsfield, from niche selection and script writing through generated visuals, voiceover, editing, and upload. He recommends dark business history for this example and lists four other potential niches. The video presents ad revenue, affiliate links, audience products, and channel sales as ways to earn, and suggests offering video production as a service if a creator’s own channel does not take off. Its workflow is detailed, but the earnings and production cost figures are presented as general claims or examples rather than verified results from the demonstrated channel.

onboarding.how: Viewers can find and subscribe through YouTube without manual onboarding; a creator still needs to set up the channel and publish.

delivery.how: Agents can draft scripts and generate media, while a person should check factual claims, edit for quality, assemble the video, and approve publication.

risks: AI output may not look or sound good enough to retain viewers; the speaker stresses that the content must be entertaining and good.
The host reports running out of Higgsfield credits during the demonstration, so usage costs could vary with production volume.
Historical and crime-related stories need careful fact-checking to avoid publishing inaccurate or misleading claims.
High production volume does not guarantee views or revenue; the speaker says results may not come from the first or even tenth video.

video.title: Forget Big Apps. These Tiny Tools Are Making Millions

summary: Chris Koerner explains 'the great unbundling': as Craigslist was split into billion-dollar companies, platforms like Apify, Clay, Zapier and OpenAI can be split into single-purpose tools. He profiles Nico, a former pasta maker turned SDR who vibe-coded a Google Maps lead scraper on an Apify actor. It charges $35/month convertible into credits and reached $3,500 MRR in about 7 months with near-zero costs and word-of-mouth growth. Chris then lists 12+ ideas built the same way, including niche scrapers, Amazon review reports, a Zapier support bot, a micro-influencer finder, an Upwork search tool, a single-feature Clay, a niche 'Zillow' for RV parks or laundromats, and a Shopify-only BuiltWith. His advice is to move fast before the window closes.

video.title: The Credit Card Side Hustle No One Talks About

summary: Colin Stroud describes Go Somewhere, a business that helps owners improve credit card rewards and helps travellers book trips with points. He grew it from a LinkedIn-led side hustle into a full-time business, with fixed-fee consulting, trip research and credit-card affiliate income. He says AI tools help with research and operations, while customers still value human advice and support. The model is learnable and mostly online, but its acquisition depends heavily on LinkedIn and its core services still require human expertise.

speakers.description: Founder of Go Somewhere and credit card rewards consultant.

ideas.name: Credit card rewards consulting for business owners
ideas.one_liner: For a fixed fee, review a business owner's spending, recommend a points-earning card strategy, help implement it and include planning for a future trip.
ideas.business_model: One-time fixed-fee consulting package; affiliate commissions are an additional revenue stream.
ideas.customer: Business owners with substantial card spending, including construction and other local businesses. Colin says his target clients spend at least $20,000 a month on cards; many have significant spending but little time or interest in optimizing rewards.
ideas.problem: Owners may use cards that return relatively few points for their spending and may not know how to transfer or redeem rewards effectively.
ideas.offer: A 75-minute consultation reviewing personal and business spending, a written credit card rewards strategy, implementation help by email or text, and planning for the client's next major trip using points.

pricing.notes: The main current offer is $875. The $400 figure is an example of what a beginner might charge for a simpler strategy, not a stated current price.

acquisition_channels.details: LinkedIn is Colin's main source of clients. He posts educational content and examples of points deals; he says client acquisition has been inbound and organic.

quote.text: I'm posting one, two times a day, six days a week, and LinkedIn has been my best friend, for sure.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

acquisition_channels.details: He also shares content and affiliate links with clients and his newsletter audience. Most of his email subscribers came from LinkedIn.

quote.text: I've got 7,000 email subscribers. So I think I could sell there.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

ideas.delivery: Colin conducts a discovery call, researches the client's personal and business spending, writes a recommended card strategy, discusses it on a live consultation, and provides follow-up help by email or text. A future trip plan is included, with the client contacting him when ready to travel.
unit_economics_claims: Colin charges $875 for the one-time business-owner package.
Colin said his software subscriptions and similar costs were about $100, with almost no other costs at that point.

A consultation client can require a discovery call, research, a 75-minute consultation, follow-up writing and potentially later trip research; he said the trip portion can take from 20 minutes to four hours.
Colin said his revenue reached $13,000 in November 2024, $231,000 gross in 2025, and $89,000 year to date by April 30, 2026.
He said he had about $40,000 in expenses in 2025, including software, travel and contractors.
tools: Credit card issuer websites and rewards programmes
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Colin said ongoing software subscriptions and similar costs were about $100, but did not specify the period.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Colin said he first made $1,000 in a month in March 2024 and started the business as a side hustle.

acquisition.how: AI could help research and draft posts, but acquiring clients currently depends on Colin creating useful LinkedIn content and building trust with a human audience.

onboarding.how: The client completes a discovery call and shares personal and business spending details; the transcript does not describe automated intake.

delivery.how: The core value is Colin's review, live advice and written recommendations. AI may assist research, but the offer is explicitly sold as a human consultation.

billing.how: A fixed fee is straightforward to charge through routine payment software, but no billing tool or automated process is stated.

support.how: Implementation help comes through email and text, and follow-up trip assistance can require additional human research.

uk_applicability.notes: The online consulting and content model can operate in the UK, but card products, rewards programmes and transfer partners differ by country. UK advice and affiliate promotions may also require careful review of financial-promotion and consumer-credit rules.

risks: The service relies on specialist knowledge of card terms and rewards programmes that can change.
The included trip-planning support can create open-ended work months after the original sale, making the effective hourly return unpredictable.
Colin says LinkedIn has been his easy source of clients and that he has little outbound-sales experience, creating platform concentration risk.
In the UK, credit-card recommendations and affiliate promotions need careful review for applicable financial-promotion and consumer-credit requirements.
A client may expect a specific award redemption that is not actually available when they are ready to book.

tactics.name: Validate demand by doing and sharing a real award-search example
steps: Choose a specific points deal and research how it can be booked.
Call the airline if needed; Colin says he spent about five hours on a Turkish Airlines-to-Hawaii example and was on hold for about an hour.
Get as far as confirming the booking path without spending money if you are practising.
Post the research and what you learned on LinkedIn, accurately saying whether you booked the trip.
Use audience response as evidence of interest; Colin says his post received almost 100,000 impressions with about 1,000 followers.

quote.text: Not for a real client just for me. Didn't book it. I got on the phone with the agent. I was on the hold like an hour.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Use LinkedIn content for inbound demand
steps: Publish useful points and rewards content one or two times a day, six days a week, as Colin says he did.
Share practical research and examples rather than relying on outbound sales.
Build an email list from the audience so there is a channel to reach people if social distribution changes.

quote.text: I've almost never done any kind of outbound marketing that's been 100% inbound organic, just from content.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Start with spending and earning rate, not card perks
steps: Ask how much the customer spends and where that spending occurs.
Compare the points earned on those categories before weighing lounge access or insurance benefits.
Recommend a simple card strategy that fits the spending pattern and explain how to implement it.

quote.text: stop focusing on the benefits of your card and start thinking about how much it's earning.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Scope trip research with a form, deposit and complexity-based fee
steps: Collect the traveller's points balance, destination, cabin and trip requirements in a website form.
Take a deposit to start work.
Quote a flat fee based on trip complexity, with multi-city and larger-family trips costing more.
Collect the remaining fee once the trip is booked.

quote.text: Anybody on the internet in the world could come to my website, fill out a form. And it's free to fill out the form.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Systematize research and delegate trip work
steps: Use an award-search tool to search multiple programmes rather than checking airline sites one at a time.
Track trips through a custom CRM and dashboard built with Lovable.
Hire experienced points researchers to handle most of the research while retaining oversight and client contact.

quote.text: So custom CRM, custom dashboard, really, really cool. So in terms of delivering that service, it's all done through AI by humans.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Learn through free resources and practise before taking clients
steps: Study points blogs and free courses, including The Daily Drop resources Colin recommends.
Practise researching an itinerary using your own points or by stopping before payment.
Build a truthful sample case study from the research and distinguish a researched example from a completed booking.

quote.text: Luckily, you can practice on yourself. Like you can go book fake trips, basically. You can get all the way to the booking stage and stop.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Keep a simple fixed-fee core offer
steps: State the package price clearly before work begins.
Keep the scope easy to understand: consultation, written strategy, implementation help and one trip plan.
Track the later trip work because it can vary substantially and affect the effective hourly return.

quote.text: I charge flat fees. So I say it, yeah, it's what you want. This is exactly how much it costs. I keep it really simple.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

video.title: How Anyone Can Make $10K+/Month From the Government

summary: Natalie describes bidding as a prime contractor on government contracts, then hiring subcontractors to do the work and keeping the difference between their quote and her bid. She discusses contracts for hazardous waste disposal, catering, landscaping and relocation assistance, as well as using AI and public procurement data to evaluate bids. Her claimed earnings and low maintenance time depend on finding reliable subcontractors and doing substantial research and proposal work up front. Chris Koerner adds a post-interview clarification about subcontracting limits, certification programs and the legal risk of pass-through schemes.

speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office.

speakers.name: Natalie
speakers.description: Government contractor and subcontracting prime; her full name is not stated.

ideas.name: Government contract prime and subcontractor broker
ideas.one_liner: Find public-sector contract opportunities, bid as the prime, hire a qualified subcontractor to perform the work and retain the difference.
ideas.business_model: Contract revenue with a markup over subcontractor cost; the prime invoices the government and pays the subcontractor.
ideas.customer: Federal, state, city and local government agencies, schools and universities procuring goods or services.
ideas.problem: Public bodies need vendors to complete work, while many small businesses know their trade but not the procurement and proposal process.
ideas.offer: Identify a suitable solicitation, prepare and submit a compliant bid, arrange subcontracted delivery and manage invoicing and contract coordination.

pricing.model: Bid a contract price based on the scope and subcontractor quote; retain the margin after paying delivery costs.
pricing.notes: No standard fee or markup is stated. Contract prices depend on the solicitation and past pricing.

acquisition_channels.details: Search SAM.gov and other public procurement systems for solicitations; she also says opportunities exist with local, state, city, school and university procurement systems.

quote.text: So the average person, how do they become a small business, well, just by having an LLC?

video.title: The Beginner-Friendly Claude AI Side Hustle Nobody Talks About

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Ryan Dozer, a solo AI marketer who runs a six-figure SEO/content agency. Dozer explains Claude skills (markdown SOPs for AI agents) and how he packaged about 20-25 of his own into a $99 'Claude Code skill stack' sold from his own site via Stripe, claiming over $3,000 in 30-45 days. He demonstrates an SEO blog-post-writer skill that turns YouTube videos into ranking articles, a LinkedIn scraper skill using Apify, and a vibe-coded marketing OS. Key takeaway: turn the workflows and expertise you already use daily into skills and sell them as digital products, but the numbers are self-reported and the sales path leans on his existing audience.

video.title: The Only Playbook You Need to Sell Anything Online

summary: Chris Koerner presents a two-day playbook for growing an audience with short-form content, collecting email addresses, and selling digital products or services. He describes selling recordings from consulting sessions as a $97 Google Drive product and walks through GoHighLevel workflows for Instagram comments, lead magnets, email, and AI voice agents. He also demonstrates building a basic bank-statement-to-P&L app with AI Studio and discusses selling automation services or software. His recurring advice is to test content and offers, build an owned email list, and publish before over-planning.

tactics.name: Turn existing expertise into a low-friction digital product
steps: Review existing recordings, notes, and files for material that solves a customer problem.
Package the useful material in a simple digital format, such as a Google Drive folder.
Test subject lines with A/B emails to relevant newsletter segments.
Deliver the link directly after purchase.

quote.text: I ended up just selling a link to the Google Drive. That's it, not like a community with moderators
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Test content formats and keep separate research and posting accounts
steps: Test formats such as carousels, infographics, picture posts, and talking-head videos.
Track both positive platform signals and whether you enjoy making the content.
Use a separate research account to train the feed toward your niche and collect content examples.
Keep the posting account focused; use a separate personal account for unrelated viewing.

quote.text: I have like a consumption Instagram account for research. And then I have a posting Instagram account from posting
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use a hook and withhold the promised payoff until the end
steps: Open with a visual or verbal hook that identifies the audience and promises a specific payoff.
Explain the situation and what you tried without revealing the key answer immediately.
Show evidence or a result, then deliver what the opening promised.
Use a call to action that fits the platform and the offer.

quote.text: And the whole time they're like, what is the thing? What, why are you hiding the idea?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Ask followers what they need before building a product
steps: Use an Instagram story poll to ask what problem followers have.
Follow up with another poll or question about the leading problem.
Repeat for several days to learn the specific product or solution they want.
Test the offer before making a large product investment.

quote.text: You don't have to guess what they want. So then when you have a big launch a month later
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Send social viewers to one simple email landing page
steps: Use a single focused landing page instead of a link page with many choices.
Ask for an email address first; collect additional details later if needed.
Use a clear lead magnet that is more valuable than the short video preview.
Send a short welcome sequence, then one relevant, valuable email each week.

quote.text: The more there is for them to click on the landing page, the more likely they are to get distracted and to never convert at all.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Build a comment-to-lead workflow
steps: Connect the Instagram account in GoHighLevel through Facebook integrations.
Choose the specific post and use a trigger phrase with a contains-phrase filter.
Track first-level comments only.
Like the comment and rotate several public replies to reduce repetitive-looking responses.
DM a clickable button to the landing page, then capture the email and deliver the lead magnet.

quote.text: you want to be sure it's just contains and not exact match.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Keep a simple lead workflow and add tags
steps: Start with the trigger and one useful response instead of adding unnecessary complexity.
Tag each contact by the lead magnet or topic they requested.
Use tags later to send relevant offers to the right subset of contacts.
Build a thank-you page and a short delivery email, with a backup link on the page.

quote.text: If you have 30 different PDF lead magnets over the course of a year, and you tag all of those people that buy it as PDF
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Demonstrate the voice agent as part of a qualified lead journey
steps: Collect a phone number only when needed and include the required consent language.
Set an appropriate delay and condition in the workflow before an outbound call.
Train the voice agent for a narrow job, such as demonstrating itself to a business owner.
Invite interested prospects to a follow-up call with a real person.
Check applicable phone and marketing rules before using automated calls.

quote.text: your express goal is to get them on a call with me, a real human to further answer questions
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Reuse a voice-agent template across clients
steps: Start from a marketplace template.
Replace the business name, voice, goals, availability, and knowledge base.
Connect the client's calendar and notifications.
Review call transcripts and update the prompt when the agent fails on repeated questions.
Duplicate a working configuration for the next client, then test the client-specific version.

quote.text: you literally just duplicate it. You just click that. Okay. Then you swap out the big and same with your new client.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Let AI improve a rough prompt and iterate on the prototype
steps: Write the idea in plain language, even if the prompt is rough.
Ask a separate AI tool to improve the prompt for the specific builder.
Build a first version and test it with dummy data.
Show the builder a screenshot and describe the specific change needed.
Do not treat a working prototype as proof that a regulated product is production-ready.

quote.text: the shortcut is to ask the AI, what to ask the AI.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Keep testing growth and offer variations
steps: Test different lead magnets, formats, offers, and workflow variations.
Keep successful versions running while testing new ones.
Make small changes and monitor what happens.
Do not assume a growth tactic will work indefinitely.

quote.text: Test all of it. Like, never ever ever stop testing.

tactics.name: Publish and learn through execution
steps: Build a small version of the offer.
Publish it and observe real customer behavior.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Mark, a 66-year-old lawyer who designs 'business in a box' ideas, about his nitro iced coffee cart built from a gutted Home Depot tool cart for under ~$1-3k. Using shelf-stable brewed coffee in bag-in-box packs and a nitro tap, he pours 24oz iced coffees in 30 seconds for ~$3 cost and ~$8.50 price, netting $400 at small events, $800-1,200 at festivals and $8,000 at his best two-day event. He also ran beer tap trucks and armoire tap bar rentals, and sets up operators (divorced moms, veterans, visa immigrants) on a ~30% profit split. Key takeaway: strip a product to what customers actually buy, keep capex tiny, and win on location.

video.title: The Most Passive $104K/M Online Business You've Never Heard Of

summary: Kyle explains his website landlord model: build and rank a basic local service website, then rent its calls and form leads to a local business for a monthly fee. He says the work is concentrated in choosing niches, building sites and finding the first client; once a site ranks and a client is in place, it can require little ongoing attention. Chris also describes an unmonetized pet and horse cremation lead site that receives inquiries. The discussion emphasizes low competition, proving lead quality with a free trial and favoring simple, predictable pricing over maximizing each site's revenue.

ideas.one_liner: Build a local service website, rank it in Google, and rent its tracked calls and form leads to a local business.
ideas.business_model: Primarily a negotiated flat monthly fee for local leads; Kyle also describes a trusted-client commission arrangement and an initial one-off payment.

ideas.problem: Small local businesses need high-intent customer leads but may not want to risk a large fixed marketing contract without proof of results.
ideas.offer: Build a generic niche-and-city website, rank it through local SEO, then forward tracked phone calls and form leads to a local business. Offer an initial free trial so the business can judge lead quality.

quote.speaker: Kyle

acquisition_channels.details: For his first sale, Kyle contacted an old high-school friend who was an attorney; he also advises starting with one's network.

quote.text: I made a screencast video where I recorded my screen and showed him how this business model works and how I could build a Macite targeting Torrance.
quote.speaker: Kyle

ideas.delivery: Create a generic website for a service in a specific city, improve its ranking with content and backlinks, and place a tracking phone number on it. The number forwards calls to the paying provider; the tracking platform can send call recordings and caller details to the client. The site can also collect form leads. Kyle says low-competition sites often need little maintenance after ranking, though building, SEO and replacing clients still require work.
unit_economics_claims: Kyle claims basic site overhead can be about USD 25 per month per site.
Kyle reports company revenue around USD 100,000 per month and overhead below USD 5,000 per month; elsewhere he says he personally makes around USD 35,000 per month.
Kyle says his first client paid USD 6,000 upfront, and later describes several changing monthly fee arrangements.
Kyle gives an example of an auto glass site producing about 50 calls per month for a USD 600 monthly fee.
Kyle says one to three free trials typically produce a locked-in business owner.
Kyle says clients who stay beyond six months may remain for about five years or more.
Kyle reports an exception where a trusted concrete contractor pays 10% commission.
ideas.startup_cost: Kyle says site overhead can be about USD 25 per month for hosting, domain and tracking phone number. Initial build and learning costs are not stated; the first client paid USD 6,000 upfront.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Kyle says his first win came after three months. He contacted a former school friend and received an initial USD 6,000 payment.

acquisition.how: Organic search can bring in leads with limited ongoing work after ranking, but site selection and SEO require work and the paying clients are found through manual calls. UK cold calling needs appropriate screening, including TPS/CTPS checks.

onboarding.how: A human negotiates and sets up the free trial, client contact details and call routing; the tracking platform can automate forwarding and notifications.

delivery.how: Call forwarding, form capture and recording can run automatically. Site building, content, backlinks and occasional ranking checks need human work; Kyle says some low-competition sites need little later attention.

billing.how: Recurring flat fees can be billed automatically, but Kyle says he manually follows up on failed cards and late payments.

support.how: Many clients reportedly need little contact after setup, but disputes, payment failures and client replacement require human follow-up.

uk_applicability.notes: Local SEO and renting lead flow to UK service businesses can work on the same basic model. The specific cities, niches, prices and search competition need UK research, and the manual cold-call step needs UK screening and privacy compliance.

risks: Google ranking changes or stronger competitors can reduce the site's lead flow.
The model depends on targeting low-competition niches; Kyle warns against entering heavily funded markets such as personal injury in Los Angeles.
A client may fail to answer calls or follow up promptly, wasting leads and weakening retention.
Without job tracking, commission or pay-per-call billing can create disputes and depends on trust.
Flat fees without contracts can make clients easy to lose; the operator needs a replacement prospect pipeline.
Late or failed client payments require follow-up.
In the UK, cold calling needs appropriate TPS/CTPS screening, and handling call recordings and lead data requires care.

tactics.name: Choose a low-competition niche and city
steps: Look for a local service and city where search demand exists but competing sites are weak.
Avoid heavily funded national or major-city SEO markets.
Compare the supply of providers with the apparent demand for the service.
Consider adjacent services and cities as separate opportunities.

quote.text: I want to compete against Joe Bill and Steve in Oram, Utah with the joke removal company where they have websites that I'm competing against, they bought those websites, maybe back in 2005 and haven't touched them since.
quote.speaker: Kyle

tactics.name: Build proof before pitching providers
steps: Build a generic niche-and-city site and let it begin generating calls.
Use tracked calls as proof that people are searching for the service.
Offer a provider a free week of calls without asking for card details.
Discuss a monthly flat fee after the provider has seen the leads.

quote.text: I connect them to you for a week for free. And I'm not going to pick a credit card information from you.
quote.speaker: Kyle

tactics.name: Start with warm contacts for the first sale
steps: List business owners already in your personal network.
Send a screen recording explaining the proposed niche and city and how leads would reach the prospect.
Use the first successful delivery as a case study for later outreach.

quote.text: I think it's so important that when anyone launches any agency digital marketing, whatever, start with your network, like it all comes down to trust.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Make a casual, specific cold-call offer
steps: Find businesses offering the service through Google, Yelp and Yellow Pages.
Record business details in a spreadsheet.
Say what niche and city the site serves and approximately how many calls it receives.
Ask for an email and phone number to route the free-trial calls.

quote.text: I go, man, I got this website that is getting like 50 calls a month for junk removal services and Austin. I'm not a junk removal company.
quote.speaker: Kyle

tactics.name: Use call tracking to prove lead delivery
steps: Use a tracking number that forwards to the provider.
Send the provider call recordings, caller number and call notifications.
Use a whisper message so the provider knows the caller came through the lead site.
Review call records if a client disputes the quality or source of a lead.

quote.text: it also automates emails to my client with the recording of the call and the phone number of the caller so they can keep track of any call that comes from me.
quote.speaker: Kyle

tactics.name: Prefer simple flat pricing
steps: Use a monthly flat fee so clients can predict their bill.
Avoid complicated call tiers if they lead to invoice questions and lead-by-lead audits.
Consider commission only when tracking is reliable and the operator fully trusts the client.

quote.text: I'd rather make less money and have this be 100% passive than squeak out next to five to 10 grand a month because I'm like over analyzing and auditing all the leads.
quote.speaker: Kyle

tactics.name: Keep the site simple and clear
steps: Use a fast, basic site that clearly states the service and location.
Keep adding relevant content until the site reaches page one.
Do not add design elements that distract from the call or form action.

tactics.name: Use content and backlinks as the main SEO work
steps: Focus most effort on content and backlinks for local, low-competition terms.
Use citations and heading structure as supporting work.
Do not assume advice for highly competitive national keywords applies to a local low-competition site.
