warnings.warning: Kyle says SEO sites should target low-competition local terms; he advises against competing against heavily funded national or major-city sites.
A site can generate leads that are not valuable to a buyer if local providers lack capacity or do not serve the relevant area.
Calls can be missed or followed up slowly; Kyle says call recordings help show whether leads arrived and how they were handled.
Commission and pay-per-call deals require reliable lead and job tracking; Kyle says he avoids them when he cannot verify closed work.
Tiered call pricing can lead clients to dispute invoices and audit individual leads, so Kyle prefers a predictable flat fee.
Kyle says some clients' cards fail and one or two clients may not pay in a month, requiring follow-up.
Kyle says the course and community he purchased no longer exist; he also advises vetting a course before spending heavily.
Kyle says the website landlord's client-acquisition step involves manual cold calls. In the UK, screen business cold calls against TPS/CTPS and follow applicable PECR and data-protection rules.
The host promotes GoHighLevel and the TKO Owners community; Kyle promotes Rent Local Sites and his TikTok account. These are promotional interests, separate from the business examples.

lessons.lesson: Prove that a business can deliver before asking a client to commit; a free trial of tracked leads lowers the buyer's perceived risk.
Start with warm contacts when possible. A trusted first customer can create urgency to deliver and provide a case study for later sales.
A strong, specific offer makes sales calls easier: describe the service, location and existing lead flow, then offer a low-risk trial.
Choose lower-competition local search terms where a basic site can beat neglected competitors, rather than chasing the largest search markets.
Use call tracking and recordings to make lead delivery visible and reduce disagreements about which calls came from the site.
Predictable flat pricing can be more valuable than maximizing short-term revenue if it reduces disputes and keeps clients for longer.
Keep operations simple. Kyle says a basic spreadsheet and a small software stack can be enough for managing clients and sites.
For a local service site, clarity and speed can matter more than polished design; the site should make its service and location obvious.
Automating a business does not remove the initial work: the site still has to be researched, built, ranked and matched to a client.
A lifestyle business can be a deliberate goal. The speakers value time freedom and sustainable income over pursuing the largest possible exit.
When selling leads on commission, use reliable tracking and work only with partners you trust; otherwise the operator cannot verify closed jobs.

evidence_quality.rationale: Kyle describes a first-hand business, concrete workflows, named tools and several specific revenue, cost, pricing and retention figures. The figures are self-reported and not independently verified; the introduction's USD 104,000 monthly figure differs from Kyle's later USD 35,000 personal monthly figure and roughly USD 100,000 company monthly figure.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host reads a GoHighLevel promotion and promotes TKO Owners. Kyle directs viewers to Rent Local Sites and his TikTok account. The course Kyle bought is said to no longer exist.

video.title: He Spends 1 Hour a Week on This Business

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jay Meldrum, who left corporate professional services to open Swing Cave Golf, a single-bay members-only golf simulator in a Texas strip mall (Allen area). Six months in he has about 28 members on three tiers (USD 175/275/325 per month), roughly USD 7,000 monthly revenue, break-even at about 15 members after three months, and claimed 50-55% net margins. The business is run with 24/7 app-based door access, scheduling software and cameras, with about an hour a week of owner time. Upfront cost is about USD 100K, and he plans a second location and eventual scaling. Takeaway: a low-opex, membership-based, physical-space business can be near-passive once built, but it needs significant capital and a physical site.

summary: William Lindholm describes a cake-sourcing and delivery business that helps companies get sales prospects’ attention with physical gifts. The business began as an automated employee birthday-cake service in Norway, then pivoted in the US to sales campaigns after birthday software proved difficult to sell at scale. William says the new model uses AI agents to find and negotiate with bakeries, while software coordinates large orders and tracks deliveries. The discussion emphasizes attention, measurable sales outcomes, and the need to keep testing which gifts produce meetings and closed sales.

Track meeting bookings and compare the result with prior outreach.

tactics.name: Tie the offer to a budget connected to revenue

Test the offer with the buyer before building extensive integrations or infrastructure.

summary: Chris Koerner explains how to start and run a farmer's market (using his wife's kids' market at a shopping centre as the example), then interviews Mike McCoy of Prep Pizza, who sold DIY pizza dough kits at farmer's markets (about $60k in a first summer, part time) before scaling online via Facebook ads to claimed $3-4M of sales. The video also covers other farmer's market products (baked goods, pickles, fresh pasta) and tips such as sampling, choosing in-city markets, and filming content. Key takeaway: farmer's markets are a cheap, fast way to validate a physical food product, and a market organiser can piggyback on a venue that wants footfall.

summary: Brett describes DesignJoy, a solo productized design subscription that he says he launched on Product Hunt and grew while keeping his full-time job. He explains its self-serve offer, rapid delivery, pricing increases, workload, and use of AI tools. The conversation also covers possible productized services, including AI-first development, branding, copywriting, video clipping, thumbnails, and podcast editing. A key takeaway is that AI can speed up digital service work, while distribution, client demand, design judgment, and human delivery still matter.

acquisition.how: Product Hunt submission and a self-serve site can be prepared and monitored with software. The launch still depended on a personal network and the service needs ongoing distribution. In the UK, favor inbound channels and consent-based promotion; do not automate unsolicited marketing to individuals or sole traders.

onboarding.how: A website can take payment and accept requests without a sales call, with occasional human review for fit, scope, or unclear briefs.

delivery.how: A designer must make and review each client deliverable. AI can assist with requirements, UX, and assets, but the transcript describes Brett personally doing the design work.

risks: Brett says rapid revenue growth and a large client load led him to work himself nearly to death and into hospital.
He says increasing prices did not reduce demand as he expected; it sometimes increased demand by moving the offer into another category.
He says monthly recurring revenue swings with churn and clients pausing.

tactics.name: Launch through Product Hunt with a small existing network
steps: Build a simple service site and make the offer clear enough to buy without a call.
Submit the product to Product Hunt on launch day.
Ask friends and family to support the launch; Brett used his school network on Facebook to request upvotes.
Share the founder story on forums, even without an established audience.
Treat marketplace exposure as a launch spike, then build a repeatable acquisition channel.

quote.text: My personal network was my friends and family I went to school with on Facebook. That was all I had at the time.
quote.speaker: Brett

tactics.name: Make a service purchasable without a sales process
steps: Turn a broad custom service into a clearly described package.
Let customers select and pay on the website instead of requesting a quote and attending several meetings.
Set an expected turnaround so the customer knows when value will arrive.
Offer pausing and resuming when demand is intermittent.

quote.text: So instead of filling in a form on a website, getting a quote, jumping on a call, having three or four meetings discussed pricing and proposals and estimates and all sorts of stuff
quote.speaker: Brett

tactics.name: Raise prices when demand exceeds capacity
steps: When demand becomes hard to manage, test a higher price rather than immediately shutting down the offer.
Watch what happens to demand and customer fit after each increase.
Do not assume a price increase will reduce demand; Brett says each increase sometimes moved the offer into a new category and increased demand.

quote.text: Every time I felt like I was hitting a wall and wanted to shut things down, I just, my gut reaction was just like, just gonna increase prices and see what happens.
quote.speaker: Brett

summary: Chris Koerner visits his neighbour Rayma, a stay-at-home mom of four in Dallas who runs Gifty Gal, a corporate gifting business focused on personalised prospecting gifts for tech sales teams. She started in 2022 with baby shower gifts, grossed about $75k (netting $7,800) in year one, and reached $357k revenue and $119k net in 2025 working about 20 hours a week from home and a shared warehouse. Growth came entirely from referrals and LinkedIn after one LinkedIn post reshared by her husband's network. She explains her pricing (about $100 per prospecting box, 30-50% net margin target, shipping billed separately), wholesale sourcing via Faire and reseller licences, and a four-step framework: connect, collaborate, curate, fulfil.

tactics.name: Connect, collaborate, curate, fulfil framework
steps: Connect: post on LinkedIn about what you do (e.g. help sales teams close more deals with personalised gifts) and respond quickly
Collaborate: discovery call with the client on what the gift must achieve and who it must reach
Curate: source products at the best wholesale price that fit the recipient's alma mater, hobbies etc.
Fulfil: assemble, collect shipping info, double-check names and addresses, ship

Confirm shipping cost after a sample is approved

video.title: The Easiest Way to Actually Make Money With AI

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Corey, who sells a $1,000 'AI assessment' (audit) to small businesses. A voice agent (Annie, built on a voice-AI platform) interviews the owner for 10-20 minutes, another AI agent turns the transcript into a report (Docx to Gamma) recommending off-the-shelf tools, and a follow-up call upsells process optimisation, Zapier/Make automations, custom GPT knowledge systems, CRM setups and speed-to-lead agents at $1.5k-$5k+. Corey then lists tactics for finding customers with no following: local AI meetups, door knocking, free audits for a peer group, and office hours. Key takeaway: you only need to be one step ahead of the client, and a higher-priced audit makes the upsell easier.

video.title: The Simplest Side Hustle You Can Start Under $100

summary: Josh sells local businesses advertising space on shared postcards sent to nearby homes, and says he started with under $100. He finds advertisers mainly through local Facebook business groups, designs their ads, and arranges printing and USPS delivery. The discussion covers pricing, print and postage costs, ways to track responses, and the limits of promising advertisers a return. Chris also suggests using the postcard business to build relationships and sell other services; the transcript includes a separate story about Chris’s wholesale iPhone-parts business.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office.

speakers.name: Josh
speakers.description: Guest who identifies himself as Direct Mail Josh.

ideas.name: Shared local direct-mail advertising cards
ideas.one_liner: Sell category-exclusive ad spaces on shared postcards mailed to selected local households.
ideas.business_model: One-off or repeat sales of advertising space; larger cards can be sold as single mailings or recurring runs.
ideas.customer: Local businesses that serve households in the selected area, especially home services and local brick-and-mortar businesses.
ideas.problem: Local businesses want exposure to nearby homeowners and may want an alternative or addition to digital marketing.
ideas.offer: Sell ad space on a shared postcard, with one business per category. Josh designs the ads, offers revisions, helps develop offers, adds a dynamic QR code, and tracks QR scans. Printing and postal delivery are arranged through suppliers and USPS.

pricing.model: One-off ad-space sales, with optional repeat mailings or multi-month runs.

price_points.label: Example price on a larger card
Transcript renders this figure as $9.99; likely a misheard $999
Suggested range for an average ad space, expressed in cents
Example rate in cents for one space
Example rate in cents for a double space
Suggested price range for a smaller-town market

pricing.notes: Josh says he adapted pricing from another operator and adjusts it by market, size, and demand. The transcript's '$9.99' figure is ambiguous and may be a Whisper error.

acquisition_channels.details: Josh posts in local business networking and contractor groups, usually once a week, describing the mailing area, household reach, and category exclusivity. Interested businesses comment or message him.

quote.text: So that's one of my favorite prospecting methods is just posting groups.
quote.speaker: Josh

acquisition_channels.details: Not stated.
He has sold one or two spaces by cold calling and called businesses he found through yard signs.
He has tried email outreach but says it is not his preferred method.

He sometimes contacts businesses through Messenger or text, including businesses he sees posting in local groups. In the UK, unsolicited marketing messages to individuals and sole traders need consent under the user's stated PECR constraint.
He has walked into businesses and met one early prospect in person.
Josh posts social-media videos about the business; he says these brought him a solo-card customer and another order.
A real-estate contact referred a warm lead who bought a space.

ideas.delivery: Josh chooses a mailing area, matches advertisers to it, designs their ads, provides revisions and offer help, and adds dynamic QR codes to track scans. He sends print files to a printing company; cards can be shipped to him or directly to a postal facility. USPS EDDM handles the mail delivery. He says cards delivered to him need to be bundled and labelled correctly for USPS.
unit_economics_claims: For a 10,000-piece run, Josh quotes $2,500 postage and about $2,300 printing, or roughly $4,800 total.
Chris estimates that filling both sides of a 10,000-piece card can generate $9,000-$10,000 revenue and $4,000-$5,000 profit; Josh confirms the estimate.
Josh says the front of the card must cover printing and postage to reach break-even.
Josh reports a bakery customer paid $350 for a three-month run and says 15-18 people redeemed its coupon over the run.
ideas.startup_cost: Josh says he started for less than about $100. A 10,000-card run is quoted at about $4,800 for printing and postage; the transcript does not explain how he financed initial runs.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Josh describes selling his first $1,100 space after about five messages, but does not state how long after starting the business that sale occurred.

acquisition.how: Agents could draft and schedule group posts, identify suitable groups, and triage inbound enquiries. Human review is still needed for group rules, local fit, sales judgement, and any outbound contact. UK law restricts unsolicited electronic marketing to individuals and sole traders.

onboarding.how: A form could collect ad copy, logo, offer, service area, and QR destination; an agent could prepare a draft and request approval. Josh currently provides design and revisions.

delivery.how: Printing and postal delivery are physical operations. Software can prepare files and coordinate suppliers, but humans or vendors must print, bundle, label, and deliver the cards.

billing.how: Invoices and payment reminders could be handled by billing software with occasional human checks; the transcript does not name or describe a billing system.

support.how: Agents could answer routine questions, share proofs, and report QR scans, while a human handles offer advice, revisions, complaints, and unusual requests.

uk_applicability.notes: The shared direct-mail model can work in the UK, but the transcript's USPS EDDM service and US postal pricing do not transfer directly. A UK operator would need a suitable local unaddressed-mail service and current UK print and delivery costs. UK outreach by email, SMS, WhatsApp, or social DM must account for PECR rules, especially for sole traders.

risks: Josh explicitly says he cannot guarantee ROI; the offer sells exposure, and advertiser results vary.
Response attribution is difficult when customers call instead of scanning the QR code or do not use a unique offer.
A weak offer, unsuitable advertiser, or poorly selected mailing area can produce poor results.
Printing a large run before checking a supplier's sample risks wasting substantial money.
The postal workflow has bundling and labelling requirements, and direct-mail vendors must be reliable.
The model depends on filling enough ad space before print and postage deadlines.
UK outbound email, SMS, and social messages may be unlawful without consent for individuals and sole traders; cold calls require TPS/CTPS screening.

tactics.name: Choose a mailing area by household fit
steps: Enter a target ZIP code in the USPS EDDM tool.
Sort routes by higher income when the advertisers are home-service businesses that need single-family homeowners.
Match advertisers to the area they serve and avoid routes dominated by apartments or condos if those households are a poor fit.

tactics.name: Pre-sell enough space to cover the mailing
steps: Calculate print and postage costs before promising a mailing.
Treat the front half of the card as the break-even target for those costs.
Treat additional filled space, including the back, as potential revenue above break-even.

quote.text: So it's like I gotta fill the front half of my card to cover printing and postage.

tactics.name: Post a short, specific offer in local business groups

video.title: You Only Need a Laptop to Start This Business

summary: Chris Koerner hosts serial entrepreneur Michael Girdley, who pitches about a dozen business ideas picked from a 30-idea list by Koerner's audience poll. They cover an OpenClaw AI-agent persona marketplace, paid AI replicas of famous mentors, an AI-assisted local news site, a curated X magazine, a printed YouTube book for kids, AI skincare, a 'distraction bot' app, admissions negotiation for parents, and AI audits for small businesses. Girdley's strongest recommendation is AI audits as a low-competition entry point that leads to better follow-on AI work. Most of the content is speculative brainstorming with few first-hand numbers.

ideas.name: OpenClaw / agent persona exchange marketplace
ideas.one_liner: A marketplace where creators sell deployable AI-agent 'personas' (marketing manager, sales rep) and the exchange takes a cut.
ideas.business_model: Marketplace commission on persona sales (subscription or licence); creators sell free/open or closed-source versions
ideas.customer: Business owners who want ready-made AI agents that act like employees; creators who want to sell their own versions
ideas.problem: Hard to find pre-built, trusted AI agents for specific roles such as cold email or marketing
ideas.offer: A searchable exchange with filters, tech stack and approximate token costs for each persona, like an eBay for agents

pricing.model: Per-month subscription or upfront licence per persona; marketplace takes a cut
pricing.notes: Buyer also pays token costs

acquisition_channels.details: The exchange itself is the platform; creators bring their own audiences and personas

ideas.delivery: Platform hosts or links personas that run on the buyer's OpenClaw setup; creators build the personas
unit_economics_claims: Marketplace takes a cut of all persona sales (no rate stated)

acquisition.how: Listings and SEO are agent-friendly, but a two-sided marketplace needs seeding of supply and demand

onboarding.how: Self-serve creator and buyer signup

delivery.how: Software distribution; vetting and quality review need occasional human checks

billing.how: Stripe-style commission splits

support.how: Disputes and broken agents need human escalation

uk_applicability.notes: Software marketplace works the same in the UK; consumer-protection and VAT on digital goods apply.

risks: Early market; depends on OpenClaw adoption
Domain names like openclaw exchange are already taken
Quality and security of third-party agents

video.title: How to Invest in Index Funds for Beginners (Step-by-Step)

summary: This solo tutorial explains index funds, compares them with ETFs, and gives a step-by-step process for opening an account, choosing a fund, automating contributions, and holding long term. The narrator recommends low-cost, diversified funds and regular investing, using US brokers and account types as examples. The video includes return and fee figures, hypothetical growth projections, and a promotion for WeBull. It does not discuss a business for customers to buy, so there are no business ideas to extract.

video.title: The Most Passive Online Side Hustle I've Ever Seen

summary: Chris Koerner argues that simple AI-vibe-coded calculator or tool websites (paycheck, calorie, mortgage, etc.) can earn passive ad and email-lead income because they capture large search volume. He cites big examples (paycheck calculator, calorie calculator, Omni Calculator) and his own pet cremation directory calculators. He then builds an AI token cost calculator in Hostinger Horizons in about 6 minutes, picks the niche with Google Trends, adds email gating and AdSense, and publishes it. Key takeaway: build many cheap niche tool sites, validate with trends and keyword data, and monetise beyond AdSense with email capture and lead sales. The video is sponsored by Hostinger, so the ease claims are promotional.

video.title: Debt Relief Explained: Who It's For, Who It's NOT For, and Best Companies in 2026

summary: Casper Capital's host explains US debt settlement, who may or may not benefit, how the process works, and its risks. The video compares Accredited Debt Relief, National Debt Relief, and Americor using claimed fees, ratings, customer complaints, and program details. It also describes debt consolidation and mentions debt management programs and bankruptcy as alternatives. Its practical advice is to compare at least two quotes, review the full cost and timeline, and get the terms in writing.

video.title: He Can't Code but His AI Agents Make Him $5K/Month

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Vadim, an 18-year-old non-coder who vibe-coded Vugola, an all-in-one clipping, scheduling and captioning SaaS, using Claude Code, Supabase, Vercel and GitHub. He claims $5K revenue in 30 days at ~80% margin, with 267 paying users on $9/$39/$99 plans, acquired mainly via Twitter after Reddit/X outreach by an OpenClaw agent. He also describes running a small team of Hermes agents (CEO, marketing, growth, coding, support) and shares prompting tips, PostHog analytics, Paperclip, and mind-mapping for niche research. Key takeaway: a solo founder can build and run a niche SaaS with AI agents cheaply, but the numbers are self-reported and the product is still in beta.

ideas.name: Agricultural spray drone application service
ideas.one_liner: Use heavy-lift drones to apply farmer-supplied crop treatments, charging by acre.
ideas.business_model: Per-acre application service, sometimes with repeat applications during a crop season.
ideas.customer: Farmers who need crops or pasture sprayed and may not want to buy, operate, or maintain their own spray equipment.
ideas.problem: Farmers need crop treatments applied, including where wet ground, trees, power lines, or rough terrain limit other equipment.
ideas.offer: Bring a spray drone and trailer to the farm, mix the farmer's chosen product, and apply it to specified acres. The farmer supplies the chemical.

pricing.model: Per acre, with price varying by terrain, alternatives, and application volume.

price_points.label: Approximate price matching an airplane on suitable fields
Possible extra charge for five-gallon rather than two-gallon application

pricing.notes: Mike says operating cost is $3 to $3.74 per acre for the work he describes. The chemical is supplied separately by the farmer. Prices and costs are US claims.

acquisition_channels.details: Visit farms with the equipment and ask to demonstrate spraying with water over the farmer's crops. The guest says to get permission before flying over the land.

quote.text: The way that I would tell people to get a customer is you you have to go to the customer or get the customer come to you to do a demonstration.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Visit agricultural co-ops where farmers buy seed and chemicals, show the drone and trailer, and introduce the service.

quote.text: I went to co-ops like where the farmers buy their seed and chemical from. So I showed up there with my drones and my trailer doing exactly what you said.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: A demonstration can lead farmers and their friends to ask for the service or book it for a later season.

quote.text: We are flying at a farmer's field and there's an airplane next to us like ripping over his corn and he walks over and he's like, That's cool. You're spraying my corn next year.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Chris suggested scraping farmland ownership data and visiting owners. Mike objected to flying over a property without permission; the suggested outreach method was not established as something Mike did.

ideas.delivery: The operator travels to the farm with heavy-lift drones and a trailer, mixes the farmer's selected chemical, fills the drone, and sprays the crop. The drone can follow automated missions, but a person must be present to supervise, refill tanks, swap batteries, and manage equipment. Mike says he avoids recommending chemicals.
unit_economics_claims: Mike claimed operating costs of $3 to $3.74 per acre and prices commonly between $10 and $20 per acre.
Mike claimed a $132,000 profit in 24 days and a separate $65,000 profit in eight days.
Mike said a 70% net margin was typical for the work he described; he said difficult rolling acres could produce 85% to 90% profit margins.
Mike said an example drone carries 26 gallons and can cover about 12 or 13 acres per load at two gallons per acre.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The operator needs spray equipment and a trailer; equipment purchase prices are not given.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated for an independent operator. The guest says one required FAA process can take three to four months; his separate Fastpass program may allow flying under his licensing in about ten days.

acquisition.how: Mike describes in-person farm visits and live demonstrations as the way to win customers. Software can help identify prospects, but it cannot perform the demonstration or close the relationship by itself.

onboarding.how: License checks, paperwork, understanding the farmer's fields and chosen product, and agreeing on application details require human coordination.

delivery.how: Automated flight missions handle much of the drone's route, but physical setup, chemical mixing, refilling, battery swaps, safety checks, and supervision require a person on site.

billing.how: Per-acre billing could be calculated from mapped acres and recorded work, but no automated billing system is described and a human would need to confirm completed work.

support.how: Farmers may need operational coordination, field-specific decisions, and a responsive operator; no automated support process is described.

uk_applicability.notes: Crop spraying and agricultural contractors exist in the UK, but the transcript's FAA certificates, US crop data, pricing, and operating assumptions do not transfer directly. UK aviation and pesticide rules would need to be followed.

risks: The service involves aircraft, pesticides, and heavy equipment, so licensing and compliance are central.
The guest says FAA authorization for heavy-lift spraying is difficult and that government processing can be slow.
Farmers may need to see the application work before buying; relying only on online discovery may not bring enough customers.
Season length, weather, crop type, field conditions, battery rotation, and repeat applications affect workload and revenue.
Mike advises not to recommend a farmer's chemical because a poor crop outcome could be blamed on both the product and the drone service.
The transcript's very high profit claims are the guest's own claims and are not independently verified.

quotes.speaker: Mike

ideas.name: Drone deer recovery service
ideas.one_liner: Use a thermal drone to locate deer that hunters shot but could not recover.
ideas.business_model: Per-recovery service fee, with a different stated fee depending on whether the deer is found.
ideas.customer: Hunters who have shot a deer and cannot locate it.
ideas.problem: Hunters may lose a wounded deer and want help finding it without walking through an area and disturbing other deer.
ideas.offer: Search the property with a thermal drone, identify a heat signature, and help the hunter recover the deer.

pricing.model: Per search, with a success-based price difference.

price_points.label: If the deer is not found

pricing.notes: Mike initially considered $250 to $350, then raised his stated prices after hearing feedback at an expo. He compared the service to a tracking dog that cost about $350.

acquisition_channels.details: Show thermal footage at the Northeast Ohio Sportsman Show using a simple booth, screen, sign, business cards, and magnets.

quote.text: I took that video to an outdoor show, a local outdoor show, and I just had a table with a cloth over it and an old iMac that I had.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Put flyers in local bow shops and rifle ranges; the flyers showed the drone, thermal view, and zoomed image.

quote.text: I printed off these brochures, like a a flyer, and I went to the local bow shops, uh local rifle ranges, that type of thing.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Hunters talked about the service with other hunters after seeing the demonstration or using it.

quote.text: And so once you got some people talking about it, they were just talking to their next people that they knew because yeah, word of mouth.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Mike started a YouTube channel alongside the service and used drone recovery content to publicize the category.

quote.text: when I came up with this business idea, it was part of the the whole thing. It was like, okay, this is my idea. I'm going to do it as a service, but I also want to create a YouTube channel.
quote.speaker: Mike

ideas.delivery: The operator flies a thermal drone over the relevant property, locates a heat signature, uses the zoom camera to identify it, and helps the hunter recover the animal. The transcript does not specify the full field workflow or how often the drone locates an animal.
unit_economics_claims: Mike said he made $50,000 during his first ten weeks of public deer recovery work in Ohio.
Mike stated a $550 fee if he found a deer and $450 if he did not.
Mike said a tracking dog cost about $350 and that customers paid a $200 premium for his service because it avoided disturbing other deer.
ideas.startup_cost: The guest bought a drone, but its price and other startup costs are not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Mike says he reached break-even within a couple of weeks and made $50,000 during his first ten weeks of public deer recovery work.

acquisition.how: Videos, listings, and search traffic can bring inbound enquiries, but the guest's launch depended on expo attendance, printed materials, and word of mouth.

onboarding.how: A person needs to understand the hunter's situation, confirm location and permissions, and coordinate a time to search.

delivery.how: A pilot must physically attend the property and operate or supervise a drone search.

billing.how: A booking and payment flow could be automated, but no billing system is described and the fee depends on the search result.

support.how: Hunters need human coordination around an urgent, location-specific search and recovery.

uk_applicability.notes: Thermal search and deer recovery could be relevant in the UK, but hunting practices, wildlife rules, land access, and drone regulations differ from Ohio and other US states.

risks: Mike says legality was unclear when he began and that he relied initially on an informal conversation with an Ohio natural resources official.
The service must not be used to locate a deer so that someone can then shoot it; the guest says the rules were later clarified in Ohio.
Mike says some hunters may take marginal shots because they expect a drone to find the deer.
A wounded deer may still be alive and could move after being found.

quotes.text: My first 10 weeks uh doing deer recovery just here in the state of Ohio, I made $50,000 in 10 weeks.
quotes.speaker: Mike

quotes.text: So yeah, it's $550 if I find your deer. If I don't find your deer, it's 450 bucks.
quotes.speaker: Mike

quotes.text: the biggest benefit of using a drone was yes, we hope that the deer has expired by the time we find it with the drone, but if it's not
quotes.speaker: Mike

ideas.name: Drone pilot locator directory
ideas.one_liner: List independent drone deer recovery pilots on a searchable website and charge them an annual subscription.
ideas.business_model: Annual listing subscription from independent pilots.
ideas.customer: Independent drone deer recovery pilots seeking enquiries and hunters looking for a nearby pilot.
ideas.problem: Hunters need to find a recovery pilot in their area, while independent pilots need visibility.
ideas.offer: A zip-code search on the Drone Deer Recovery website shows nearby listed pilots and lets visitors contact them.

pricing.notes: Mike calls the listing price super cheap. The host estimated six figures in annual memberships from the listing count; that is the host's back-of-the-envelope estimate.

acquisition_channels.details: Hunters search for drone deer recovery pilots and use the website's zip-code lookup.

quote.text: And people that search for deer recovery people in their area. If they're on the drone do recovery website, they put in their zip code.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: The guest's videos help drive attention and traffic to the directory.

quote.text: we're getting anywhere from 2.5 to 3 million views on YouTube, Tik Tok, Instagram. So maybe some of those weren't literally looking for a a pilot.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Mike says he drives traffic to listed pilots through the website and social content.

quote.text: It gives you a drop down of who's close by and then they just click on contact pilot and then it'll text them the phone number so we can track exactly how many people go to the website
quote.speaker: Mike

ideas.delivery: The site accepts pilot listings, takes a visitor's zip code, displays nearby operators, and provides a contact action that texts the pilot's phone number. Mike says the website tracks traffic and contact clicks.
unit_economics_claims: Mike charges $500 per year for a pilot listing.
Mike said there were about 200 to 300 pilots listed.
Chris estimated six figures in annual membership revenue; this was an inference, not a reported result.
tools: Website contact form or contact action

acquisition.how: Search traffic and existing video audiences can bring pilots and hunters to the site, though content and directory growth still need ongoing work.

onboarding.how: Pilot sign-up and listing details could be collected online; the transcript does not describe whether review or approval is manual.

delivery.how: The website's zip-code lookup, nearby pilot results, and contact action are software-delivered.

billing.how: An annual subscription is suited to recurring online billing, but no automatic renewal or payment workflow is stated.

support.how: Listing questions, disputes, and directory maintenance may require human help; no support system is described.

uk_applicability.notes: A searchable directory and subscription model work in the UK, but the number of operators, hunting market, and rules for drone use in wildlife recovery may differ.

risks: Mike says he did not trademark the three-word name early enough, after it had become generic language, and that similarly named businesses caused market confusion.
Directory value depends on traffic, accurate listings, and enough pilots in the areas where hunters search.
The host's six-figure revenue estimate is not a verified figure from Mike.

tactics.name: Launch a service with a simple live demonstration
steps: Buy or borrow a drone capable of producing useful thermal footage.
Film a simple demonstration on your own property, such as showing a thermal view and then identifying the subject with a zoom camera.
Display the footage at an event attended by likely customers.
Bring business cards and small takeaways; Mike says he ran out of both.

quote.text: Your like foray into the whole industry was to just take a low stakes video of your own property of some deer. That's it. Go to an expo with your target audience right there
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use customer feedback to set an initial price
steps: Ask potential customers what they expect the service to cost.
Treat feedback carefully when respondents may not be the buyer, but use specific comparisons to understand the value they see.
Mike initially considered $250 to $350, heard that the service was worth more, and later set a higher price with a different fee if no deer was found.

quote.text: And so I took all that info that they were giving me that I was like, Geez, maybe I start high, right? I can always come down.
quote.speaker: Mike

tactics.name: Place simple flyers where the target customer already goes
steps: Print a flyer with the equipment, thermal image, and corresponding zoomed image.
Ask local bow shops and rifle ranges if you can display it.
Use the flyer to explain an unfamiliar service visually.

quote.text: I printed off these brochures, like a a flyer, and I went to the local bow shops, uh local rifle ranges, that type of thing.
quote.speaker: Mike

tactics.name: Talk to the regulator and local enforcement before launching
steps: Ask the relevant state department how the intended drone use fits current rules.
Explain the service's purpose and boundaries.
Meet local game wardens and demonstrate the equipment.
Check the current written regulations rather than relying only on an informal conversation.

quote.text: I did talk to the the Ohio Department of Natural Resources head guy and told him what I planned on doing
quote.speaker: Mike

tactics.name: Build a niche directory around a service audience
steps: Let visitors enter a zip code and see nearby operators.
Give each operator a clear contact action.
Charge listed operators an annual subscription.
Use traffic and contact tracking to show operators the audience they receive.

quote.text: It gives you a drop down of who's close by and then they just click on contact pilot and then it'll text them the phone number so we can track exactly how many people go to the website
quote.speaker: Mike

tactics.name: Win farmers by demonstrating the result on their own crop
steps: Bring the trailer and equipment to the farm.
Ask permission to demonstrate with water over part of the crop.
Show the farmer the droplets on the plant and explain where the drone can spray.
Follow up on fields where conventional equipment has trouble reaching or operating.

quote.text: I take my rig, I go to his farm, I introduce myself, and I say, Hey, can I just show you how this works?
quote.speaker: Mike

tactics.name: Use agricultural co-ops as an introduction point
steps: Identify co-ops where local farmers buy seed and chemicals.
Visit with the drone and trailer visible.
Explain the service and show that the equipment is real and ready to work.

quote.text: I went to co-ops like where the farmers buy their seed and chemical from. So I showed up there with my drones and my trailer doing exactly what you said.
quote.speaker: Mike

tactics.name: Keep the product recommendation with the farmer
steps: Ask the farmer which chemical and application they want.
Apply the farmer's selected product rather than recommending a product outside your expertise.
Avoid having a poor product outcome become confused with the performance of the drone service.

quote.text: So, I'll just do what you you want me to spray.

tactics.name: Prepare licensing before buying into agricultural spraying
steps: Obtain the remote pilot certificate and the required state commercial pesticide applicator license.
Contact the equipment seller about the remaining paperwork for heavy-lift drone operations.
Ask how any temporary operating program works and confirm its eligibility and terms.

tactics.name: Protect time and delegate in deliberate seasons
steps: Set family and personal commitments as priorities on the calendar.
Batch email and text replies rather than responding to every notification immediately.
If a busy period requires extra work or travel, decide when that period ends and plan time off afterward.
Delegate tasks when the quality trade-off is acceptable.

warnings.warning: Do not rely only on informal legal advice for drone deer recovery. Mike says the rules were initially unclear, and he later met local game wardens and watched the regulations change.
Do not use a drone to locate a deer so that it can then be shot. Mike says the official he contacted supported recovery only, not using the drone to find and shoot the deer.
Chris's idea of flying a drone at a farmer's property without permission was challenged by Mike, who said he needed permission to fly over the land.
Mike says he waited too long to trademark Drone Deer Recovery; the phrase became generic and similarly named operators caused customer confusion.
Mike says he does not recommend farmers' chemicals because a poor result could lead them to blame both the product and the drone application.
The guest says heavy-lift spraying requires multiple licenses and FAA paperwork, and describes that process as difficult and slow.
Mike says some hunters may take marginal shots because they expect a drone to find the deer, creating an ethical concern.
The host's AI employee promotion for HighLevel and promotion of TKOowners.com are promotional segments, not evidence about the guest's drone business.

video.title: This Might Be the Easiest Way to Sell AI to Businesses

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates a GoHighLevel AI agent that texts people after a local service business misses their call, answers questions and helps book an estimate. He shows how to tailor and duplicate the workflow, then prospect for customers using scraped business phone numbers and ringless voicemail. The video pitches a $500–$2,000 monthly service and shows a callback asking about price, but no sale is closed. Its core lesson is to automate the first response and lead qualification while giving the business owner a way to take over.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; demonstrates the workflow and describes the offer.

ideas.name: AI missed-call text-back service for local businesses
ideas.one_liner: Set up a tailored AI SMS agent that responds to missed calls, answers basic questions, qualifies leads and helps book estimates.
ideas.business_model: Recurring monthly service fee per client; the video also describes a 90-day money-back offer.
ideas.customer: Small service businesses that receive customer calls, such as tree-trimming companies, plumbers and HVAC businesses.
ideas.problem: Businesses miss calls and callers may not call back. A static text-back message does not answer follow-up questions or move the caller toward an appointment.
ideas.offer: Configure a GoHighLevel workflow that detects a missed call, sends a tailored SMS, has an AI agent ask about the customer’s need and details, and routes qualified, urgent or unqualified contacts appropriately. The owner or an employee can take over the conversation.

pricing.model: Monthly fee per client; a 90-day payback guarantee is presented in the sales agent’s response.

price_points.label: Price stated in the sales conversation

pricing.notes: No setup fee is stated. The host says the service is offered with a refund if it does not pay for itself within 90 days. The demonstrated prospect asks about price, but the host says no sale has closed.

acquisition_channels.details: The host exports local business phone numbers from Outscraper, uploads them to a ringless voicemail service, and leaves a broad message asking the business to call back. The callback triggers the missed-call text-back workflow; the AI answers questions and flags hot leads for a human follow-up. The transcript does not establish that this outreach method is compliant for UK use.

quote.text: I went to outscraper.com. I typed in treeming businesses in Dallas, Texas. It gave me this info. And all I care about is the phone number.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The provider configures a GoHighLevel workflow and adapts its prompts and branches to the client’s trade. After setup, the software sends SMS messages, handles routine conversation, records lead details and sends owner notifications. The business owner or employee handles handoffs and carries out estimates and physical service work.
unit_economics_claims: The host states a target price range of $500–$2,000 per client per month.
The sales conversation states a $500 monthly price with a refund if the service does not pay for itself within 90 days.
The host reports no money received from the demonstrated prospecting test so far; the callback is not a closed sale.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The host mentions a GoHighLevel free trial; paid platform, phone and ringless-voicemail costs are not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. The demo generates a callback and price question, but no sale is closed.

acquisition.how: The demonstrated campaign uses software to send ringless voicemails, but a person selects and cleans the list, creates the recording and campaign, and closes interested leads. The UK legality and suitability of this outbound method are not established in the video.

onboarding.how: A human must gather the client’s services, coverage area, questions, phone setup and handoff rules, then adapt and verify the prompt and workflow. The workflow can be duplicated to reduce repeated setup.

delivery.how: Once configured, the agent can handle routine SMS conversations and qualify leads without the owner in each exchange. It sends notifications and supports a human takeover; the client still performs estimates and physical work.

billing.how: The video states monthly pricing but does not show invoicing, payment collection or subscription management.

support.how: The agent answers routine questions, but the owner or employee needs to handle emergencies, qualified leads and cases the bot cannot resolve. Ongoing client support is not described.

uk_applicability.notes: The missed-call response and appointment-qualification service can suit UK trades, but the video’s acquisition tactic uses ringless voicemail to numbers gathered from a business list, with no compliance discussion. summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates going from a physical product idea to a sourced product in one sitting, using the AI sourcing agent Accio (transcribed 'Axio'). He validates demand for a discreet 'porch pirate' parcel box via Google Trends, searches Accio in natural language, generates a tech pack, and compares supplier prices to Amazon listings. He claims a $27 sourced box sells for $143 on Amazon, about 75-80% gross margin and 20-30% net after shipping and fees. The video is sponsored by Accio, so the takeaway is that sourcing and validation tools make starting a physical product business faster, but the numbers are an unverified back-of-envelope demo.

summary: Kip Roland describes moving from Amazon resale to live auctions on Whatnot, then testing TikTok Shop. He explains how he sources liquidation goods, chooses items, runs streams, fulfills orders, and hires presenters, while sharing revenue, profit, audience, and staffing figures. The discussion also covers food, soccer jerseys, fashion, and other product categories, with warnings about testing returns, buying too emotionally, and handling fulfillment. His main advice is to buy with the numbers, find products with high perceived value, start with low-cost inventory, and build an audience around the presenter.

tactics.name: Research the live format before buying stock
steps: Watch top sellers in the category and note their formats and presentation.
When a stream loses your attention, ask whether the host, product, or price point caused it.
Check whether the category is already represented and look for products viewers have not seen on the platform.

quote.text: I looked at the top sellers. I looked at the formats that they were selling.
quote.speaker: Kip Roland

tactics.name: Buy with math and sell with emotion
steps: Set a maximum purchase cost using expected bids, fees, shipping, defects, and returns.
Avoid bidding emotionally on brands just because they look attractive or perform for another seller.
Prefer low-cost inventory with high perceived value and room for multiple bids.

quote.text: Buy with math, sell with emotion. Buy with math, sell with emotion.
quote.speaker: Kip Roland

tactics.name: Test and grade returned inventory
steps: Test appliances before selling when practical.
Grade condition and completeness consistently; the guest used grades such as A, S tier, and C tier.
Do not describe an item as working unless it has been tested to that level.
Refund a buyer when an undiscovered fault, such as a leaking coffee maker, is reported.

quote.text: I kind of had to systemize it like, you know, is it A grade? Is it S tier? Is it C tier? Is all the parts here?
quote.speaker: Kip Roland

tactics.name: Start with low-cost, high-perceived-value products
steps: Prioritize products buyers can recognize as valuable in a short auction.
Start some items at $1 to create immediate engagement.
Avoid paying a premium for a brand buyers do not recognize or value.

quote.text: Focus on those high perceived value items. And with that kitchen electronic show, man, that that I learned that so much.
quote.speaker: Kip Roland

tactics.name: Use small tests and audience bookmarks before expanding categories
steps: Ask viewers whether they want to see a new product category.
Put the planned show on the account and ask interested viewers to bookmark it.
Use bookmark interest as a signal before buying a new lot.
Review returning and new buyer proportions after the test.

quote.text: So, I had enough people bookmark it, I'm like, 'Okay, let's go make this purchase.'
quote.speaker: Kip Roland

tactics.name: Plan fulfillment before going live
steps: Estimate how many items the show may sell and make sure storage, packing supplies, and labor can handle it.
Prepare a repeatable packing process before running long or frequent shows.
Use the platform's integrated shipping labels when available.

quote.text: So think about those creative things to get those bids a little bit higher and then also help people overcome that shipping objection early.
quote.speaker: Kip Roland

tactics.name: Reduce shipping friction with bundles
steps: Bundle small, low-cost items so the buyer pays shipping on a higher-value order.
Consider adding a small extra item when it raises perceived value and encourages bidding.
Explain the bundle early in the show to address the buyer's shipping objection.

quote.text: Well, let's bundle five of them together. So, now you're paying $6 in shipping for a $15 item.
quote.speaker: Kip Roland

tactics.name: Hire presenters for product interest and coachability
steps: Look for someone who naturally likes the product category and can present it authentically.
Give feedback based on show performance and treat it as a chance to improve, not a personal criticism.
Keep product cost and margin pressure with the owner rather than passing it to the presenter.
The guest's stated pay model was $17 per hour plus 1% commission.

steps: Do not copy the most visible sellers automatically.
Try a product that is distinct, obtainable at a good cost, and has a plausible audience.
Compare the net amount received after platform fees and shipping with the sourcing cost.
Repeat only if the result and sourcing are workable.

video.title: He Turned $400 Into $2.5M Using AI (No Coding)

summary: John Cheney describes starting Gen AIPI with about $400 and winning an enterprise customer after building an initial AI assessment product. The business shifted from automated tests and courses to AI strategy, staff training, and ongoing implementation for larger companies. Cheney says he reached about $2.5 million in annual recurring revenue and describes a path toward larger recurring contracts, while emphasizing direct sales, public progress updates, and coaching clients to build their own solutions. The service relies on substantial human selling and consulting, so its current model is not close to unattended operation.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office.

speakers.name: John Cheney
speakers.description: Founder of the General AI Proficiency Institute, also called Gen AIPI.

ideas.name: Gen AIPI: AI strategy, training, and implementation for businesses
ideas.one_liner: Help owner-led companies understand AI, train employees, and install or manage AI systems that improve operations.
ideas.business_model: Initially one-off assessment and training, then monthly fractional chief AI officer and AI system implementation retainers.
ideas.customer: Mostly larger businesses without a CTO or someone driving technology; Cheney says most customers are around $20 million to $30 million in annual revenue.
ideas.problem: Companies use AI lightly or not at all, lack the expertise to identify useful applications, and often have manual work or weak operational data.
ideas.offer: AI readiness assessment, executive strategy, employee education, process transformation, dashboards, and ongoing installation or management of AI systems. Cheney later emphasized coaching client employees to build their own solutions.

pricing.model: One-off assessment and training, followed by monthly retainers or system management packages.

price_points.label: Package described as roughly 12 to 15 hours of service per month
Price mentioned for a one-call close
Package described as roughly 50 to 60 hours of service per month

pricing.notes: Cheney says he initially priced by headcount, then by packages and hours, and more recently shifted toward installing and managing systems.

acquisition_channels.details: Cheney says he began calling businesses and continued after closing his first customer. For UK use, calls need appropriate TPS/CTPS screening.
He messaged people he knew who owned companies; after about six messages, one prospect asked for a call and bought.
He publicly posted progress on LinkedIn and recommended posting about work on personal Facebook or LinkedIn, even with a small audience.
He says many later deals came through referrals and that referral prospects were often close to buying before the call.

ideas.delivery: Cheney first delivered local assessments and in-person training, then also ran Zoom training for groups of employees. He described connecting company systems through APIs, building executive dashboards and agent workflows, and coaching client staff. He started solo using AI tools and a few contractors, then says he hired a full-time team.
unit_economics_claims: Cheney says the business cost about $400 to start and secured a $15,000 customer by the following Tuesday.
He says revenue reached about $180,000 over roughly six weeks and annual recurring revenue was about $2.5 million after a little over a year.
He says the first million in revenue had almost 100% profit, largely because the main cost was his time.
He describes monthly packages from $10,000 to $25,000, with different service-hour allocations.
ideas.startup_cost: About $400, including a domain, email, Stripe setup, and credits.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: He started on a Thursday, finished the initial product in about three days, and says his first customer signed by the following Tuesday.

acquisition.how: Agents can research and qualify company leads and prepare outreach, but the described sales process depends on human calls, relationship building, and closing. In the UK, software must not send unsolicited marketing messages to individuals or sole traders without consent; cold calls need TPS/CTPS screening.

onboarding.how: Online assessments, intake forms, and scheduling could be automated, with human review needed to understand company priorities and scope work.

delivery.how: Agents and integrations can automate reporting and repeatable workflows, but strategy, training, system design, and coaching still require people.

billing.how: Monthly invoices and payment collection can run through billing software, while humans still set terms and resolve exceptions.

support.how: Agents can answer routine questions and track tasks, but ongoing consulting and troubleshooting require a knowledgeable person.

uk_applicability.notes: The B2B service can transfer to UK firms, but outreach rules and handling client data need to reflect UK requirements. The transcript describes a US operation and does not discuss UK delivery.

risks: A high-touch consulting and training offer depends on expert staff and may not run almost entirely without human involvement.
Cheney warns that promising to build many custom processes can turn the offer into a dev shop with ongoing maintenance obligations.
AI outputs, integrations, and client data need review, security controls, and clear ownership.
The transcript gives self-reported growth figures and does not independently verify them.

tactics.name: Build a quick first version to test an idea
steps: Use an AI coding tool to turn a written proposal or problem description into a working prototype.
Set a short build window and test whether the core experience works before committing to a large development budget.
Cheney says his own initial build took about three days; treat his timing and cost as a personal claim, not a universal estimate.

quote.text: I just dragged it into Replet and said, "Build this." And like 20 minutes later, it was built.
quote.speaker: John Cheney

tactics.name: Find prospects and call them
steps: Use a research assistant to identify 20 businesses in a target area and gather decision-maker details.
Call prospects and keep doing outreach after the first sale.
For UK prospecting, screen cold calls against TPS/CTPS and do not use unsolicited marketing texts or DMs to individuals or sole traders without consent.

quote.text: Really what you can do is you can go on to something like Manis right and just say hey find me 20 customers
quote.speaker: John Cheney

tactics.name: Use a concise AI readiness pitch to start conversations
steps: Contact business owners you know and explain that you can measure employee AI readiness.
Offer to build a plan to help the company adopt AI.
Ask for a call, then scope the customer's needs and quote a paid package.

quote.text: I'm measuring, you know, I want I can measure all your employees, see how good they are at AI and, you know, then kind of build a plan
quote.speaker: John Cheney

tactics.name: Show progress publicly to create trust and inbound interest
steps: Post what you are building and what you are learning on LinkedIn or a personal Facebook page.
Do not wait for a large audience; explain your work in plain language.
Use personal interests as well as work topics to give potential customers a way to connect.

quote.text: The best way to get no customers, the best way is to make sure nobody knows what you're doing.
quote.speaker: John Cheney

tactics.name: Convert one-off training into an ongoing retainer
steps: Listen for a customer who wants continuing help after an initial training engagement.
Offer a recurring fractional chief AI officer service with follow-up and ongoing business impact work.
Explain the fee against the customer's potential cost savings or revenue impact.

quote.text: I don't like the idea of you just coming in and teaching us and then being gone. Like do you have a model where you'd kind of stick around?
quote.speaker: John Cheney

tactics.name: Structure the sales conversation around strategy, transformation, and education
steps: Discuss how AI could affect the customer's industry and competitors.
Ask which tasks or roles the customer wants to improve or hire for, then show a practical automation example and its possible ROI.
Explain how employee training could improve productivity after process changes are in place.

quote.text: we really help in three ways, right? We want to help you with strategy, right? To figure out how your industry is going to be affected
quote.speaker: John Cheney

tactics.name: Coach clients to build their own solutions
steps: Work alongside the employee who owns the problem instead of selling only custom code.
Help the client get an early, satisfying result so they feel capable of building more.
Let the client do the implementation work and provide support when they get stuck.

quote.text: The best customers we have, they're vibe coding their own solutions, right? They're they're director of operations
quote.speaker: John Cheney

tactics.name: Create an early win in training
steps: Start a class with a fun, simple build such as a small game.
Let learners change the output and see that plain-language instructions can create something usable.
Use the early success to build confidence before introducing more work-focused applications.

quote.text: The first thing we're gonna do here is we're gonna open up Ched PT or Grock or something and we're gonna vibe code a game.

tactics.name: Use referrals to shorten the sales process
steps: Ask referred prospects about their business and where they see room for help.
Connect the offer to the trusted referrer's experience and move to a close sooner when fit is already established.

steps: Begin with a CEO's need to see the business clearly.
Connect relevant business systems through APIs and build a dashboard that can answer questions and generate reports.
Use the work to identify further process improvements and repeatable tasks.

video.title: How AI Makes Facebook Marketplace a Gold Mine

summary: Chris Koerner pitches many ways to make money from Facebook Marketplace, then demos no-code scraping of listings with Oxylabs' AI Scraper (prompting a JSON schema, exporting CSV to Google Sheets, scheduling via Zapier). Ideas include an arbitrage sniper, deal feeds and alert tools for resellers, lead generation for local businesses, a 'gone wild' media account and niche 'radar' micro-SaaS. He also shares a second-hand story of a friend flipping sheds for $600k/yr net. Key takeaway: scrape public Marketplace data to be first on underpriced deals or sell the data/alerts to resellers and local businesses.

video.title: They Banned My $35K/Month Page So I Started a Business

summary: Host Chris Koerner describes losing a Facebook page that had generated substantial income, then launching Plans of Grandeur by selling previously unpublished creator training to his newsletter. He tests prices and email formats with randomized subscriber groups, takes payment through Stripe, and later organizes the material in a community. He reports that the launch generated tens of thousands of dollars in revenue and profit, while presenting his process as a repeatable way to sell useful content to an existing audience. The video also discusses his former creator consulting, Facebook monetization, newsletter tutorials, and small-list sales of courses and events.

acquisition.how: An opted-in newsletter can be segmented, emailed, and measured with software. UK marketing rules still require a valid basis to email subscribers and functioning unsubscribe handling.

onboarding.how: Stripe can take payment and redirect buyers to the materials; tagging and invitations can be automated. The transcript describes manual setup and some manual community invitations.

tactics.name: Start from an unfair advantage
steps: List assets or experience that give you a useful starting point, such as a newsletter, work history, or knowledge of an industry.
Choose an offer that can be sold to people you already understand or can reach through that advantage.

quote.text: Anytime anyone starts a business, you need to go to your unfair advantage. Everyone has an unfair advantage.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Randomize the list before an email price test
steps: Export active subscribers and put the addresses in Google Sheets.
Add a RAND formula, sort the list by the random values, then split the randomized rows into groups.
Keep the sample below 10% of the full list so the initial lower-price test does not reach too many subscribers.
Tag and segment each group, and exclude unsubscribed subscribers.

quote.text: So, I want to perfectly randomize this list because what I'm about to do is what's called an AB test or a split test.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Test price with the same email and different payment links
steps: Create the same one-time offer at $47 and $97.
Send identical emails to randomized groups, changing only the payment link and price.
Compare the revenue and conversion results, and allow time for higher-priced purchases to arrive.
Repeat tests when results are uncertain before sending the selected offer to the rest of the list.

quote.text: If I send both of those identical emails, it's the same email, same subject, same wording, same everything. The only thing that's different is the payment link with the price, right?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Reduce checkout friction
steps: Use a direct payment link and avoid asking for information already held in the subscriber list.
Do not add optional fields unless the value of collecting that data justifies the conversion cost.
Check that the payment link is one-time rather than recurring and test the link before sending.

quote.text: The more friction you add to the checkout process, the more your conversion rate will drop.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Build the presale offer from existing assets
steps: Inventory training videos, spreadsheets, documents, and guides that already exist.
Describe the outcome the material supports and bundle it as a practical library.
State what future material and live sessions buyers will receive, and make the one-time lifetime terms clear.

quote.text: I have a treasure trove of videos, spreadsheets, and docs in my Google Drive account that has never been published.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Segment and send the test campaigns
steps: Import each randomized CSV group into the newsletter platform and add a separate tag.
Build dynamic segments from the tags and filter to active subscribers.
Duplicate the email so the copy stays consistent, change the link and price, then send each version to its assigned group.
Exclude prior test groups from later campaigns to avoid sending the same offer repeatedly.

quote.text: We want to AB test the entire email which I think you can do in Beehive as well but I haven't learned it yet so I'm not trying to learn it right friction momentum time kills all deals etc.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: State the price in the email
steps: Compare a price-disclosed email with one that hides the price, using separate payment links to track sales.
Koerner reports that the disclosed-price version converted better in his test and chose to show the price in later emails.

quote.text: So the lesson, tell them the price in the email.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Organize delivery after validating sales
steps: Start with an existing file folder and a payment redirect to deliver the material.
After purchases arrive, organize the materials into clear folders in a community platform.
Invite buyers and provide a short walkthrough video.

quote.text: So, we basically downloaded all of the Google Drive content and uploaded it here uh into separate folders.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use a small list to test, then scale the winning email
steps: Use a small randomized sample to test price, copy length, and payment destination.
Track each payment link and email campaign separately.
Send the best-performing version to subscribers who have not received the earlier tests.

quote.text: After a few more AB tests, I'm going to know exactly what people need. And then I'll send the right price with the right messaging to everyone on my newsletter.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

video.title: He Asked AI To Make Money. It Did.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Robbie, a non-technical operations employee who gave an OpenClaw AI agent ('Ron') $100 and 90 days to make money, inspired by the 2023 HustleGPT experiment. Ron's first idea (SWOT analysis gigs on Fiverr) failed for lack of visibility, but Ron scraped 200 TikTok comments from people wanting their own Ron. Robbie then launched 'AI Co-Founder Club', hosted containerised OpenClaw agents on rented Contabo servers, took $10 pre-orders and converted them to $29/month memberships. He claims about $8.4k MRR after 13 days with ~$2.6k monthly costs. Key takeaway: document the build publicly, validate with paid pre-orders, and sell to the audience your experiment attracts.

video.title: He Turns Abandoned Driving Ranges Into Cash Machines

summary: Chris Koerner visits Golf Ranch in Richardson, Dallas, whose founding team (ex-Topgolf and long-time paid-ads operator) buys dated or abandoned driving ranges and modernises them. They upgraded ball and mat quality based on customer surveys, added covered bays, lights to midnight, music, string lights and a putting green, and replaced prepaid bucket cards with a $20/month Ranch Pass membership (40% off buckets); they now have 8,000 members across four sites and claim an LTV:CAC of about 10. Volume at this site went from about 3.5 million to 12 million balls a year. The key takeaway is that an old, underserved industry with a low bar can be won by listening to customers, a membership loop, loss-leader amenities and modern digital marketing; the goal is 50 sites and 100,000 members.

video.title: The Simplest $7M Business You've Never Heard Of

summary: Michael Clark describes how he and his wife built The Flower Letters, a business that sends serialized stories and illustrated extras by post. They started with Instagram and Facebook ads, built an email list, and now sell multiple stories through monthly and prepaid subscriptions, gift products, and some retail placement. Clark credits prepaid plans, repeat and gift buyers, and continued investment in marketing and new stories, while describing high manual fulfillment needs and seasonal peaks. The host also explores other postal subscription ideas and shares his wife’s planned recipe-by-mail club.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; also pitches side ideas and narrates the introduction.

speakers.name: Michael Clark
speakers.description: Co-founder and CEO of The Flower Letters.

ideas.name: The Flower Letters
ideas.one_liner: A mailed subscription that delivers an illustrated, serialized story in letters and themed inserts.
ideas.business_model: Monthly or prepaid annual subscriptions, with one-off sales of tins and other add-ons.
ideas.customer: Primarily women aged 35 and older, including people buying a sentimental gift for a mother, sister, friend, or themselves.
ideas.problem: Customers want a distinctive, giftable experience and something enjoyable to look forward to; buyers also want stories and gifts that feel personal.
ideas.offer: Two sequential story letters a month for a year, with artwork and varying inserts such as postcards, bookmarks, and era-related items. Customers can choose from several story subscriptions, mostly historical fiction, plus fantasy.

pricing.model: Monthly subscription or prepaid annual story; one-off add-ons and shipping may be charged separately.

price_points.label: Shipping when charged; free shipping is used in some promotions

pricing.notes: Clark says the annual prepaid option is attractive to customers and reduces reliance on conventional month-to-month subscription billing. The transcript mentions other possible add-ons, but gives no prices for them.

acquisition_channels.details: Facebook and Instagram ads became the main acquisition channel. They started testing ads with small spends after launching; an early marketing collaborator later ran the ads. Clark says the current acquisition cost is much higher than in the early days.

quote.text: So early on we started trying to acquire email addresses and so we can connect with people that way.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

acquisition_channels.details: The founders created a Flower Letters Instagram account and posted the product. Clark says the company initially got sign-ups after putting the offer out; his wife had previously sold paintings through her own Instagram.

quote.text: No, we just we started a flower letters Instagram, put it out.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

acquisition_channels.details: Clark says customers refer friends and that a loyal customer base is excited to try new stories.

quote.text: A lot of people referred this to their friends.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

acquisition_channels.details: The website asks visitors for an email address in exchange for a discount. The email list is used for campaigns, including win-back campaigns for previous customers.

quote.text: That's the first sort of on-site funnel is you ask for their email address for a discount.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: The company has a product in the Newport Mansions gift shops. Clark describes Costco placement as an aspiration, not a confirmed channel.

quote.text: One of their the person that runs their gift shop signed up, reached out like, "What if you wrote a story about the Gilded Age and we could put it in our shops?" We were like, "Yeah, that's totally cool."
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

ideas.delivery: Hanny writes the stories and creates the art and inserts; Clark handles the business. A team in a Utah warehouse handles each item and stuffs the letters by hand before mailing them. They built a redemption website for retail gift purchases where buyers scan a QR code and enter an address.
unit_economics_claims: Monthly price is $12; prepaid annual price is $100.
Materials and postage-related contents cost about $2 to $3 at their volume, according to Clark.
Early customer acquisition cost was roughly $15 to $20; Clark says it later rose to $40 to $50.
Clark reports annual churn of about 5% and lifetime value of about $180 across 12 months.
Clark says email drives 38% to 50% of revenue at times.
The company spent $2.6 million on Meta advertising last year, according to Clark.
tools: Retail redemption website and QR codes
Unnamed subscription software for monthly billing
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated as a specific amount; the host describes the initial launch as having almost no money.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated precisely. The first letters were sent at the end of August; the host says the business reached about $36,000 in monthly recurring revenue within its first four months.

acquisition.how: Paid social campaigns, website email capture, and email win-back campaigns can be run with agents and routine human review. Creative, audience choices, ad spend, and UK-compliant email consent still need oversight.

onboarding.how: A website can collect orders and addresses, and the retail redemption flow uses a QR code and web form. Exceptions and gift recipient details may need human help.

delivery.how: Writing and illustrating the stories are creative work, and staff handle and hand-stuff physical letters. Agents can assist with planning or operational analysis but cannot perform the core physical fulfillment.

billing.how: Online monthly billing can use subscription software, but Clark says annual prepaid subscriptions are handled through their own process rather than subscription software.

support.how: Agents could answer routine order questions, but the company promises to make problems right and Clark describes calling upset customers, so sensitive cases need a person.

uk_applicability.notes: A serialized postal gift subscription can work in the UK. The business would need UK postage and fulfillment economics, applicable VAT and consumer rules, and UK-specific seasonal planning. Email acquisition should use appropriate consent or another valid UK basis; the transcript's Utah warehouse and US ad costs do not transfer directly.

risks: Every letter must arrive in the right order for the story to work; missed or confusing contents can undermine the promise.
Writing a complete serialized story is harder to produce and operate than a standalone monthly letter.
The business has sharp seasonal peaks, especially around Mother's Day, and needs enough fulfillment capacity and staffing.
Meta ad costs have risen substantially from the early acquisition costs Clark reports.
Physical fulfillment remains labor-intensive and exposed to postage, supply, and staffing constraints.
An insert was removed after the team learned that customers found it offensive.
Gift recipients may dislike the product, prompting the purchaser to cancel.
Reliance on paid Meta acquisition creates platform and margin risk; Clark says email is important as an owned audience.
