tactics.name: Validate with real customers, not only friends and family
steps: Put the offer in front of people outside the founders' immediate family and friends.
Use sign-ups and purchases from people who fit the target market as evidence of interest.
Avoid treating supportive family purchases as proof that the product has found its customer.

quote.text: If you're launching a product or service, don't tell your family and friends. They'll give you a false positive.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Start with a small paid-social test
steps: Launch the product page and initial social presence.
Test Facebook and Instagram ads with small spends.
Track customer acquisition cost and bring in someone with advertising skills when the early tests show promise.

quote.text: October, we started dabbling in ads, just spending a few bucks here and there and people started showing up.
quote.speaker: Michael Clark

tactics.name: Capture email addresses from paid traffic
steps: Send website visitors to an on-site email form.
Offer a discount in exchange for an email address.
Use the list for customer communication and win-back campaigns, and treat consent and UK direct-marketing rules as part of the setup.

tactics.name: Make prepaid annual plans attractive
steps: Offer a prepaid annual story alongside monthly billing.
Set the annual price so buyers see a lower monthly equivalent.

Give a customer options to choose another story rather than relying only on one story renewing.

tactics.name: Use win-back campaigns for completed or inactive customers

video.title: How to Make $1.6K/Day on Facebook Marketplace

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Matt (Jackson, Michigan), a former high school math teacher who started flipping couches, appliances and church pews on Facebook Marketplace/Craigslist, then moved to riding and zero-turn lawnmowers. He claims $20-30K profit in his first summer, quit teaching, built a helper network (drivers, a mechanic, 'Family of Flippers'), sourced volume from dealers who dislike used stock, and now runs a Toro/Bad Boy etc. equipment dealership with a best month of $1.1M. The episode is heavy on tactics: speed to lead, deposits, negotiation (make the seller name the number first), outsourcing driving first, and calling dealers for under-advertised used inventory. Key takeaway: the edge is buying underpriced at speed and selling at market value, not fixing items.

video.title: Stop Buying Things. Start Buying Assets that Pay for Themselves

summary: Chris Koerner interviews David (Fort Wayne, Indiana), a 'multipreneur' running several small rental businesses. He details a tote (moving box) rental business sold via a realtor gifting subscription, a travel-trailer (RV) rental business that made about $7,000 net in its first season, and a side-hustle recording/video studio. The takeaway is that small rental businesses need little capital, reuse the same asset repeatedly, and can be validated by asking existing operators and using marketplaces as lead-gen before moving customers to your own site.

video.title: How I Use Web Scraping to Find Products That Sell for 20x the Price

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates how to use the Oxylabs web scraper API (his sponsor) to scrape Amazon best-seller lists in three categories (pet accessories, household/health, children's education books), then analyse them in Google Sheets and Claude to find products with strong sales rank but low review counts. He then finds near-identical products on Alibaba via image search and works through landed-cost and Amazon fee maths (about 30% net margin claimed on a cat feeder). He adds extra screening tactics: one-star test, fee-tier size shrinking, variations, rating distribution, Google Trends, Amazon Choice badges. Key takeaway: pick Amazon products by data (rank vs review mismatch) rather than personal interest, but the margin maths is rough and the evidence is promotional.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; says he has imported from Alibaba/AliExpress for 17 years; Oxylabs sponsor affiliate

ideas.name: Amazon FBA product arbitrage using scraped best-seller data (Alibaba sourcing)
ideas.one_liner: Scrape Amazon best-seller lists, find products with high sales rank but few reviews, source a near-identical item from Alibaba and sell it via FBA.
ideas.business_model: One-off product sales on Amazon; margin between Alibaba landed cost and Amazon price less FBA fees
ideas.customer: Amazon shoppers in the chosen marketplace (US .com in the demo)
ideas.problem: Most Amazon sellers pick products by personal interest rather than data, so they enter saturated or low-margin niches.
ideas.offer: A copy or slightly improved version of an under-reviewed best-selling product (e.g. a bundled gravity-fed cat feeder and water dispenser), differentiated by colour, material or size.

pricing.model: Match competitor price on Amazon, or slightly under

price_points.label: Stainless paper towel holder Amazon price

pricing.notes: Leave extra margin for Amazon ads

acquisition_channels.details: Amazon search ranking; seller aims to take the position of a product with few reviews. First listing image is stressed as critical; use lifestyle photos not Alibaba stock photos. Fewer returns boost ranking. Amazon ads suggested.

quote.text: I cannot emphasize enough how important that first image is on your Amazon listing.

video.title: The Easiest $3K/Day Business Nobody Is Talking About

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Sariah (27, Utah), who started Memory Magnets Co with under $1,000 in 2024 after her husband's low pay and second job left the family broke. She sells custom photo magnets online, at markets and as an on-the-spot wedding/event service, and sells magnet-making machine kits plus refill supplies and courses. She claims $1.63M online revenue in her first full year (about $600K profit), a $233K best month and a $100.5K first six-figure month after six months. Key takeaway: a simple, high-margin physical product plus a service at price-insensitive events (weddings), marketed through short-form video, grew fast, and teaching others to copy the model became a second revenue line.

video.title: The Most Overlooked $13K/Day Business Anyone Can Start

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Hunter about starting a parking-lot maintenance business with line striping, then adding seal coating and crack filling. Hunter describes learning with a small free job, finding customers through local Facebook posts and email, and growing from small striping jobs to larger contracts. He shares pricing, equipment costs, job economics, and the physical work involved. The main takeaway is that low-cost striping can open the door to higher-value maintenance work, but delivery still requires people, equipment, and attention to weather and job conditions.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office.

speakers.name: Hunter
speakers.description: Parking-lot striping and asphalt maintenance operator; surname not stated.

ideas.name: Parking-lot line striping
ideas.one_liner: Repaint parking lines, symbols, and directional markings for churches and other businesses.
ideas.business_model: Per-line and per-stencil job pricing, with a minimum charge; striping can lead to seal-coating and crack-filling work.
ideas.customer: Churches and other businesses with parking lots that need new or refreshed lines and markings.
ideas.problem: Faded, missing, or poorly aligned parking lines and markings make a lot look neglected and can make it harder to use.
ideas.offer: Repaint parking stalls, handicapped symbols, arrows, fire lanes, and no-parking areas. Hunter sometimes covers poor old markings and gives a small number of blue handicapped symbols as a free extra.

pricing.model: Per line, per stencil or marked area, with a minimum job price.
pricing.notes: Hunter said travel and hard-to-see lines that need to be realigned can raise his per-line price. He said he quotes some stencils at $10 or $25. The transcript also includes a $760 quote for a particular church lot and estimates for materials and labor.

acquisition_channels.details: Hunter bought scraped prospect lists from a contractor on Upwork and emailed churches and businesses. His message said he was new, would offer a good price, and wanted to make the church look good for Christmas. He said he sent about 50 emails on his first day and around 300 total in an early campaign.

quote.text: So email I I work with a guy overseas just on Upwork found him and I pay him five or six bucks for a list that he provides.
quote.speaker: Hunter

acquisition_channels.details: He posted in his town's Facebook page asking people to vote for a business that should get a new lot. He used the free job to get his name in front of local business owners and then contacted nominated businesses about paid work.

quote.text: So, I went on Facebook, made a post in our town's page, and just said, "Hey, I'd love to help out a business. Vote below for for who you want to see have a new lot."
quote.speaker: Hunter

acquisition_channels.details: He tried door knocking but found it was not the best use of his time. He also preferred to meet prospects in person to quote jobs when possible; he said his close rate was better in person.

quote.text: So, I I did go door knocking. That was hard. It didn't feel like it was the best use of my time, so I yeah, jumped into email.
quote.speaker: Hunter

ideas.delivery: Hunter practices on an old lot with water, then does a small free nonprofit job before taking paid work. He visits sites to quote when possible, measures and prices the lines and stencils, and applies water-based paint with a striping machine. A roller and paint can be used when machine access is unavailable, but require more taping and time. Hunter said he sometimes hires help when work exceeds his capacity.
unit_economics_claims: Hunter said he spent $5 on paint for his first small free job.
He quoted one church $1,190, later completed a similar church job for around $1,000 to $1,200, and said his first month brought just over $2,800.
Hunter said first-month profit was about 75% because he did the work himself.
A particular church lot with 82 parking stalls was quoted at $760; Hunter estimated about $130 in materials and Chris estimated about $200 in total costs and $550 in profit.
Hunter said his minimum job price had risen to $500.
tools: Graco line striping machine, models 3400 and 3900
ideas.startup_cost: Hunter said he started the business with just over $3,000. He described a lower-cost roller-and-paint route, but the transcript gives different figures: Chris mentioned a $10 roller, while Hunter later said rollers cost $20. Hunter bought a used striping machine for $2,300 and a stencil pack for $800.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Hunter first practiced with water, did a small nonprofit lot for free, then obtained paid work through email.

acquisition.how: Lead-list preparation and email drafting could be assisted by software, but targeting, replies, site visits, and in-person sales require human judgment. In-person selling caps practical automation.

onboarding.how: A form could collect site details, but someone still needs to inspect the lot, assess faded lines and stencils, and confirm the quote.

delivery.how: People must prepare the site and physically paint the lines and markings.

billing.how: Quote IQ can prepare quotes; routine invoicing could be automated, though Hunter said many church customers pay by check.

support.how: Agents could answer routine scheduling and quote questions, but complaints and site-specific changes need a person.

uk_applicability.notes: The service transfers to UK car parks, but markings, accessible-bay requirements, insurance, and site-safety practices need to fit UK rules and customer expectations. UK cold-email rules allow unsolicited marketing to corporate subscribers, but not to individuals or sole traders without consent; prospect lists must be screened accordingly.

risks: Door knocking was a poor use of Hunter's time.
Church board approval took a couple of weeks, delaying paid work.
A used machine required replacement parts and learning how to repair it.
Hunter said he spilled two gallons of paint in his minivan.
Faded or misaligned lines can take longer and cost more to fix than a simple repaint.
Work is weather-sensitive; Hunter described a rush to finish before it got too cold.
Unsolicited UK marketing email must follow PECR; avoid sending to individuals or sole traders without consent.

ideas.name: Parking-lot seal coating
ideas.one_liner: Apply a protective asphalt coating to extend the life and improve the appearance of parking lots.
ideas.business_model: Per-square-foot job pricing, with larger projects often sold alongside striping.
ideas.customer: Churches and other owners or operators of asphalt parking lots.
ideas.problem: Asphalt deteriorates and looks worn; sealing is intended to protect the pavement and make it look better.
ideas.offer: Spray a thin layer of asphalt seal coating over a prepared parking lot. Hunter added this service after customers asking for striping also requested seal-coating quotes.

pricing.notes: The $9,000-plus lot quote is an example, not a universal price. The speakers discussed labor and profit estimates for that example.

acquisition_channels.details: Hunter said customers who first wanted striping also asked for seal-coating quotes. He added the service because he found that subcontractors were busy or unsuitable.

quote.text: I started when I would go meet these these people to give them quotes. I I would try to always go in person and they always wanted striping and sealing.
quote.speaker: Hunter

acquisition_channels.details: Hunter's email outreach targeted churches and businesses for parking-lot work, which created opportunities to quote sealing as well as striping.

quote.text: So email I I work with a guy overseas just on Upwork found him and I pay him five or six bucks for a list that he provides.
quote.speaker: Hunter

ideas.delivery: Hunter tows a 275-gallon tank and spray system behind a truck and sprays the asphalt surface. The work takes a full day for the example lot. He said he uses two workers for some jobs and charges 50% upfront because material costs are higher. Freshly sealed pavement may require more careful striping and chalk-line layout afterward.
unit_economics_claims: Hunter quoted just over $9,000 to seal a 46,900-square-foot lot.
He said material cost was about $0.06 per square foot and his selling price was usually $0.15 to $0.25 per square foot.
For the example lot, Chris estimated around $3,000 in material, two workers at $300 each, and about $4,500 profit; Hunter agreed the job could have about a 50% net margin after overhead.
Hunter said his best one-day seal-coating job brought in $13,000; striping the same site was done the next day for $1,700.
He said a large church job was worth $26,000.
ideas.startup_cost: Hunter bought a used seal-coating trailer with a tank and pump for $6,000. He did not state the total cost of starting this service.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Hunter took a seal-coating job after customers began requesting quotes; he said he drove three hours to collect equipment for an early job.

acquisition.how: Existing striping customers can be identified in a CRM, but site visits, quoting, and relationship-based sales remain human work.

onboarding.how: Satellite measurements can help estimate area, but site condition, preparation, access, and scope need human review.

delivery.how: Workers must tow equipment, prepare the site, spray the coating, and manage the physical job.

billing.how: Invoices and 50% deposit requests can be automated, but payment timing and job completion need human oversight.

support.how: Automated scheduling and routine updates are feasible; site problems and customer decisions need a person.

uk_applicability.notes: Commercial asphalt lots exist in the UK, but material specifications, local climate, waste handling, site safety, and customer expectations need local adaptation. Weather affects when work can be done. UK cold-email rules apply to prospecting.

risks: Hunter said subcontractors could not take the work soon enough or were poor-quality options, so offering the service may require buying equipment and learning the work.
Weather can compress the working season and create long, demanding days.
Material costs are high enough that Hunter takes 50% upfront.
Faint lines after sealing may need to be measured or re-laid with a chalk line.
Oil-based striping paint on a seal-coated surface can turn yellow and hazy, according to Hunter.
The example profit calculations were estimates and did not fully itemize insurance, gas, and overhead.

ideas.name: Parking-lot crack filling
ideas.one_liner: Fill asphalt cracks to slow deterioration and reduce the chance of larger cracks and potholes.
ideas.business_model: Per-linear-foot pricing or an estimated project price for lots with many cracks.
ideas.customer: Churches and other owners or operators of asphalt parking lots.
ideas.problem: Cracks can widen and develop into potholes, shortening the useful life and harming the appearance of a parking lot.
ideas.offer: Measure and fill asphalt cracks with heated material. Hunter said he sometimes estimates rather than measuring every crack in a complex lot.

pricing.model: Usually priced per linear foot, with total job prices depending on the number and depth of cracks.
pricing.notes: Hunter corrected himself from square-foot to linear-foot pricing. He said material use varies substantially with crack depth.

acquisition_channels.details: Crack filling was added after customers who asked for striping and sealing also requested quotes for it.

quote.text: So, I started with striping and then everyone wanted those quotes for seal coating and crack filling.
quote.speaker: Hunter

acquisition_channels.details: The same church and business email outreach used for striping could lead to quotes for crack filling.

quote.text: So email I I work with a guy overseas just on Upwork found him and I pay him five or six bucks for a list that he provides.
quote.speaker: Hunter

ideas.delivery: Hunter pushes a measuring wheel along cracks, heats material with propane using a crack-filling machine, then walks the crack and applies the material. Heating takes about 20 minutes, while the example 38-foot crack took about two minutes to fill. The work is physical and material use varies with crack depth.
unit_economics_claims: Hunter said he charges $0.30 to $1 per linear foot.
He gave an example of a 38-foot crack priced at $38 and estimated $5 to $10 in material for that crack.
He said the smallest crack-filling job he had was over $400 and most jobs were $2,000 to $3,000.
Hunter said a badly misquoted job with cracks six or seven inches deep took two days and left him with no profit.
He estimated a safe gross margin of around 70%, while saying results depend on crack depth.
ideas.startup_cost: Hunter bought a new crack-filling machine for $1,500. He did not state total startup cost for this service.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Hunter said he bought equipment after landing his first crack-filling job.

acquisition.how: Existing customer records and automated email workflows can identify prospects, but quotes and site assessment remain human-led.

onboarding.how: A customer can submit site details online, but someone must inspect crack depth and estimate material needs.

delivery.how: Workers must heat material and physically apply it along the cracks.

billing.how: A quoting and invoicing system can automate routine billing, though the scope and final amount may change after inspection.

support.how: Agents could handle scheduling and routine questions, but variation in site conditions requires human support.

uk_applicability.notes: The service is relevant to UK asphalt car parks, but materials, safety procedures, local climate, and disposal requirements need to be checked against UK practice. UK cold-email rules apply to prospecting.

risks: Crack depth can be difficult to judge from appearance and can consume far more material than expected.
Hunter described working two days on a badly quoted job and making nothing.
Heating material and applying it are physical, equipment-dependent tasks.
Very small isolated cracks may not justify mobilization; Hunter said his smallest job exceeded $400.
UK customer outreach must follow PECR rules.

tactics.name: Practice before taking a paid job
steps: Find an old parking lot and practice following existing lines with water in the machine.
Do a very small free job for a nonprofit to learn how the work feels and build confidence.
Track material use and adjust technique before quoting larger sites.

quote.text: I went down to just an old parking lot. Here's the machine, I put some water in it and I just tried to run follow along the lines
quote.speaker: Hunter

tactics.name: Use a local Facebook post to create a first proof job
steps: Post in the town's Facebook page and ask residents to nominate a business for a free refresh.
Use the free job to get local attention and show the result.
Contact the nominated businesses to ask whether they want paid quotes.

quote.text: I wanted to reach out to all of them to see if they would pay after. Yeah. For you know, we'll we'll choose the winner
quote.speaker: Hunter

tactics.name: Build an email prospect list and follow up
steps: Buy a targeted local list from a list provider found on Upwork; Hunter paid $5 to $6 for a list.
Email prospects with a simple introduction, a good-price offer, and a specific seasonal reason to act.
Start with a manageable batch, track replies and quotes, then follow up rather than endlessly adding new prospects.
Filter UK contacts so unsolicited marketing email is sent only where PECR permits.

quote.text: And so my close rate is better in person but it is what it is. What is your close rate? Um it's like 40 to 50%.

tactics.name: Quote in person when practical
steps: Visit the site and count lines, stencils, arrows, no-parking areas, and difficult sections.
Ask whether old lines need to be redrawn or realigned.
Send a written quote with Quote IQ; Hunter said some customers do not need an in-person meeting.
Price travel and difficult visibility or layout work higher.

quote.text: Some of them just want to they don't want to meet me. They they don't need to. Okay. Yeah. Yeah and so my close rate is better in person
quote.speaker: Hunter

tactics.name: Start with a roller and buy a machine after demand is proven
steps: If capital is tight, start with a roller, paint, and an email address.
Expect more taping and slower delivery than with a striping machine.
Use early job revenue to buy a machine once demand and job size justify it.

If subcontractors are too busy or unreliable, decide whether to buy equipment and learn the service directly.

warnings.warning: Hunter said a crack-filling job with cracks six or seven inches deep consumed enough material that he worked for two days and walked away with no profit.
Used striping equipment was cheaper but required Hunter to replace some parts and learn repairs.
Church customers may need board approval, which Hunter said can take a couple of weeks.
Seal coating and striping work is exposed to weather; Hunter described rushing to complete jobs before colder conditions arrived.
For asphalt Hunter recommended water-based paint; he said oil-based paint on a seal-coated surface can turn yellow and hazy.
Hunter said he initially tried door knocking but found it was not the best use of his time.
The host's sponsor segment makes claims about LLC liability protection and tax write-offs; those are promotional claims, not independently established in the interview.
The host promoted a paid business community, and Hunter promoted online guides and in-person training, creating promotional conflicts around business advice.

For UK outreach, do not copy the US-style email tactic without checking PECR: unsolicited marketing email to individuals and sole traders generally requires consent, while corporate subscribers may be contacted subject to applicable rules.

video.title: Overlooked Businesses You Can Start for Almost Nothing

summary: Chris Koerner interviews franchise adviser and entrepreneur Alex Smerzneck about franchising as a way to own a business with a proven playbook. Alex recommends private insurance adjusting, home sale preparation, and custom window boxes, then discusses artificial turf and cleaning franchises. They also cover franchise financing, evaluating disclosure documents, and how multi-unit ownership can scale. Alex promotes Franzy, his franchise-matching platform, which creates a promotional conflict when he discusses franchise opportunities.

tactics.name: Match the franchise to the buyer
steps: Start by asking what the buyer wants from the business, their risk tolerance, operational background, and financial goals.
For risk-averse buyers, look for established brands with around 80 to 100 open units and 5 to 10 years or more of history.
For buyers seeking greater upside, consider earlier systems with protected territory while recognising that the risk is higher.

quote.text: I start with the individual like what do you want? What's your risk tolerance? What are you good at?
quote.speaker: Alex Smerzneck

tactics.name: Use franchise financing to reduce initial cash
steps: Ask lenders about SBA financing for the franchise.
Estimate the cash contribution after financing before committing.
Alex says friends or family may fund the remaining amount if the buyer lacks it.

quote.text: And if you don't have $10,000, you can get friends or family to finance that.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Check the franchise disclosure document and Item 19 footnotes
steps: Review the FDD for units sold and closed, closure reasons, lawsuits, litigation, and bankruptcies.
Read Item 19 financial disclosures and inspect footnotes for adjusted EBITDA or revenue.
Compare the stated earnings with franchisee costs and operating requirements before deciding.

quote.text: Look at the footnotes and make sure you're you're getting the whole whole set of information.
quote.speaker: Alex Smerzneck

tactics.name: Build a referral engine for home-sale preparation
steps: Use the franchisor's referral playbooks to approach real-estate agents and brokerages.
Build repeat relationships with agents who handle multiple home sales.
Create a dependable bench of electricians, plumbers, drywall workers, and other subcontractors.
Offer an option to pay at closing if the brand supports it.

quote.text: And if you get a high-volume realtor on your team, like that could be dozens of closings a year.

video.title: I Tried OpenClaw for a Month and I'm Never Going Back

summary: Nick describes how he has been learning AI agents and applying them at a large company, where leaders have little experience with the tools. He demonstrates an earnings-call preparation prototype and a personal OpenClaw assistant built around organized, searchable data. He suggests businesses in corporate AI consulting, executive education, data cleanup, custom tools, and meeting follow-up. His central advice is to learn by applying AI to real workplace problems and to keep testing ideas as the technology changes.

tactics.name: Learn company problems from inside the organization
steps: Consider working at a company to see how its teams operate.
Notice where employees struggle, where spreadsheets are used, and where work slips through the cracks.
Use those observed pain points to identify possible AI services or tools.

quote.text: If you're on a meeting that could have been an email, that's an opportunity. If somebody let something slip through the cracks, that's an opportunity.
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Use a short AI update to open executive conversations
steps: Identify publicly traded companies and find executive contact information from public sources.
Write a concise, relevant message that offers a short briefing on practical AI changes.
Expect rejection and improve the pitch based on responses.
Use the first meeting to demonstrate a concrete workflow rather than just describe AI.

quote.text: If you can get on their calendar and just have like what I had with that executive team, like within a couple of minutes, they're going to be like, "Oh, I get it. I get it."
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Treat an AI demo as a prototype, not proof of demand
steps: Build a small demo around one real workflow.
Show it to people who do that work and ask what the process currently costs them.
Use their feedback to decide whether to refine, sell, or abandon the idea.

quote.text: And so, from this, like I I showed some of the people at my company like, "Hey, this is pretty cool."
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Keep a human review stage in AI-generated earnings scripts
steps: Collect the company strategy and current reporting data.
Generate an initial draft from prior transcripts and the new data.
Workshop the recommendations, refine the script, and export only after people review it.

quote.text: The thing that people miss here is they think AI just does everything. It doesn't. It's a good help but like you still have to work shop things.
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Create a clear taxonomy before building AI retrieval
steps: Inventory where files are stored and identify inconsistent folder and naming conventions.
Agree on a hierarchy and common naming structure.
Use AI to categorize files, then have an experienced person resolve ambiguous cases.
Prepare the resulting data for search and retrieval.

quote.text: Now, clean data would be clear taxonomy, which a taxonomy would just be a hierarchical way for you to to uh identify information.
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Start with meeting capture and follow-up
steps: Record meetings with appropriate participant notice.
Transcribe and summarize the meeting.
Save the transcript and summary in a searchable location.
Extract commitments and create reminders for agreed follow-up.

tactics.name: Use multiple models to review plans and specifications
steps: Ask one model to turn an idea into a product requirements document.
Send the document to other models for an adversarial review.
Revise the specification through several review rounds.
Repeat the review for the implementation plan before building.

Try specific products such as team shirts, customized spikes, tumblers, phone cases, and stickers.
Ask which products and colors customers prefer and what they will pay.
Follow customer demand instead of committing early to one product.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Matt and Joanie, who started Sonoma Strong Hauling junk removal in Sonoma County when Matt was 35 and just out of jail and rehab. Starting part-time with a pickup and a free Craigslist post, they did $87k in year one at ~70% margin and now do $50k/month at ~35% net with a small crew. The episode focuses on free, old-school marketing: candy dishes at every real estate office, friending 2,000+ realtors on Facebook, daily local Facebook group posts, bandit signs, partner referrals and YouTube. Key takeaway: scrappy local relationship marketing plus professional branding can fill a low-capital service business, and growth spending should follow demand.

summary: Chris Koerner has Tyler Denk, co-founder of Beehiiv and early Morning Brew employee, walk through starting a newsletter from zero on Beehiiv (website, template, welcome automation, recommendations, Boost, magic links) and monetising it. Tyler's own 120,000-subscriber weekly side-project newsletter, Big Desk Energy, has generated about $500k: $5-7k per sponsored send, ~$80k per $10,000-a-head founder mastermind in Costa Rica, and $10-25k from Boost. Both argue niche lists (even 500-5,000 high-value readers) can earn well through sponsorships, events or consulting, and that paid acquisition at ~$1.45-2.50 per subscriber becomes a flywheel when Boost/recommendation income and sponsorships return more. Chris shows how he segments his list and uses surveys to build a media kit. The episode is effectively promotional for Beehiiv.

video.title: Laid Off 2 Days Before Christmas, Now He Makes $60k/Month Reselling

summary: Jim Row describes building a resale business from restaurant equipment and liquidation goods, then growing it into a local retail store and broader delivery operation. He explains sourcing through auctions, selling through Facebook Marketplace and live videos, using referrals from food distributors, and testing items before committing more capital. His examples include furniture, restaurant equipment, industrial hinges, a truck, and other returned or surplus goods. The main takeaway is to learn to sell with items you already own, then reinvest carefully; the business still depends heavily on physical handling, local marketing, and personal sales work.

ideas.delivery: Jim and his wife received, sorted, tested, cleaned, displayed, and sold physical inventory. They moved stock inside and outside the store each day, and either the customer collected goods or Jim, his family, or a helper delivered them. Facebook lives and Marketplace listings supported sales, but fulfilment was local and hands-on.
unit_economics_claims: Jim said the store did $60,000 in sales in its first month and maintained about that sales volume for several months.
A Saturday furniture sale generated about $3,000 in profit, according to Jim.
Jim said a Facebook post hinting he might close brought in the store's biggest day of the year, with $15,000 in sales.
Jim started with a $1,200 purchase and reinvested the proceeds.
The tow-shop rent was about $3,200 a month; the later store rent was $4,500 a month.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated as a total. Jim described starting with a $1,200 purchase and later setting a fixed inventory budget.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. The first reported sale event followed shortly after he began buying and selling returned furniture.

acquisition.how: Listings and social content can generate inbound interest, but store traffic relied on location, visible stock, regular promotion, and personal relationships.

onboarding.how: Customers browse, ask questions, reserve goods, and arrange collection or delivery through direct human contact.

delivery.how: Physical stock must be inspected, cleaned, sorted, moved, displayed, and often delivered by people.

billing.how: Payments were taken in person; no automated checkout or billing system was described.

support.how: The seller personally answers product questions, handles reservations, and builds relationships with buyers.

uk_applicability.notes: The retail and resale model could work in the UK, but the speaker's sourcing and suppliers are US-specific, including Costco returns, B-Stock, and GovDeals. A UK operator would need local liquidation sources, suitable premises, and a local audience. Marketing described was inbound social content and listings, rather than unsolicited messages.

risks: Sales dipped after moving from a visible roadside location to a large downtown store without drive-by traffic.
A large inventory can require daily moving, cleaning, testing, sorting, and display work.
Buying inventory is easier than selling it; unsold goods tie up cash and space.
The model depends on local demand, accessible premises, and physical fulfilment.
Customer response to a product can be unpredictable; the speaker says his own preferences were not a reliable guide to what would sell.

tactics.name: Learn selling before buying inventory
steps: Start with items already owned so the first test does not require taking on debt.
List the items and practise answering low offers while keeping the buyer relationship open.
Ask buyers who cannot afford the current item whether they want to hear about a cheaper one later.
Use the responses and sales to learn what moves before committing to larger auction purchases.

quote.text: I want you to understand how to respond to those and still keep them as future customers.
quote.speaker: Jim Row

tactics.name: Turn an adjacent sales workforce into a referral channel
steps: Identify people who already visit the same customer type, such as food-distribution salespeople visiting restaurants.
Offer a clear commission for qualified leads, then let the reseller handle the rest of the sale.
Test the approach across several contacts; Jim said about 20 contacts led to three reliable referrers.
Reward useful help with payment or a thoughtful gift, while recognising that some people may decline commissions.

quote.text: I'd pay them 10% commission on any lead that they would give me.
quote.speaker: Jim Row

tactics.name: Use a visible storefront to create curiosity
steps: Place a small amount of appealing inventory where passing customers can see it.
Use an open sign and a reader board to make the shop visible.
Keep the entrance open when possible; Jim found people stopped coming when he shut the shop door.

quote.text: People would drive by and just pull in and they're like, "What are you doing here?"
quote.speaker: Jim Row

tactics.name: Sell through an existing local audience
steps: Build a social-media audience and customer database before a sale event.
Go live to show the products, explain the new offer, and demonstrate unfamiliar features.
Use customer testimonials to show that people are buying.
If the seller lacks an audience, partner with a business that has one and create a mutual benefit.

quote.text: If someone else has the database, I just team up with them.
quote.speaker: Jim Row

tactics.name: Use auction downside protection before bidding
steps: Check comparable online listings and estimate the value of the material or parts.
Set a maximum bid based on a conservative fallback such as scrap value.
Bid only when the downside case is acceptable to the business.
For unusual lots, call potential manufacturers or business users to test whether there is a buyer.

quote.text: I did the math on how much the aluminum weighed and then I looked up the scrap price and I was like, I'll just put in a max bid for that number.
quote.speaker: Jim Row

tactics.name: Sell a batch to cover the cost, then improve the deal
steps: Offer a first batch at a price that can recover the lot cost.
Once the first buyer accepts, ask whether they will buy another batch.
Offer to save the buyer freight by delivering personally when that makes economic sense.
Use the delivery visit to build a relationship and learn about other needs.

quote.text: If you guys can do another hundred, I'll save you the freight and I'll personally personally deliver them to you and that way we get to meet and we can build a relationship
quote.speaker: Jim Row

tactics.name: Make a slow listing more useful to a buyer
steps: When a reseller has multiple identical ovens, offer a warranty backed by the remaining units as potential replacements.
Update the listing to state the warranty clearly.
Jim said the listing sold within two days after the change.

quote.text: I changed the ad to warranty. It sold in two days.
quote.speaker: Jim Row

tactics.name: Treat unsold stock as a marketing and pricing problem first
steps: Do not assume an item has no market because the seller personally would not buy it.
Test a different price, description, or positioning before writing the item off.
Match the product to a different customer or location if it is slow in the current market.

quote.text: I'm not my own customer because I don't buy cracked patio furniture, but other people do.
quote.speaker: Jim Row

tactics.name: Choose stock for a different local market
steps: Notice which products sell slowly in the current town because of local customer preferences.
Move suitable items to a larger or better-matched market.
Use a local helper or meet buyers there to complete the transaction.

quote.text: I take anything that fits that market over there and I put it in their warehouse and uh and then I just meet people there
quote.speaker: Jim Row

tactics.name: Use flexible pricing and honest service in window sales
steps: When a customer presents a lower competing quote, ask to see the quote and understand the difference.
If discounting is not possible, offer a concrete non-price value such as a yard sign and reference calls, without making false claims.
Address the customer's specific concern; Jim offered a clean worksite and brought his mother to check it.
Avoid sales tactics that do not align with how the operator wants to treat customers.

quote.text: I was like, "How do I lower the price? I want the job still. How do I lower the price without looking like an idiot?"

tactics.name: Keep an inventory budget
steps: Set a buying budget when auction buying becomes exciting and easy to overdo.

evidence_quality.rationale: Jim is a first-hand operator and gives concrete sourcing, sales, and operating examples. Several claims lack supporting records or clear definitions, and the host's introduction says half of first-month sales were profit while Jim's own account clearly confirms sales but not that profit figure. The hinge purchase cost is also inconsistent in the transcript.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Chris Koerner includes a Beehiiv sponsor read and promotes the paid TK Owners community. These promotions are separate from Jim's interview and were excluded as business ideas.

video.title: 7 Low-Cost Business Ideas for Beginners in 2026

summary: Chris Koerner ranks seven food business ideas for 2026, from grill cleaning to watermelon products, and also discusses related side ideas and sales tactics. Examples include a pancake pop-up, dehydrated fruit, luxury picnics, frozen grapes, unattended bakery stands, and watermelon snacks. The video mixes reported operator examples with the host’s own estimates and hypothetical calculations. Its recurring advice is to test ideas cheaply, use local demand channels, and learn by doing.

video.title: Now is the Best Time to Make Money with Content (AI Tutorial)

summary: Chris Koerner argues now is a great time to earn from content inspired by other creators' content in any niche. He walks through building an n8n workflow on a Hostinger VPS (about $5/month) that reads YouTube channel RSS feeds on a schedule, appends the videos to a Google Sheet and emails a digest. Setup covers the Google Cloud Console APIs and OAuth consent, an RSS Read node, Google Sheets and Gmail nodes, and an Aggregate node to fix email spam. He suggests the tool could be resold, for example as a $30/month competitor-monitoring email to YouTubers, or sold as n8n templates. The video is promotional for Hostinger.

tactics.name: Build a YouTube competitor-tracking digest in n8n
steps: Buy a Hostinger VPS with n8n preinstalled
In Google Cloud Console create a project, enable the Gmail and Google Sheets APIs, configure the OAuth consent screen with external audience and test users
Add Gmail read/send/modify and Sheets read/write scopes
In n8n add a Schedule trigger, then an RSS Read node per channel
Get each channel's RSS URL from the page source by searching for RSS, which avoids third-party sites that harvest your email
Append publish date, channel name and title to a Google Sheet
Add an Aggregate node (titles, links) before the Gmail node so you get one digest email, not one per video
Limit to the latest 10 items per channel and schedule daily

quote.text: I'm going to add a node right here between RSS and Gmail. Hit the plus. It's going to be called aggregate.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

video.title: I Built an AI Agent in 5 Minutes (And Sold It Live)

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates a campaign to sell AI voice agents to local service businesses, using ringless voicemail drops to contact tree-care companies. He shows lead selection, campaign setup, several callbacks, and a GoHighLevel voice-agent build. The campaign generated calls and conversations, but the transcript does not report a sale. His main takeaway is that the agent is quick to build; finding customers and handling follow-up are the harder parts.

The provider handles setup and may connect a new or ported-in phone number. Any physical service work and on-site quotes remain with the client business.

acquisition.how: Lead scraping and voicemail sending can be software-assisted, but list selection, offer creation, callbacks, and closing were human-led. Chris's demonstrated cold voicemail method would need a legally compliant alternative in the UK; inbound marketing or compliant outreach to corporate subscribers could be more automatable.

support.how: Routine questions may be handled by the agent, but the transcript does not show a support process for client issues, failures, or changes to the agent.

uk_applicability.notes: The core voice-agent service can work for UK trades and other local businesses. The US ringless voicemail campaign should not be copied without legal review: UK rules restrict unsolicited automated marketing calls, and contact data and call handling also need appropriate privacy compliance. Pricing, phone-number setup, and the chosen outreach channels may need adaptation.

risks: The demonstrated ringless voicemail campaign is not shown to close a paid sale; callbacks can be accidental or low-intent.
Some recipients may be angry or confused by unsolicited outreach, and Chris reports that some people were angry.
UK rules restrict unsolicited automated marketing calls; screening against a do-not-call list alone does not establish compliance.
The agent can sound robotic or provide inappropriate answers if its voice, knowledge base, or settings are poorly chosen.
A business may still need human follow-up to confirm availability, quote jobs, and perform physical work.
Chris says a single standalone marketing touch may not produce strong results; multiple touches may help, but those channels have their own legal requirements.

tactics.name: Choose a niche and check demand
steps: Start with a service niche that has a clear missed-call problem; Chris considered pool-service and tree-trimming businesses.
Use Google Trends to compare search interest for related services over time.
Compare related terms, such as gutter cleaning and gutter repair, and use the Google Keyword Tool to check local search demand and keyword bidding competition.
Treat higher search interest as a clue about demand, not proof of profit or low competition.

quote.text: No, it's like there could be even more um supply to meet this demand. And this could be the most saturated category.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Scrape and prepare a focused lead list
steps: Search for relevant business categories and locations in Outscraper; Chris selected three pool-related categories for one example, then used already-cleaned tree-trimming leads for the live campaign.
Filter for businesses with phone numbers and set a maximum results count based on the number of campaign credits available.
Use existing free lead lists when available; Chris says his group lets members request them through Typeform.
If scraping directly, compare the estimate with the stated cost and turnaround time; Chris reports paying about USD 4 for the displayed list.
Keep only the fields needed for the campaign, then remove blanks and invalid numbers.
Randomize lead order in Google Sheets before taking a sample, to reduce location or alphabetical-order bias.

quote.text: And so whatever I'm doing, even if it's probably already randomized, I like taking 10 seconds and randomizing them again just in case.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Keep lead cleaning proportional to the value of the data
steps: Prioritize the first phone number in the scrape rather than spending extensive time checking every extra phone-number column.
Upload lists to Slide Broadcast's list manager to add a cell-versus-landline column, even without running a campaign.
Treat the added classification as a second check; Chris says the scrape data and validation are not perfectly accurate.

quote.text: because like if you can scrape unlimited leads for next to nothing, like why spend a bunch of time cleaning and scrubbing and validating a bunch of stuff.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Write a short voicemail around one customer pain
steps: Keep the message brief because Chris expects many recipients to listen for only a few seconds.
Lead with a problem that fits the niche, such as missing calls while working on a tree job.
Personalize only with information actually known about the prospect; in this example Chris knew they owned a tree-trimming business in Texas.
Give a clear callback instruction and use a callback voicemail greeting that matches the offer.

quote.text: We want to speak to a painoint. We want to solve a problem. We want to personalize as much as we can.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Prepare to answer callbacks
steps: Set the callback number and voicemail greeting before sending the campaign.
Turn off call screening and check that the number will ring as intended.
Avoid sending all messages at once if the operator cannot answer the callbacks; Chris says he would normally throttle the campaign.
Treat callbacks as an opening for a conversation, not proof that a prospect heard the pitch or wants to buy.

quote.text: Now, if I were being like responsive and dutiful, I would not let these go to voicemail. I would answer all of them and I would throttle them to not send 500 all at once because I want to be able to answer these calls because that's how you're going to close it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Test a multi-touch sequence
steps: Use a voicemail drop as one touch rather than assuming a single message will produce strong results.
Test other appropriate channels, such as email, a call, or LinkedIn, and track which combination produces meaningful conversations.
The audience participant reports a sequence of voice note, email, then text; Chris says he would test it, but the transcript does not establish UK legal compliance for those touches.

quote.text: But like like any marketing, you want multiple touches and preferably you want multiple touches in different mediums.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Build an initial voice-agent knowledge base quickly
steps: Create an agent with a clear name, language, voice, and initial greeting.
Use ChatGPT to draft a simple knowledge base for common questions and the intended next step, such as arranging an on-site quote.
Add the client's website to the HighLevel web crawler to pull in existing FAQs and business information.
Review the generated material, connect the knowledge base, choose the information to collect, and test the agent with a realistic call.
Use an email notification to pass completed call details to the business team.

quote.text: I'm building a simple AI voice agent to receive inbound calls at a tree trimming business called Chris's tree trimming. It needs to answer typical questions about scheduling an on-site quote for a trimming or removal job.

tactics.name: Use a template or marketplace to reduce setup friction

For clients already using HighLevel, consider selling or installing the agent through the HighLevel app marketplace.
Use a new HighLevel number or port the business's existing number, depending on the client's setup.

video.title: She Makes $1k/Day Sending Letters

summary: Hannah describes how she started Tiny Post, a monthly snail-mail club, after building a neighborhood farmers market in Austin. She grew the club through TikTok and other organic social posts, then hired help to pack and mail its physical contents. The conversation also covers related letter-club niches, direct-mail ideas, and ways to extend the product. Its strongest lesson for a founder seeking an agent-run business is that the customer-facing storytelling can use software, but making and mailing the distinctive product still takes substantial human work.

A monthly physical product is exposed to postal delays, damage, postage changes, and production errors.

tactics.name: Start with a small local event and show up consistently
steps: Set up a simple first market in a space you control.
Invite neighbors with flyers and offer a welcoming reason to attend, such as free drinks.
Repeat the event monthly so the community knows when to expect it.
Invite small makers and hobbyists to participate, then add activities that fit the event's mission.

quote.text: And I decided I would be really consistent with it and just show up every month on a Saturday.
quote.speaker: Hannah

tactics.name: Use a personal story as the content
steps: Explain why the product exists and what personal experience led to it.
Show the work and the process rather than only making a direct sales pitch.
Use comments and questions to explain the product to people who have not encountered it before.
Keep publishing and learn from how the audience responds.

quote.text: I shared a lot about why I was doing it and where the idea came from.
quote.speaker: Hannah

tactics.name: Use a waitlist carefully
steps: Use a waitlist if demand exceeds the team's capacity.
State clearly on the signup form that the product costs money.
Tell people when signups will open and how long they may wait.
Measure how many waitlisted people actually buy before assuming the list represents demand.

quote.text: I just threw up a little Google form like I wasn't even like thinking, but I didn't say that it cost money.
quote.speaker: Hannah

tactics.name: Protect the one-ounce mail limit
steps: Design each mailer around the weight restriction for the intended postage rate.
Weigh the final assembled envelope before dispatch.
Treat extra inserts and seasonal items as a postage decision, not only a creative decision.

quote.text: the weight is what restricts us the most because I can't go over one ounce.
quote.speaker: Hannah

tactics.name: Batch and standardize packing
steps: Split the monthly mailer into repeatable steps such as stamping, addressing, inserting, and sealing.
Batch the work into a defined production week.
Bring in and train additional helpers when the original family group becomes overloaded.
Measure letters completed per batch and labor hours before deciding whether machinery is worthwhile.

quote.text: This month is the first month we've like really standardized and brought in more people and that has like truly been a huge game changer.

tactics.name: Use unboxing posts as feedback
steps: Watch subscriber unboxings and posts about the physical mailer.
Note what customers like, misunderstand, or share.
Use the feedback to improve future issues while keeping the product's creative direction.

Offer the channels actually used, including Instagram, TikTok, and Pinterest, plus an other option.

steps: Check whether a new revenue stream changes how subscribers experience the product.
Decline advertising if it would make the mailer feel less personal or trustworthy.

video.title: AI is STEALING These Jobs! Here's How to Profit

summary: Chris Koerner argues that AI exposes a large share of US jobs (claims 25% fully performable, 70% exposed) and pitches business ideas for workers in healthcare, retail and professional services. Ideas range from licensed clinical businesses (IV therapy, mobile Botox, GLP-1 services) to product sourcing, reselling, dashboards, buying accounting practices, fractional CFO agencies and AI implementation. He is most excited about AI implementation for SMBs and promotes his own community Playmakers AI. Most content is listicle-style with rough numbers and little process detail.

video.title: How to Buy Big Things with Little Money

summary: Chris Koerner explains ways to acquire property, businesses, and other valuable assets with little upfront cash, drawing on his own purchases and negotiations. He focuses on seller financing structures, building trust with sellers, staying flexible about the asset, and documenting a project publicly to attract customers or investors. His examples include real estate, short-term rentals, RV parks, and a landscaping business. The main takeaway is to reduce risk for the seller, negotiate terms creatively, and be ready to walk away if the deal does not work on the numbers.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; shares personal acquisition experience and examples.

ideas.name: Buy businesses and assets with little cash using creative financing
ideas.one_liner: Acquire a business or asset by negotiating seller financing, flexible terms, and a relationship of trust.
ideas.business_model: Acquire an existing business or asset, improve or operate it, then earn from its cash flow or resale.
ideas.customer: Sellers of businesses, real estate, or other assets; the buyer is the founder or operator.
ideas.problem: The buyer wants an asset but lacks the cash for a conventional down payment or financing terms.
ideas.offer: A purchase proposal that adjusts the down payment, timing, payment schedule, collateral, or future profit share to suit both parties.

pricing.model: Negotiated purchase price and financing terms.
pricing.notes: Terms depend on the asset and seller. The transcript gives several hypothetical structures rather than one standard price.

acquisition_channels.details: Find owners in an asset class, build a relationship, visit in person more than once, follow up, and explain how the buyer can add value.

quote.text: Visit him in person multiple times, follow up with him, bring your spouse and kids if that's the case.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Document the project on free social platforms to build an audience and attract prospective customers or investors.

quote.text: If you bring the world along with you through these free media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, Tik Tok, whatever, then you can skip the line.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The buyer operates or improves the acquired asset. The seller may receive installments, interest, a balloon payment, future appreciation, or another negotiated form of consideration.
unit_economics_claims: Chris says he bought an $800,000 business with $50,000 down.
The transcript gives hypothetical buy-and-resell math for a landscaping business.
tools: ChatGPT for generating alternative financing structures
Banks for conventional or alternative loan options
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; the purpose is to reduce the amount of cash required upfront.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; depends on the asset and financing terms.

acquisition.how: Finding and persuading an owner depends on trust and often repeated personal contact; software can assist with research but cannot replace the relationship.

onboarding.how: Document collection and deal administration can use software, but parties and advisers must agree and review the contract.

delivery.how: Operating a purchased business or physical asset requires human oversight and may involve physical work.

billing.how: Scheduled payments can be automated, but payment terms and servicing need human setup and monitoring.

support.how: Seller relations and operational issues require human judgement and communication.

uk_applicability.notes: Seller financing and negotiated purchase terms can work in the UK, but legal, tax, lending, and property rules differ and need local advice.

risks: A balloon payment may become due before the buyer can refinance or sell; default can return the asset to the seller.
A seller with a second lien position may recover little or nothing if a senior lender is paid first.
Interest-only payments do not reduce principal and interest may compound.
A lease-to-own or master lease can leave the buyer with operating risk and no ownership if the option is not exercised.
Borrowing from friends and family can damage valuable personal relationships.
Do not become emotionally attached to a deal; be willing to walk away.

quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

quotes.text: You've got to be willing to build a relationship of trust.

tactics.name: Document the project publicly
steps: Start a social account before launch, even with no followers.
Use a phone and informal videos to show planning, building, and fundraising.
Study other creators in the niche: hooks, music, posting frequency, asset type, and comments.
Paste comment text into ChatGPT to identify themes that may resonate with viewers.
Optimize for shares, comments, and average view duration, not likes alone.
Repeat the formats that work and try to improve each video.

tactics.name: Broaden the asset search and build seller trust
steps: Choose an asset class, then stay flexible on geography, price point, size, and type within it.
Look for an owner who is willing to get to know you and whom you also like.
Learn about the owner's asset class and acknowledge what they know.
Offer value, compliment the property sincerely, visit more than once, and follow up.
Share relevant personal context and common ground to make the relationship more familiar.

quote.text: You've got to be willing to build a relationship of trust.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Ask for alternative bank loan options
steps: If a bank presents a costly loan condition such as PMI, ask what other options exist.
Explain that the proposed cost makes the deal unaffordable.
Keep speaking with banks until one offers terms that work.

quote.text: I read that I don't have to pay that. and they were like, "Uh, all right. I don't think it's going to work, but let me see if there are other options."

tactics.name: Frame seller financing around the seller's benefits
steps: Present the tangible benefits of the proposed terms to the seller.
Explain the buyer's story and relevant industry experience.
Use a specific plan for improving the asset and show how the seller can be protected.
Consider an ongoing profit share if the seller believes the asset has untapped potential.

quote.text: You've got to frame it in a way that really highlights the positives for them. Both the tangibles and the intangibles.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use a balloon payment to defer principal
steps: Negotiate a small initial payment and manageable monthly payments.
Set a balloon due date in the contract.
Plan to refinance or sell the asset before the balloon is due.
Check the default and lien terms before signing.

quote.text: The idea with this structure is to either refinance or sell the asset before then.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Offer graduated payments to build seller confidence
steps: Start with payments the new business can afford.
Increase payments on a schedule as the buyer establishes a track record.
Use the schedule to show the seller that payments begin immediately and the buyer is acting in good faith.

quote.text: suggest graduated payments because they can almost have the same purpose, which is to save you money in your payments upfront
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Combine bank debt with a seller carryback
steps: Calculate the down payment required by the bank and the buyer's available cash.
Ask the seller to carry the funding gap as a note.
Discuss the seller's junior lien position and the risk of being behind the bank.
Consider bringing in friends or family for part of the buyer contribution only after weighing relationship risk.

quote.text: A partial seller carryback would be for the seller to put 150 grand on the line

tactics.name: Trade future appreciation for better terms
steps: If the seller believes the asset can be worth more after improvements, ask them to improve the current financing terms.
Offer a defined share of future rents or profits tied to specific milestones.
Write the valuation triggers and payment share into the agreement.

quote.text: How about you give me better terms on the seller financing and then I cut you into those future profits.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use a master lease with an option to buy
steps: Lease the property while the seller keeps title.
Set a monthly payment and a predetermined purchase price and date.
Define the right to walk away and what happens to the property if the buyer does not exercise the option.
Use time under the lease to test whether the improvement plan works.

quote.text: It's a master lease agreement with the option to purchase at a predetermined price at a certain predetermined time in the future.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Swap price, rate, down payment, services, or collateral
steps: Offer a higher interest rate or purchase price in exchange for less cash down.
Consider consulting or marketing services in place of a cash down payment.
Consider offering collateral only after reviewing what default would mean.
Use ChatGPT to generate alternative term combinations, then review them with appropriate advisers.

quote.text: How about 8% interest and 0% down?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Consider subject-to or delayed down payment terms
steps: For a subject-to structure, discuss taking over payments while the existing loan remains in the seller's name.
For a delayed down payment, propose a future payment date and define what happens if it is not paid.
Review the existing loan and contract terms carefully before proceeding.

quote.text: The debt stays in the seller's name and you come out of pocket little to nothing.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Stay willing to walk away
steps: Evaluate the deal on its numbers and risks.
Do not treat one asset or seller as the only opportunity.
Walk away if the financing, operations, or downside protection do not work.

quote.text: You've got to be willing to walk from any deal at any time. It should only be math to you.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

video.title: People Are Selling One Prompt Websites for $1K+ (Full Tutorial)

summary: A sponsored tutorial in which Chris Koerner uses the AI website builder Wegic (transcribed as Ouijic/Weedic) to build a site for his planned Secret Pickleball club, with court booking, leaderboard and members-only merch, in about two and a half minutes, then a Dallas pizza restaurant site with payment buttons, menu and a lead-capture chatbot in about one minute. He pitches it as a way to save $3-5k on a designer or to start a web design agency selling sites for thousands of dollars. His advice is to pick an industry you understand, dig into owners' booking and lead-handling headaches with why/how/who questions, and price on value rather than time. Evidence is promotional: the video is an ad for Wegic.

video.title: The 11 Best Side Hustles for 2026

summary: Chris Koerner counts down 11 side-hustle ideas for Q1 2026, from wall-printing services to importing cheap Chinese jet boats. Most are second-hand data points from social media, YouTube and chance encounters, with sparse and unverified numbers. The recurring themes are low startup cost, visual short-form video marketing, arbitrage and middleman positioning, and testing demand (for example on Facebook Marketplace) before spending money.

video.title: OpenClaw is BOOMING! Do This to Profit

summary: Chris Koerner introduces the viral Moltbook social network for AI agents and outlines several ways people might build businesses around OpenClaw. He recommends packaged agent setup and managed AI services, then demonstrates building an SEO news site with AI-generated articles, a newsletter signup, and search analytics. He reports 12 unique active users during the first 30 minutes after launch, but gives no revenue results. The main takeaway is to explore practical agent services and use fast, AI-assisted publishing to test interest, while carefully restricting agent permissions.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; the transcript also spells his name as Chris Kerner.

ideas.name: Packaged OpenClaw installation and AI implementation service
ideas.one_liner: Set up and configure AI agents for individuals, executives, and business owners, then maintain and service them.
ideas.business_model: One-off setup fee followed by an optional monthly maintenance and service fee.
ideas.customer: Individuals, busy executives, and business owners.
ideas.problem: Customers may not know how to install, configure, secure, or connect an AI agent to the apps and workflows they use.
ideas.offer: An agent-in-a-box setup that connects the customer's channels, locks down permissions, and solves practical problems; ongoing maintenance is also offered.

pricing.model: One-off setup plus recurring maintenance and service.
pricing.notes: The host suggests these as possible charges; he does not report having charged them.

acquisition_channels.details: The host recommends trying agents personally, then talking about them with friends and people encountered in person, including at church. He says interested people may ask for help.

quote.text: And then just start talking about it on the internet to your friends, in person, at church, wherever. And people will want help with it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Install the agent on the customer's computer or server, connect it to the relevant apps and channels, restrict permissions, and configure it to perform useful tasks. The host says the service should solve problems, not stop at installation. He suggests charging for setup and ongoing maintenance.
unit_economics_claims: The host proposes a USD 300–1,000 setup fee and USD 50–350 per month for maintenance and service; these are hypothetical price suggestions.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. A Mac Mini is not required; the host says an existing computer or old laptop can be used.

acquisition.how: The host's proposed customer discovery relies on personal conversation and in-person word of mouth, which requires human participation.

onboarding.how: An agent may help with setup, but connecting personal apps, configuring permissions, and understanding the customer's workflows need substantial human review.

tactics.name: Package agent setup around a solved problem
steps: Choose a clear customer group such as individuals, executives, or business owners.
Connect the agent to the channels and apps the customer already uses.
Lock down permissions before enabling actions.

Offer maintenance and service after the initial setup.

quote.text: Make sure their permissions are locked down. Make sure it's tied together to all the right channels and make sure it's actually doing things for them.

steps: Install the agent on a computer you already have; the host says a Mac Mini is not required.
Tell ChatGPT what you do during a typical day and ask for agent use cases.
Try one useful workflow yourself.
Talk about the result with friends and people you meet in person, including at church, and offer help to people who ask.

quote.text: And then just start talking about it on the internet to your friends, in person, at church, wherever. And people will want help with it. And you can charge them.

Sell managed AI assistance as a software-as-a-service product so customers do not have to manage their own server or computer.

quote.text: This is the lower friction route, which I think usually wins in most cases.

video.title: The Most Profitable One-Man Business You’ve Never Heard Of

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Alex, who runs a forestry mulching and land-clearing business near Cincinnati. Alex explains how he spotted local demand, priced jobs, used video ads and YouTube to educate leads, and scheduled large farm jobs in winter to reduce seasonality. He reports strong revenue and margins, while also describing equipment costs, maintenance, and other Bobcat services such as snow removal. The central takeaway is that clear local demand and a video-led sales funnel helped a capital-intensive, physical service business grow quickly; the work itself still depends on people and machinery.

ideas.name: Forestry mulching and land clearing

ideas.delivery: Alex goes out to quote and marks the area to be cleared. One operator then arrives with the forestry-equipped machine and runs it through the marked area. They ask customers to remove metal, tires, and other debris; if the customer does not, the crew does that work as billable time.
unit_economics_claims: Alex reported about $3,300 as the average job size.
Alex reported a $20 cost per lead and about 49% of quotes closing.
For a roughly $6,000 job, the host estimated about $4,000 profit; Alex agreed with the calculation.
Alex reported spending about $80–$100 per day on diesel and setting aside about 8% for repairs.
Alex reported gross profit of about 70% in the first operating period and net profit of about 40% later.
ideas.startup_cost: Alex financed the first machine and attachment with about $5,000 down, paid about $11,000 cash for a trailer, and bought a used truck for about $8,000. He said a used first machine cost about $74,000 and the first used attachment cost $15,000; the transcript does not give a full startup-cost total.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: The first deal closed two days after ads were published; the first job was about $6,500.

acquisition.how: Agents could help produce ad variants, manage targeting, and route inbound leads, with a person checking the videos, local targeting, and ad spend.

onboarding.how: A person currently visits properties, assesses density and terrain, marks the area, and prepares the operator.

delivery.how: A person must operate heavy machinery and handle site conditions; this is physical work.

billing.how: Billing tools could handle invoices and payments, but the transcript does not describe their billing process.

support.how: Customer questions about property, debris, timing, and results require human judgment.

uk_applicability.notes: The service and video-led local marketing could work in the UK, but demand, equipment financing, land access, and environmental or wildlife rules would need local adaptation.

risks: Forestry mulching wears equipment and parts; Alex says used equipment can be hard to assess and recommends starting with a new machine and warranty.
Metal, tires, and barbed wire can damage teeth or equipment, so the work area needs checking.
Fuel, repairs, insurance, machine payments, suitable towing capacity, and a CDL for some equipment combinations add operating costs and constraints.
Weather and wet ground affected the business's season; Alex adapted by booking suitable large farm properties for winter.
The work is physical, equipment-dependent, and cannot be run unattended.

video.title: This Business Makes Vending Machines Look Dumb

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Forest, a 34-year-old former Pepsi/Coke/Bang merchandiser and beverage brand rep. He bought a failed pastry route for $15k, grew it to about $800k a year and sold it in two parts for about $185k. He then moved to Billings, Montana and started a small-distributor business selling jerky, candy and novelty snacks to independent gas stations and grocery stores. He reports about 95 accounts, roughly $50k a month in sales, 30% net margin and one lost account. The takeaway is that a hands-on, relationship-based route business that merchandises and buys back unsold stock, using local products, net-10 customer terms and net-14 to net-30 supplier terms, can start with very little capital. It is physical, driving-heavy work, not agent-run.
