ideas.name: Independent-store jerky and candy micro-distributor (merchandising route)
ideas.one_liner: Drive a route to independent gas stations, grocery and hardware stores every 14 days, selling jerky, candy and novelty snacks by the case, merchandising the shelf and buying back unsold stock.
ideas.business_model: Wholesale resale margin: buy from manufacturers, mark up 30-45%, sell by the case to stores on net-10 terms. No service fee.
ideas.customer: Independent gas stations, small grocery stores, hardware stores, lumber yards, liquor stores and auto parts stores, mostly rural; small regional chains (e.g. 8-store and 20-store accounts).
ideas.problem: Big wholesalers drop product and leave, with no upselling or relationship, no regional or local products, and store owners carry the mental load of ordering and forecasting inventory. Out-of-stocks and outdated stock are not bought back.
ideas.offer: Visit every other week, place the order, merchandise and rotate the shelf, take over whole sections (e.g. jerky), supply products the big wholesaler does not carry (especially local brands), buy back credits on unsold or outdated items, and supply free manufacturer racks and displays. Positioned as an addition to the store's existing wholesaler.

pricing.model: Per-case wholesale with 30-45% markup over cost, net-10 customer terms

price_points.unit: per delivery at best grocery store
price_points.label: best grocery account

price_points.unit: per jerky case (some cases over $100; about $30 profit)
price_points.label: case price

pricing.notes: Markup 30-45%, so the example $1,000 order yields about $350-400 gross profit. Net margin about 30% when owner-operated, about 20% if staff run it. Sells by the case only.

acquisition_channels.details: Walks into independent stores with the product in the truck or trailer, a price sheet and a fun one-pager, and offers to fetch the display on the spot. Re-visits non-buyers every other Tuesday; the second follow-up is usually when they say yes. Early close rate about 4 in 10.

quote.text: you give them the one pager that has some fun photos. And I always tell them like, "Hey, let me go grab the product now."
quote.speaker: Forest

acquisition_channels.details: Relationship-based; owners help other local businesses. Existing accounts and regional chains bring more stores (e.g. a 30-store owner, a 25-store regional account, a four-store chain asking him to bring in a brand).

Manufacturers want distributors; one jerky brand sent a salesman to open stores for him. Called competitor owners for market insight and brand intros. Used Google to find cool local or non-saturated brands and pitched them using a list of about 50 independent stores.
Used Google Maps and satellite or street view to find stores that look independent, ignoring fuel branding like Shell or BP, and built the route list from that.

ideas.delivery: Owner drives a pickup with an enclosed trailer (now a box truck) 10-12 stops a day, about 6-8 hours, in a radius of about 2.5 hours around Billings. He is salesperson, driver, merchandiser and order-taker. Monday is warehouse day: pallets are received by staff at a local storage facility and the family helps put away stock. Invoices are made in a cheap app and printed. Buy-backs are rare because he picks products himself.
unit_economics_claims: About $50k/month revenue from about 95 accounts at roughly $500/month each
Gross margin about 35-40%, net margin about 30% owner-operated
Warehouse about $1,400/month for 1,500 sq ft; earlier two storage units about $500/month
One account lost in about 16 months
Full route could gross about $800k/yr with a $50-70k/yr driver
tools: Local storage-facility warehouse with staff receiving
ideas.startup_cost: Very low: a first manufacturer order of about $2,500 on 14-day terms (free racks), a car or trailer, and a cheap invoice app. Claimed it can be started with almost no money.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: About $20,000 in sales in the first month in Billings (claimed, per host)

acquisition.how: Door-to-door walk-in sales to store owners is in-person and relationship-based. Agents could help build target lists from Maps and manage follow-up schedules, but the selling is human.

onboarding.how: Setting up a store means a physical display install and a verbal agreement, with no contracts. Account records could be digitised.

delivery.how: Driving, carrying cases, merchandising shelves, receiving pallets and buy-backs are all physical work done every visit.

billing.how: Net-10 invoices from an app could be automated with accounting software and payment reminders. Stores currently pay by cheque or cash on the next visit.

support.how: Support is an owner relationship on the next visit; order changes could be handled by messaging but the model depends on face time.

uk_applicability.notes: Independent convenience stores, farm shops, garages and pubs exist in the UK, and cash-and-carry or van-sales models are established. The UK is much denser and smaller, so competition is higher and the large-radius rural advantage is less relevant. Food labelling, hygiene registration and shelf-life rules apply. Selling to stores is B2B, so PECR is not a barrier to visits, but cold email or call to sole traders needs care. Prices would be in GBP with local British brands.

Perishable or dated goods cause write-offs and buy-backs
Relationships are fragile and scaling needs staff
Heavy physical driving workload, weather (-20°C) and rural distance
Brands may limit territories or terms
Chain stores are hard to enter

summary: Chris Koerner shows how he makes $10k-$35k/month profit on Facebook's creator program by adding commentary to viral content (claimed fair use), spending about 3 hours a week. He walks through sourcing reels on a fresh Instagram account, scripting with Gemini, editing green-screen overlays in CapCut, posting natively everywhere, and tagging creators. He funnels Facebook traffic to a Beehiiv newsletter (96k to 250k subscribers in a year) and monetizes signups via SparkLoop. A sample video critiques a junk removal claim and lays out a no-truck bootstrap plan.

video.title: He Watched This Channel and Started a $2,600/Week Side Hustle

summary: Tim describes testing a mobile RC construction play experience at fairs and private events, then preparing a permanent store with construction and rock-crawling zones. He shares session prices, event costs, startup spending, early sales, and the software he built in Replit to manage sessions and other operations. The store is a larger, less-proven expansion, with memberships and an outdoor course planned. The main takeaway is that event testing helped him learn about demand and operations before committing to a permanent location, though several store projections remain estimates.

ideas.name: Mobile RC construction play trailer
ideas.one_liner: A trailer-based sand pit where children and adults pay to operate remote-controlled construction machines at fairs, festivals, and private events.

pricing.notes: The $5 session price is equivalent to $1 per minute. Tim says the store will use a different pricing model.

acquisition_channels.details: No marketplace was named. The business booked space at county fairs and festivals; event fees and access requirements varied.

ideas.delivery: Tim and his wife run the trailer at events. They set up a sand pit, hand out remotes, take payments, answer questions, monitor session times, change batteries, and right vehicles that flip over. A customer can use different machines during their paid session.
unit_economics_claims: Tim says 1,700 sessions sold at $5 each over the summer and seven private parties booked at $399 for two hours.
He says changing from $5 for 10 minutes to $5 for 5 minutes doubled the business.
Fair fees were reported as $100 to $550 per week.
The first fair sold 10 sessions and generated about $50 in revenue, which Tim says was effectively lost to food bought by his daughter and her friend.
He reports typical bad-day revenue of $200 to $300 and best-day revenue of $800.
He reports about $2,600 in revenue at a five-day fair.
The trailer version cost about $10,000 to $11,000 to start.
tools: Custom session-tracking and POS app built in Replit
RC excavators, front loaders, crane, trucks, and other vehicles
Trailer, sand pit, remotes, batteries, and session display
ideas.startup_cost: Tim estimates about $10,000 to $11,000 for the trailer version, including a $6,000 trailer, machines, four-wheel-drive vehicles, and marketing materials.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; Tim says it took roughly six to eight months to break even.

acquisition.how: Event attendance, networking, and in-person promotion require a person. In-person sales and event relationships are not unattended software tasks.

onboarding.how: The app records a customer's name, optional email, and session length, but a person still interacts with the customer and starts the sale.

delivery.how: A person must set up and operate the physical trailer, hand out remotes, change batteries, answer questions, and reset flipped vehicles.

billing.how: The custom app supports sales, but staff take payment and handle the customer interaction.

support.how: Staff answer questions, explain the activity, and manage equipment and session issues in person.

uk_applicability.notes: The event-based activity could work in the UK, but venue access, event fees, insurance, seasonal weather, and local demand would need adapting. The reported US fair prices and customer economics do not establish UK pricing.

risks: Tim says the trailer walls were too high for passers-by to see the activity, and that it could look like an ordinary trailer among other event vendors.
Some visitors thought the business sold the machines, so the offer needed explaining.
Demand at outdoor events depends on crowd size and weather; a high event fee does not guarantee a good result.
Parents sometimes thought the session price was too expensive.
The RC cars flipped often, creating staff work, and the first trailer layout did not work well for both operators inside.
Machines ran through their batteries during a very busy paid event.
Tim says a pair of dump trucks did not work in the sand pit as designed.

The transcript says customer names and emails are retained for marketing but does not describe consent or another legal basis. For UK marketing, the business would need to follow PECR and data-protection requirements.

video.title: 40 Ways to Make $400,000 from Unwanted Land

summary: Chris Koerner presents dozens of ways to earn money from unwanted or underused land, using examples from his property and businesses he has seen. Ideas range from camping, storage and rentals to food, trees, construction, equipment and land resale. He repeatedly recommends testing demand before making large investments, using existing marketplaces, and finding ways to repurpose low-cost assets. Many examples are US-specific, rely on physical work, or are anecdotes about other operators rather than independently verified results.

speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; presents land monetization ideas and recounts his own experience and examples from other operators.

ideas.name: Tent camping on private land
ideas.one_liner: List quiet plots of land for tent campers who do not need hookups.
ideas.business_model: Per-night campsite rental through peer-to-peer camping marketplaces.

video.title: How to Get Your First Service Clients Paying Tens of Thousands

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jamison, a former private-equity professional who launched West Coast Decks in Southern California with no trade experience. He closed $60,000 of jobs in month one using paid lead services, and says he reached just under $1M in year one and now does $4-8M a year. The video is a tactical playbook for launching a high-ticket home service business: pick a low-decision-count, high-order-value niche, invest in branding early, respond to leads in seconds, hire a well-paid VA, cultivate referrals from adjacent trades via social media, and bid at 50% gross margin (2x COGS).

ideas.name: West Coast Decks (premium deck building)
ideas.one_liner: High-ticket deck design and build company in Southern California, started with no trade experience using strong branding and fast lead response.

Posts daily on Instagram and Facebook plus an email newsletter; consistent branding and profiles on Google, Yelp, Houzz, BBB and Chamber of Commerce.

Instagram-driven referrals from other trades (mostly landscapers, roofers) said to produce about $400k in year one and $600k in year two; also meets lumber yards and supplier sales reps in person who send leads.
No ads for the first 3 years; PPC, Google LSA and Meta ads are a 2026 initiative.

video.title: How To Get Paid $2,500 + Monthly Checks for "Drag & Drop" AI Employees

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Danny, a member of his TK Owners community, who builds AI voice agents (on Go High Level) for local businesses such as barbers. He built a free missed-call voice agent and website for his own barber, which produced a referral chain and several inbound calls from barbers. Danny plans to charge $2,500-$5,000 upfront plus $200-$500 per month. His sales method is to build a Replit website mockup or a live voice agent demo before the first meeting, then reconnect a week or two later to close. The takeaway is to start with a free, high-quality build for someone in your circle and use the result as a showcase and referral source.

video.title: Companies Are Panic Paying for This Skill. Here’s How to Get In

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Brandon Gdosc, a Dallas-based former corporate 'AI operations' lead who five months earlier started a solo AI consulting and services business. He claims roughly $30k of small projects in the first six weeks, then growth to an ~$800k annual run rate (about $60-80k/month). He sells audits ($10-15k), fractional AI-executive retainers ($20-35k/month) and custom builds, mainly to 400-6,000 employee companies. Key takeaways: price high, ask discovery questions instead of solutioning, use a three-level solution framework, and build solutions yourself rather than just advising. The host promotes his own Playmakers community.

video.title: How to Build & Sell Micro Apps in 2026 (Using Only AI)

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates building a niche CRM micro-app for independent pool service operators using only AI, with no coding. He uses Claude to pick a growing niche, then compares Claude Code, Replit and ChatGPT on the same prompt: Claude Code built it in about 2 minutes and was best, Replit took about 16 minutes, ChatGPT was fast but gave code without a preview. He then runs a back-of-envelope market sizing (79,000 US pool businesses, 1,000 customers at $20-$100/month) and outlines customer-finding methods: Facebook groups for feedback, Gummy Search for Reddit pain points, Claude deep research, Google Trends, scraping and cold outreach, and Facebook custom-audience ads. Key takeaway: niche vertical SaaS is cheap to prototype with AI, and validation and distribution are the real work.

video.title: I Tested This "Genius" Side Hustle (Is It A Goldmine?)

summary: Chris Koerner tests a disc golf 'ace challenge' inspired by a New Zealand floating golf green that reportedly nets $500k a year: players pay for throws and win $1,000 for a hole-in-one. In a Dallas park, security stopped him charging or paying out, so revenue was $0. At DFW Disc Golf in Arlington, with proceeds going to the owner's homeless charity, players threw from 95 feet and one skilled player aced it after about 180 shots, with $780 in fees against the $1,000 prize. Key takeaway: skill-challenge businesses are a statistics problem, so test for free to measure hit rates by distance and skill, then price accordingly and partner with tournaments and shops.

He pairs each with an antidote: Gratitude, Reminders, Interaction, Traction. The video contains no detailed business model; the only business idea is a brief mention of local newsletters, which coincides with a Beehiiv sponsor read. Key takeaway: entrepreneurship is emotionally volatile, so spread risk, stay connected, and notice small wins.

video.title: Craigslist is a Goldmine. Here's Where the Gold Is

summary: Chris Koerner shows ways to use scraped Craigslist listings to find arbitrage, source leads, and build niche products such as a job board. He demonstrates a scraping workflow with Oxyabs, spreadsheets, and ChatGPT, then discusses his earlier phone-unlocking, iPhone-parts, and car-auction businesses. Most Craigslist ideas are proposals or examples rather than businesses he says he has tested. The key principle is to find supply where fewer buyers are looking, then reach a larger audience or match sellers with motivated buyers.

video.title: How I Turned A Gas Station Visit Into A Multi-Million Dollar Business

summary: Chris Koerner walks through the Buc-ee's mega gas station that supplies his Texas Snacks business, where he and his partner spend millions a year at full retail and resell Buc-ee's-branded snacks and merch online via Shopify. He gives store vs online prices (shirts 18 to ~33-35 USD, Beaver Nuggets 5 to 9 USD, jerky only ~40% markup) and explains the logistics: pre-ordered pallets, box truck, warehouse, listing and email blasts. He recounts the origin: spending ~3,000 USD on one of everything because Buc-ee's did not sell online, then doing 160,000 USD in month one. Key takeaway: the gap is real but margins are thin, competition is heavy and the business depends on the brand's goodwill.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Co-owner of Texas Snacks; narrates a store tour

ideas.name: Buc-ee's merchandise reseller (Texas Snacks)
ideas.one_liner: Buy Buc-ee's-branded snacks and merch at full retail in bulk and resell it online through a Shopify store to fans who cannot reach a store.
ideas.business_model: Retail arbitrage / e-commerce markup on third-party branded goods; one-off product sales.
ideas.customer: Buc-ee's enthusiasts and Texas expats around the world
ideas.problem: Buc-ee's does not sell online, so fans outside Texas cannot buy its branded products
ideas.offer: Online store (texassnacks.com) shipping Buc-ee's branded shirts, Beaver Nuggets, jerky, candy, plushies and hats

pricing.model: Markup on retail: roughly 1.4x-2x the store price
pricing.notes: Jerky only marked up about 40% because higher prices are hard to justify; Buc-ee's-logo items sell best, non-branded and generic Texas items sell poorly.

acquisition_channels.details: Launched by buying one of everything (~3,000 USD) to get Buc-ee's attention and went massively viral; first month did 160,000 USD.

quote.text: I spent about $3,000 buying one of everything to get By's attention. It got their attention. I ended up launching a business that did $160,000 its first month
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Email list: after each restock they list items and send an email to customers.

ideas.delivery: Pre-order a large palletised order with the store, collect with a box truck or Sprinter van, unload into own warehouse, list on Shopify, email the list, pick/pack/ship; about a dozen employees.

ideas.startup_cost: About 3,000 USD initial inventory (one of everything); later a warehouse and staff

acquisition.how: Email and content to an existing fan base can be automated; viral launch was a one-off stunt.

onboarding.how: Standard Shopify checkout, no onboarding.

delivery.how: Physical buying trips, truck loading, warehousing and shipping need people every time.

billing.how: Shopify payments.

support.how: Order-status and FAQ support can be handled by agents with human escalation for damaged goods.

uk_applicability.notes: The model (reselling a cult regional brand to people who cannot reach it) can work in the UK, but Buc-ee's itself is US-only; UK equivalents need a brand with cult demand and no online store. Selling branded goods and food requires trade-mark care and UK food labelling/hygiene compliance.

risks: Dependent on an unofficial relationship with the brand; the brand can stop it (Buc-ee's asked them to stop selling fudge)
Thin margins and many competitors
Brand could launch its own e-commerce
Food freshness and refrigeration constraints
Inventory risk on gimmick items (a ~2,000 USD giant beaver never sold)
Trade-mark/IP risk when reselling branded merchandise

video.title: She Buys $1 Pallets And Sells Them For $5,000 (30 Mins/Day)

summary: Mindy describes buying school book and curriculum pallets cheaply, sorting and listing useful items on eBay with ChatGPT’s help, and donating the books she does not want to sell. She says her first two pallets generated about $5,000 in revenue over roughly two months, with about three hours of work per week. She later used book-sale proceeds to buy Rent the Runway liquidation clothing and began selling it through Whatnot live shows. The main takeaway is that AI can reduce the research and listing work, while sourcing, handling, shipping, and live selling still require human effort.

ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Five days for the first curriculum set she listed for $350; she says she had bought the pallets weeks earlier and did not initially intend to resell them.

acquisition.how: Auction searches and listing review can be assisted by software, but a person must judge inventory, bid, arrange pickup, and handle physical books. Community giveaway sourcing also requires local coordination.

onboarding.how: AI can identify books and organize titles into bundles and pick lists, but a person must inspect the inventory, photograph it, and decide what to list or donate.

delivery.how: The work requires a person to collect, sort, store, retrieve, pack, and ship physical books; the guest also describes donating unwanted books.

billing.how: eBay can handle marketplace checkout and payment processing after a listing sells, with routine human reconciliation and fee review.

support.how: AI can draft listing information, but questions about condition, completeness, and custom teacher requests need human review and replies.

uk_applicability.notes: The general resale model can work in the UK, but the transcript's school auction sources and examples are US-based. A UK operator would need to identify local liquidation and surplus sources and account for local marketplace, postage, and school-procurement practices.

risks: Auction pallets may contain unknown, incomplete, damaged, or low-value inventory.
The work involves lifting, transport, storage, photography, packing, and shipping physical books.
Platform fees and postage reduce gross revenue; the guest says her net is lower than the headline sales total.
ChatGPT's suggested resale prices can be inaccurate, so Mindy checks current listings and sold listings herself.
Some curriculum has few or no eBay sold listings, making pricing and demand harder to verify.
A large unsorted lot can consume time and space; Mindy donated most chapter books rather than listing them individually.
Auction sourcing and local pickup availability may differ substantially outside the US.

video.title: Stop Guessing. Here’s How to Build What People Will Actually Pay For

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates a 'validate before you build' workflow: he polls 100 US small business owners via PickFu on which website feature they'd pay for, then uses the Mocha vibe-coding app to build an appointment booking widget (BookFlow) in under 20 minutes. Appointment booking tied with chatbot for first place; ChatGPT analysis of the written responses suggests bundling booking, forms, price calculator and a chatbot layer, leading with scheduling in ads. Key takeaway: poll your target buyer first, mine the free-text answers with an LLM, then prototype quickly with AI and sell before fully building. Mocha is described as a 'friend of the pod' (promotional link).

video.title: “Stupid Simple” Apps Are Making Millions While You Overthink

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Will Cannon, who built the B2B lead-data SaaS UpLead and the e-signature SaaS Signaturely. Will describes going from a failed mortgage company to selling email lists, then an agency, then UpLead (about $1M ARR in year one, cold email plus SEO). He then explains how he cloned the e-signature category by mining G2 reviews, building a 'stupid simple' product and proving he could get customers before building. The pair also pitch a free vertical CRM monetised through payments and payroll, and both stress selling before building and that 10k a month is a life-changing target.

video.title: Stop Wasting Money on Bad Ideas. Do This Instead.

summary: Chris Koerner argues that a low-effort way to build a product business is to take a proven product and change its form factor (e.g. gummy vs pill, caffeine in gum). He demonstrates how to use Higgsfield (AI image/video platform, with Nano Banana Pro and Kling 2.5 Turbo) to produce realistic ad creative before building the product, so demand can be tested with Facebook/Instagram ads. He pitches several product ideas: a feminine/colourful rucking vest, nose filters repackaged for cyclists, and niche-targeted creatine gummies. Key takeaway: validate before investing by generating AI ad creative, and reverse-engineer winning Amazon products using Jungle Scout, then niche them down. The video is partly a sponsored/affiliate demo of Higgsfield.

video.title: I Tried the Costco Gold Hack (How Much I Actually Made)

summary: Chris Koerner tests buying a 1 oz gold bar at Costco and describes a CollectPure workflow for selling bullion online. Local buyers offer less than his $4,209 purchase price, so the proposed profit depends on a better online resale price and stacked card rewards. At the end of the video, the bar has been shipped and he is waiting to be paid; no completed sale or realized profit is shown. The video also mentions buyers who use gold bars to make jewelry, sometimes outsourcing manufacture overseas.

ideas.delivery: The seller buys and physically handles the gold, lists it, triple-packs it, takes photos and keeps receipts, then drops it at FedEx using the marketplace label. CollectPure receives and tests the bar, repacks it, pays the seller and ships it to the buyer. The host says the test bar was shipped and he was waiting for payment.
unit_economics_claims: The host opens with a second-hand claim of $2,000–$20,000 weekly profit; the video does not substantiate it with completed sales or accounts (metric_claims item 2).
The test bar cost $4,209, while the intended resale price was about $4,150–$4,160; local offers were lower (metric_claims items 14–18).
The host estimates that card and Costco rewards could offset the resale discount, but the rewards and net return are not verified in the video (metric_claims items 23–30).
Shipping overnight was estimated at $30; CollectPure's fee and the actual shipping cost are not stated (metric_claims item 21).
ideas.startup_cost: The test bar cost $4,209; other startup costs are not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; at the end of the video the bar had been shipped and the host was waiting to be paid.

acquisition.how: A marketplace listing can attract buyers, but checking stock, obtaining the bar and comparing local offers involve manual calls and a physical purchase.

onboarding.how: An online marketplace can handle account setup and listing workflows, but a person must provide the bar details and create or review the listing.

delivery.how: A person must obtain, handle, package and physically ship the gold bar.

billing.how: Marketplace escrow and payout can automate payment steps, while card selection, reward tracking and reconciling a high-value transaction need human checks.

support.how: The marketplace performs authentication, but a seller may need to handle shipping questions, payment delays or buyer disputes.

uk_applicability.notes: The buy-and-resell model could transfer, but the video depends on US Costco pricing and card rewards, Venmo, CollectPure and local buyer quotes. A UK version would need equivalent bullion stock, a suitable marketplace and locally available rewards; check UK tax and product rules.

risks: The host does not show a completed sale or disclose realized profit; the opening weekly profit range is not substantiated in the demonstration.
The local quotes are below the $4,209 purchase price, so the host depends on an unconfirmed online sale price and reward eligibility.
Gold prices can move between purchase, listing and sale, changing the spread.
The transcript does not state CollectPure's fees, payout timing, shipping insurance cost or the actual reward payout.
The transaction ties up substantial cash in physical inventory and requires secure packaging and shipping.
The host says card cashback can depend on whether Costco is categorized as a grocery purchase, and that not all cards categorize it that way.

summary: Chris Koerner tours a concrete-leveling (polyurethane foam lifting) operation in Houston with Jeff, a W-2 employee and father who started 90 days earlier and subcontracts all the physical work. Jeff claims almost $20k revenue, 30-40% gross margins and a $2,500 average job. He gets leads via Facebook ads, Nextdoor, Google, referrals, a Replit-built site with chatbots and HighLevel texting, and quotes jobs remotely from photos. Koerner shows the maths that about 36 leads a month and about 5 quoting hours a week could yield $10k/month profit. Key takeaway: a drop-servicing model, where you sell, quote and coordinate while insured subcontractors do the work, can run part-time, though the claims are early-stage and self-reported.

summary: Chris Koerner explains how to sell database reactivation as a service to small businesses using GoHighLevel templates. He proposes a no-brainer, performance-based offer (10% of revenue generated from emailing/texting a client's past-customer list), walks through importing contacts, triggering a workflow, auto-replies, and A/B testing offers. He then suggests upselling other services (AI voice agents, missed-call text back, review automation, chatbots). The video is promotional for GoHighLevel via his affiliate link, and the revenue maths is hypothetical.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Spencer (Lonear Trash, Texas), a software founder who started a residential trash subscription business by pre-selling 3-month service to ~150-200 neighbours on Facebook after the incumbent hauler degraded. He bought a used under-CDL side-loader truck 100% financed, sourced used bins, and grew via referrals (free month per referral), Facebook ads (CAC $35-100), and branded bins. Claimed ~$50-60k/month revenue, ~$300k first-year revenue and ~40% margin on rough maths, with very low churn. They also discuss municipal truck auctions as a flip or list-selling side hustle, city contracts, and starting cheaper with bulk junk pickup.

video.title: He Tried an Idea From My Video and Made $46k in One Month

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Hunter (Rogersville, near Springfield, Missouri), who started a parking-lot line striping and seal coating business after hearing an earlier Koerner Office episode with Sinko. In his first two months he claims about $22.9k then $46.8k in revenue (just under $50k total), roughly $20k net profit, on about $3k startup cost. Customers came mainly from a single cold email to about 300 Springfield churches (claimed 7-12% response), followed by in-person quotes. Key lessons: offer both striping and seal coating, show up in person, hire help early, and buy reliable equipment.

video.title: The Easiest Way to Build a Local Newsletter

summary: Chris Koerner builds a local newsletter live for a random US city (Roswell, New Mexico) on Beehive in about 90 minutes. He launches a Meta lead-ad campaign with an instant form, connects it to Beehive via Zapier, and gets his first subscribers within about 10 minutes at roughly $1.15 per lead. He explains monetisation through CPM sponsorships, Beehive boosts and recommendations, referrals, paid tiers and merch, with the claim that a subscriber is worth about 50 cents a month. The key takeaway is to acquire subscribers first with cheap paid ads, then sell sponsorships to local businesses. Beehive is an affiliate partner, so the content is promotional.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office, based in Dallas-Fort Worth, runs several newsletters on Beehive

ideas.customer: Readers: local residents (e.g. ages 25-45) of a town of about 50k+ people. Paying customers: local businesses that sponsor the newsletter.
ideas.problem: Local residents don't know what is happening in their town. Local businesses lack a cheap, targeted way to reach residents.
ideas.offer: A free weekly (or more frequent) email with local news, events, deals and places to visit, with sponsor ads included.

pricing.model: Sponsor ads priced per CPM (per thousand opens); the subscriber side is free, with optional paid tiers.
pricing.notes: Publishing more often multiplies ad revenue because ads are sold per send, but it increases workload.

acquisition_channels.details: Meta (Facebook/Instagram) lead-gen campaign with an instant form asking for email only. Geo-targeted to Roswell, NM, with 'reach more people likely to respond' ticked, placements left open, and a 16-second talking-head phone video with captions. Started at $100/day for one day, then dropped to about $20/day. Got 8 leads in about 10 minutes at about $1.15 per lead.

Publish editions to the Beehive-hosted website so search engines and ChatGPT can index them.

acquisition.how: Paid Meta ads plus Zapier sync to Beehive run on their own once set up. Creatives and budgets need occasional human or agent tuning, and ad assets can be generated by AI.

onboarding.how: Welcome email, surveys and Zapier sync of leads into Beehive are fully automated.

delivery.how: Agents can research and draft local news from public sources and send it via Beehive. Human review is needed for accuracy, local credibility and hyperlocal facts.

He explains targeting, follow-up sequences, testing, deliverability, and how to combine cold email with other acquisition channels. video.title: You Don't Need to Invent New Products. Just Do This.

summary: Chris Koerner and Connor brainstorm businesses built by changing a product’s form factor, positioning, or distribution, using Billy Mays products and newer consumer brands as examples. They pitch products including stain-remover stickers, race tattoos, athlete filters, supplement verification, and food-label testing. They also explore service ideas such as home-environment audits and short urban meditation retreats. The recurring lesson is to find an existing demand or pain point, make the solution easier or more appealing to use, and test whether the product can earn repeat purchases.

tactics.name: Repackage a proven product through a new form factor
steps: Start with a product category that people already buy.
Identify a format that is inconvenient, unpleasant, or hard to carry.
Change the format while keeping the familiar underlying use case, such as putting greens in a gummy.
Use direct-response demonstrations to explain the new format.

quote.text: take something that's already really popular and just change the form factor.
quote.speaker: Connor

tactics.name: Sell a visible solution to an embarrassment problem
steps: Identify a problem customers feel in public, such as a stain on clothing or a visible pimple.
Design the offer around making the problem easier to face, even if it does not solve the root cause.
Make the solution easy to carry and use in the moment.
Consider consumable packs to create repeat purchases.

quote.text: You're solving embarrassment. the parent kid doesn't care, right? If I'm out with my kids and they get a big stain on their shirt
quote.speaker: Connor

tactics.name: Use retail buyer relationships to expand a product line
steps: Build a relationship with a category buyer at a retailer.
Ask which products in the category sell well and what customers want next.
Use the buyer's answer to develop a differentiated product.
Return with the new product and use the existing relationship to seek additional shelf space.

quote.text: then that's your channel right and so now it's it is let me sell as much as possible and make sure that the product is good but now let me get more products to also sell to you

warnings.warning: The episode contains an AutoDS sponsor read with unverified earnings, customer-count, and product-catalog claims. The host also promotes his TK Owners paid community.
The $500 million Grüns sales figure is explicitly presented as the guest's confidence or estimate, not verified financial reporting.
The cyclist filter concept is speculative; the speakers say they do not know how well the product works. Do not make pollution-protection claims without evidence.
The mouth-tape discussion includes unverified breathing and athletic-performance claims; the speaker says it is not medical advice.
The home environmental audit could create a conflict if the consultant profits from selling the products recommended.
The supplement and nutrition-label examples are anecdotal. The transcript does not establish that the cited products or labels were independently tested.
A bomb calorimeter result alone may not establish all nutrition-label values or biological effects; test method and interpretation matter.
The host's 10% adoption estimate and 5,000-person sponsor exposure calculation for race tattoos are hypothetical.
The festival tattoo and custom gummy ideas depend on production, permissions, and customer demand that the speakers have not validated.
The quiet-session concept needs a clear customer safety process if customers hand over their phones or become distressed.

lessons.lesson: Look for a familiar product that is awkward to use, carry, or consume, then test whether a different form factor makes it easier to adopt.

quote.text: take something that's already really popular and just change the form factor.
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: A product can succeed by addressing the moment a customer feels embarrassed, even if it does not solve the underlying cause.

quote.text: You're selling a very cheap thing for a pretty high markup because you're solving that embarrassment problem.
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: Repeat purchases are easier to build when the product is consumable and fits into an existing habit.

quote.text: And it's consumable. Mhm. So, you buy more and more of them.
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: Direct-response product marketing still uses familiar techniques: strong visual hooks and demonstrations that make the benefit easy to understand.

quote.text: It was classic direct response marketing like to the tea.
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: Retail relationships can reveal what buyers want next and create an opening to pitch differentiated products.

quote.text: And you build up those relationships really strong.
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: Packaging can be part of the product innovation, but a novel packaging format may require manufacturers to change their process.

quote.text: they literally had to go to every single one of these co-ands and have them reinvent one of their processes
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: Physical-world concepts often hinge on manufacturing, distribution, or event partnerships, so validate those dependencies early.

quote.text: This depends on depends on how hard it is to make custom temporary tattoos. So, hinges a lot on the manufacturing.
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: Trust can be a product feature when buyers cannot easily verify quality; independent testing and avoiding affiliate conflicts are possible ways to support it.

quote.text: you're selling trust, right?
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: In supplements and health products, efficacy matters because customers are buying an intended outcome, not just taste or convenience.

quote.text: And so if it's not accomplishing that goal, the efficacy is just really important for this type of stuff.
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: Do not confuse a plausible idea or a large market with proof of demand; the speakers repeatedly leave pricing, adoption, and market size open questions.

quote.text: Would people pay that? I don't know.
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: Optimisation can become counterproductive when small measurements dominate how someone feels about their health.

quote.text: when you are obsessed with getting the perfect thing, whether it's the perfect level of fish oil in your bloodstream or like the perfect weight on the scale or whatever, you're actually never going to feel good no matter what.
quote.speaker: Connor

lessons.lesson: Make a lengthy experience more accessible by testing a shorter version that fits into a normal day.

quote.text: You didn't do a seven-day silent meditation retreat. You did a 48 hour silent meditation retreat or four hours or like an afternoon, honestly.
quote.speaker: Connor

evidence_quality.rationale: This is an idea-generation interview, not a documented operator case study. It includes some specific firsthand anecdotes, but most proposals are unvalidated, several market and product claims are second-hand, and the Grüns sales estimate is explicitly uncertain.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The episode contains an AutoDS sponsor read, and Chris Koerner promotes his TK Owners paid community.

video.title: I Built an AI Agent That Works While I Sleep (Cheap & Easy)

summary: Chris Koerner explains the difference between automations and AI agents. On camera, he builds a 'content multiplication' agent in n8n self-hosted on a Hostinger VPS that turns his latest YouTube transcript into short, medium and long LinkedIn posts with GPT-5. He warns about n8n cloud costs and pitches selling such agents to creators and businesses for $300-800/month plus a $2,000 setup fee, projecting $10-30k/month with 10-30 clients. The video is sponsored by Hostinger and the income figures are hypothetical.

video.title: Marcus Lemonis Opens Up: Depression, Regrets, & Losing Millions

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Marcus Lemonis (The Profit, now The Fixer on Fox; Camping World; Bed Bath & Beyond) in New York. Marcus says he lost about $50 million personally investing in businesses on the shows, has funded over 100 small businesses of which fewer than 10 worked out, and now gives no-strings money (e.g. $55k) instead of taking equity. He talks openly about depression, anxiety, work as self-medication, regret about not having children and about doing TV, and his push to try uncomfortable things like anchoring live news. Advice for beginners: pick one thing, take calculated finite risks, start with small side hustles and never bet the house. His next-decade idea is an 'everything home' platform with homes recorded on blockchain via Bed Bath & Beyond and tZERO.

video.title: How to Make $15k/M on FB Marketplace Selling This ONE Item

summary: Chris Koerner re-interviews Alex Nelson, 'the Shelf Dude' from Utah, who makes custom wooden shelving for storage totes and sells it exclusively through Facebook Marketplace. Alex charges about $40 per tote space, spends about $150 in materials on a $1,000 shelf, quit his job in May 2024 and reached about $15k/month net profit. Since then he has added digital plans, an eight-module course and an installer network on a 70/30 split, because shelving brings no repeat customers. They discuss Marketplace best practices: many free listings, price testing, boosting in competitive markets, and in-person visits that close 100% of the time.

video.title: Beginner's Guide to Dividend Investing: Build a Stock Portfolio That Pays You $5,000/Month

summary: A beginner-oriented explainer on building a dividend stock portfolio targeting $5,000/month in passive income. It covers stock categories (blue chip, dividend growers, high yield, growth), valuation metrics, staggering payout months, contribution milestones assuming 7% total return and 3% yield, and the 4% rule. Key takeaway: it needs roughly $1.2M-$2M invested and decades of consistent reinvestment, so start small and avoid chasing high yields. The speaker promotes a Blossom portfolio and a Webull transfer bonus.

video.title: How Anybody Can Start This $15k/Month Business

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Tim Mloud ('The Full-Time Flipper'), a former nurse in Muskoka, Ontario, who flips premium used couches bought on Kijiji/Facebook Marketplace in dense city neighbourhoods and resold from five storage units. He did $183k sales and ~$120k gross profit in 2023 working part-time, targeting ~$1,000 profit per couch, with video inspections, keyboard-shortcut scripts and deadline-driven sourcing. video.title: The New Best Way to Make Money Reselling Online?!

summary: Chris Koerner and reseller Shannon Gene discuss buying liquidation inventory and selling it through wholesale deals, online marketplaces, and live auctions. Shannon argues that live selling can make low-cost apparel lots worthwhile by replacing much of the work of photographing and listing items, while he also stresses audience building, freight costs, and starting with small batches. Chris pitches vending machines stocked with mystery packages, and they discuss bin stores, returned goods, reseller software, and collectible card breaks. Many of the earnings figures are examples or estimates rather than verified results.

Planting an Xbox in a mystery machine to create excitement could mislead buyers if the promotion does not clearly explain the odds and contents.
The guest promotes ResellBot and reseller learning groups, and the host promotes TK Owners and a paid mastermind; recommendations and claims may have promotional motives.

video.title: 5 Jobs You Can Get WITHOUT A College Degree in 2026

summary: The video presents five degree-free career paths: pet care, remote sales, electrical and solar work, digital marketing, and AI automation. It gives suggested learning and entry steps for each, alongside earnings and industry figures that are not independently verified in the transcript. The host also mentions building Casper Capital and growing faceless Instagram pages, but gives little detail about how either was monetised. Most of the featured paths require substantial human work; AI automation consulting has the clearest potential for software-led delivery, though the video does not explain a mostly autonomous operating model.

They argue that $500-$1,000/month-per-customer or high-ticket local service businesses (e.g. garage cleanouts at $700) reach $20K/month far more easily than $10-$40/month subscriptions or ecom. They also pitch local newsletters as an audience asset and an agent that buys available city+service domain names. Key takeaway: pick high-ticket offers, start building an asset or audience, and keep working on what works rather than chasing shiny objects.

summary: Chris Koerner and Brandon Doyle each vibe-code a lawn care instant-quote web app in the Emergent tool in under an hour, for about $10 of credits. Brandon builds a polished landing page with lawn size, services and frequency discounts; Chris builds a lead-capture form with lot math, scaled discounts, minimums and a Stripe link, meant to be sent via missed-call text-back. They argue that cheap custom tools beat paying for bloated SaaS like Jobber or Salesforce and can be a free lead magnet into home service businesses. video.title: I Built a Money-Making App in 1 Hour With AI (Bolt v2 Review)

summary: Chris Koerner tests bolt.new V2 (now integrating Claude Code) by building a PR outreach app live in about an hour with 15-20 prompts. The app stores company and campaign info, accepts a CSV of journalists, generates AI pitches via OpenAI, sends them through Resend, and tracks opens and replies. Several things broke along the way (saving data before Supabase was connected, a select-all bug, fallback templates until the OpenAI key was added, needing a Resend marketing account) and were fixed by describing errors and pasting screenshots. Bolt refused to scrape journalist emails for privacy reasons. Key takeaway: non-coders can build working internal automation tools quickly, but expect iterative debugging; the video also contains a .online domain sponsor read.

video.title: Watch Me Build an AI Agency in 24 Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner builds a sample AI voice agent for roofing contractors, scrapes local business listings, and tests a cold-text campaign to find potential customers. The agent answers common roofing questions and offers to schedule a roof inspection; the video does not show a paying customer or a completed sale. Koerner reports replies and warm leads from a 100-contact experiment, then estimates what those results might mean at larger volumes. He also recommends testing several local-business industries and promotes his AI implementation community.

speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; also identifies himself in the video as Chris.

ideas.one_liner: Build and configure a branded phone agent that answers roofing questions and helps callers arrange inspections.

ideas.offer: A customized, local-number voice agent that answers calls 24/7, responds to common roofing questions, and offers inspection appointments. Koerner first creates a sample, then proposes personalizing it for an interested roofer.

ideas.delivery: Koerner creates a voice agent in GoHighLevel, selects a voice and local phone number, writes a roofing knowledge base with ChatGPT, and inserts business-specific details after a prospect agrees to test it. The agent handles calls and can offer appointments; the roofer would perform the physical inspection and roofing work. No paid customer onboarding or live customer delivery is demonstrated.

Koerner reports 15 replies and three warm leads from 96 delivered texts in this experiment.
ideas.startup_cost: The lead pull was estimated at $1.50–$10. GoHighLevel voice usage was quoted at $0.02 per minute. Other setup costs were not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: No paying customer or revenue is shown. Koerner reports obtaining warm leads during the experiment, but does not report when or whether any paid revenue followed.

acquisition.how: The demonstrated channel is unsolicited text outreach, which cannot be automated legally in the UK for individuals and sole traders without consent. A compliant inbound channel or appropriately screened business outreach would be needed.

onboarding.how: Lead lists and templates can be prepared with software, but a person still needs to confirm the customer, add accurate business details, and configure the agent.

delivery.how: The voice agent can answer routine calls and offer appointments on its own, but a person must build and check its knowledge base and the contractor must perform inspections and roofing work.

billing.how: The transcript gives no billing workflow. A recurring charge could be automated, but the service and usage charges would need human setup and oversight.

support.how: Call transcripts and ratings can help review performance, but a person would need to handle incorrect answers, customer-specific changes, and escalations.

uk_applicability.notes: The voice-agent service could work for UK roofing firms, with UK-specific business details and call handling. The demonstrated unsolicited SMS prospecting is not suitable for UK individuals and sole traders without consent under PECR; local consent and data-protection requirements would need to shape acquisition.

risks: Unsolicited marketing texts to UK individuals and sole traders without consent create a PECR compliance risk.
The demo agent gives generic or potentially invented business information, including claiming the company has served the area for years; inaccurate answers could harm a roofer's reputation.
The sample knowledge base and appointment flow are not shown to be checked against a real contractor's services, availability, or service area.
Voice usage and model costs can rise with call volume or long calls.
Roofers may receive heavy marketing outreach; Koerner says competition varies by area.
The reported campaign produced warm leads, not confirmed sales, so the revenue projections remain unproven.

summary: Shannon Gene and host Chris Koerner discuss how to start reselling with free or cheap goods, then use research and reinvestment to move into larger auction lots. They show examples ranging from couches and books to rugs, pressure washers, furniture, vehicle parts and specialist equipment. Their main growth example is Joe, who built a used pressure-washer resale business in Sacramento. The central lesson is to check local demand, item condition, transport and resale prices before bidding; most of the examples still require substantial physical handling.

tactics.name: Research local demand before bidding
steps: Choose the resale venue first, such as eBay, Whatnot, Poshmark or Facebook Marketplace.
Search the category and inspect sold listings rather than relying on active asking prices.
Check what top sellers list and what appears to sell in the local market.
Use an incognito browser session when researching competitor listings, as Shannon suggests.

quote.text: The thing is is trying to find what sells in your market. That's the first one.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Match inventory to an unfair advantage
steps: List practical advantages such as storage, a warehouse, a barn, helpers, repair skills or a useful network.
Choose products that fit those advantages; avoid bulky appliances if there is no space or moving help.
Use product knowledge to focus on a niche where other bidders may have less expertise.

quote.text: And then you match those products to your what your advantages are.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Use image and listing research to investigate obscure lots
steps: Screenshot unclear auction photos and use image research as a starting point.
Treat AI identification and price estimates as leads, not proof.
Call the auction contact to confirm brand, completeness and condition.
Avoid public questions that expose useful research to competing bidders.

quote.text: The great thing about Gov Deals is you can contact these people. You can ask a question.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Start with low-cost items and build experience
steps: Start with free or cheap local goods such as couches or books.
Make small mistakes and learn what sells before committing to expensive lots.
Reinvest as the seller gains knowledge and can evaluate inventory more quickly.

quote.text: Start small, make some mistakes, figure it out. What do you like to sell?
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Create visual listing content that shows the work
steps: Film time-lapse cleaning or preparation with a phone.
Show visible restoration or condition improvements in the listing.
Use the video to stop local marketplace users while they scroll.

quote.text: You're going to show them doing that as well. And that is the first thing people are going to see when they're scrolling through Facebook Marketplace.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Use local listings to clear a consistent furniture lot
steps: Count the inventory and create separate listings for repeatable item types.
Set a low, clear price and include the pickup address and collection hours.
Say that an item is available while it remains listed and avoid spending time replying to repetitive availability messages.
Offer a room set as a bundle where useful, and state whether prices are firm.

quote.text: If you're seeing it here, it's in stock right now. If you message me, is this still available? I will not respond to you.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Check manifests, photos and freight before buying
steps: Get the manifest and calculate the delivered cost per unit.
Compare freight cost with the auction bid before deciding whether the lot is viable.
Inspect item photos for poor stacking, exposed surfaces and likely damage.
Prefer items protected in their boxes when possible.

quote.text: You want to always have a manifest. They tell you exactly what you're going to get.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Use low-margin staples to bring customers into a store
steps: Stock frequently needed goods that local customers have to travel to buy.
Price them near a familiar retailer's price to encourage visits.
Use the visit to expose shoppers to the rest of the store's changing inventory.

quote.text: He's like, 'I sell it the same price Costco does.' And I just bring it in, bring it in, bring it in. It gets them in the store.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Make a home-based liquidation operation welcome locally
steps: Offer neighbours first access to discounted goods.
Let local families buy items so the business is seen as useful to the community.
Manage delivery times and noise so nearby residents are not surprised by trucks.

quote.text: So everybody gets a deal in your neighborhood. Everybody gets a $100 Blackstone.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Sell liquidation as a treasure hunt
steps: Show buyers the unusual deal and invite interest rather than using pressure-heavy sales language.
Offer a clear discount on recognizable products.
Build repeat local buyers by letting them know more stock may arrive.

quote.text: It's like, wow, I got all this stuff. It's amazing. would you I have these Blackstone grills I could sell for half price.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Avoid emotional bids in efficient markets
steps: Estimate realizable resale value rather than relying on a high reference price.
Subtract buyer fees and likely selling costs before setting a maximum bid.
Walk away if the spread depends on winning at an unrealistic price.

quote.text: someone's going to be bidding with emotion, which is a big mistake.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

video.title: AI Lets You Start This Amazon Side Hustle in Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates how to research, create and publish AI-assisted books through Amazon KDP, with BookBolt as the main research and formatting tool. The examples include coloring books, journals, activity books and puzzle books, alongside second-hand case studies with reported sales. He recommends looking for specific demand, checking competition, and customizing templates rather than publishing generic material. The key takeaway is to treat early books as experiments: test consistently, learn from results and build on the products that find buyers.

tactics.name: Use marketplace research before choosing a book topic
steps: Start with a topic you know well enough to edit and judge.
Use BookBolt keyword and product research to compare search interest, competition and estimated sales.
Try specific long-tail phrases rather than broad topics alone.
Check whether searchers appear to want books; the host notes that Texas barbecue searches may be restaurant searches.
Look at movers-and-shakers and evergreen product lists for ideas, then validate the niche further.

quote.text: the more specific and niche your keywords are the better your search results will be.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Choose a topic the publisher can review
steps: List topics the publisher knows and cares about.
Use that familiarity to review AI-written material and spot content that does not make sense.
Do not assume AI removes the need for subject knowledge or editing.

quote.text: we need to be able to edit it so the book or piece of content reads in a way that just makes sense, that doesn't sound like AI.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Differentiate and test journal titles
steps: Study existing journal titles and identify a clear, relatable angle.
Use ChatGPT to brainstorm related title ideas.
Publish a small batch of ideas to learn which gets traction.
Customize templates rather than using default output unchanged.

quote.text: Give me 10 more journal ideas with funny titles like these.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Put advertising behind products that show signs of demand
steps: Publish and test products first.
Identify a product that appears to be a winner.
Then put Amazon ads behind that product.

quote.text: Then once you find a winner, then you can put Amazon ads behind it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use BookBolt Studio to prepare KDP-ready files
steps: Choose a journal size and interior format.
Set the paper type and page count.
Use the studio's formatting for Amazon KDP, then review the design before publishing.

tactics.name: Run a short initial experiment and keep learning
steps: Try the process for 30 days.
Start with one product to learn the workflow.
Then test other product types such as coloring books, planners, calendars and graduation guest books.
Treat the first book as practice rather than assuming it will be a winner.

video.title: He Built a Simple App and Sold It for $200 Million

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Dan Porter, former teacher and CEO of OMGPOP, who designed Draw Something, a friends-only drawing game that hit #1 in 60 countries with 25M daily players and sold to Zynga for $200M. He explains the key ingredients (simplicity, streaks, friends-only play, live drawing playback) and how a bug fix made it take off. He later led digital at WME and founded Overtime (110M followers, own leagues) and launched 67 Water from a meme. Key takeaway: building is research, small tweaks matter, and hits need all ingredients together.

video.title: We Copied His $10K+/Month Business From Scratch in a New City

summary: Chris Koerner and Kyler (22, Utah) replicate Kyler's Facebook Marketplace washer/dryer rental business from scratch in Dallas-Fort Worth, a market saturated after their earlier viral video. They skip name, LLC and website, post a $60/month listing, boost it for $20, buy a cheap set at a garage sale for $125, and deliver and install. In one afternoon they rent two sets for $70/month recurring in about 4 hours of work. They argue competition grows the market, a $20 boost can acquire a customer worth around $1,300, and the bottleneck is the owner's time. Revenue extrapolations are hypothetical and promotional (Koerner sells a membership).

summary: Chris Koerner and regular guest Sam discuss one-person businesses that can reach $20K/month profit without employees. Sam describes testing an AI-written divorce book ($29 ebook, $17 bump, $300 back-end) sold via Facebook ads at roughly break-even CAC, then printing 300 physical copies until Facebook restricted the ads as 'personal hardship' targeting. Chris adds the idea of monetising the book buyers by referring them to divorce lawyers for pay-per-lead or consulting/referral fees, and extends it to niche legal books (DUI, car accident, etc.). The key takeaway is to test quickly rather than over-research, start with the simple pay-per-lead model, and that $20K/month solo is far easier than scaling to a million-dollar team business.

summary: Tyler describes starting a stump grinding service in Utah while keeping his full-time job, then going full-time after demand grew. He found early work by subcontracting for tree companies, then added homeowner jobs through Google Business Profile and reviews. He explains his pricing, equipment costs, outreach, operating routine, and some risks from underground utility lines. The hosts also discuss selling a stump grinding playbook, a possible mulch sideline, and other business paths.

tactics.name: Piggyback on trades with an existing stump problem
steps: List tree companies in the surrounding service area, along with landscape installers, fence installers, and concrete contractors who sometimes encounter stumps.
Prioritise businesses that rent a grinder or already use a subcontractor.
Contact a small batch at a time so the full lead list is not used at once.
Ask whether they grind stumps themselves, subcontract the work, or own a machine.
Call businesses that respond and explain how the service could save them time or improve turnaround.

quote.text: The P stands for piggyback. So we want to piggyback off of existing businesses that have a pain point, which are tree companies that don't want to do stuff.
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Ask for a review after the job
steps: Introduce yourself to the homeowner as the stump grinding operator, even when a tree company brought you to the job.
After finishing, explain that you are growing your own company and ask directly for a review.
Make it easy for the customer to submit the review while you are there.
Keep a record of completed jobs and customer contact details so past customers can be asked later.

quote.text: Hey, I run a different company. I just started and I'm I'm working really hard to grow my company here in Utah County. Would you please give me a review?
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Make quoting simple with photos and measurements
steps: For a remote quote, ask the customer to text a photo and stump diameter.
Measure the widest point of each stump.
State a rough estimate and explain that the confirmed quote depends on the photo and measurements.
Offer the next available schedule once the customer accepts.

quote.text: If I can just text you real quick and you can text back a picture of the three stumps and just a diameter measurement. And if you get me that, that's all I need for a full quote.
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Price for travel, machine wear, and site conditions
steps: Set a minimum charge for a visit.
Use the widest stump diameter for per-inch pricing.
Account for access, stump condition, equipment depreciation, and any requested chip hauling.
Do not treat a short job as costless just because the grinding itself takes a few minutes.

quote.text: You got to be careful cuz you're not just including your own man hours. Like this is a very expensive machine and it depreciates.
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Test demand before committing to equipment
steps: Keep the existing job while testing the local market and doing early work around the work schedule.
Rent equipment at first instead of buying a grinder immediately.
Use early jobs to learn the service, gather reviews, and see whether contractors keep sending work.
Consider buying or financing a grinder after demand is clearer.

quote.text: You didn't buy the machine right away. You didn't hop into, you know, large expenses. You tested it on the side.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Win contractor work through responsiveness
steps: Answer inbound calls consistently.
Quote quickly, including by text when the job is straightforward.
Schedule promptly when a tree company needs a stump ground before it can collect payment.
Communicate immediately if something goes wrong and explain how it will be fixed.

quote.text: Responsiveness is a huge one. Second one is having the equipment that isn't the rental equipment once you get to that point.
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Turn repeat questions into a reusable product
steps: Share visual work examples on social media.
Notice repeated questions from people asking how to start.
Write the answers into a playbook instead of repeating the same introductory call.
Use a community or course for buyers who want more guidance.

quote.text: I was getting tons of DMs like, "How do you do this? How do you do this?" Really basic questions and I got really sick of hopping on every call.

video.title: You Can Now Build Apps for Free With Google AI Studio (w/ Google Insider)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Logan Kilpatrick, who leads the developer product team for Google AI Studio and the Gemini API at Google DeepMind. They discuss how vibe coding in AI Studio makes it nearly free to build and ship many small AI apps, and they live-build two apps: a video analysis engine and a voice AI lead-gen agent. Ideas covered include niche single-purpose AI apps, bundles of AI tools for one persona, an AI implementation agency for small businesses, voice AI agents and a text-based AI travel companion. Key takeaway: the cost of building software is now trivial, so take many niche shots, iterate through about 10 prompts, and use vibe-coded demos as outreach. Chris states this is not sponsored but he is a Google shareholder.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Wesley, owner of a Grounds Guys franchise in Keller, Texas (DFW), about adding a Christmas lights installation line to a lawn business. They cover pricing by linear foot, a leasing model where the operator keeps and stores the lights, rising margins in repeat years, labour and time per job, insurance, marketing (door hangers, Facebook, yard signs) and low startup costs. Wesley claims one Grounds Guys owner does $1.25M in Christmas lights alone. Key takeaway: recurring, route-dense, leased holiday lighting can have high repeat-year margins, but it is physical, risky work that agents cannot do.

video.title: 9 Beginner-Friendly Ways to Make $10K

summary: Chris Koerner and his business partner Brandon brainstorm ideas to make $10k in a year, month, week or day. Ideas include vibe-coded apps for die-hard hobby communities (board games, quilting, gardening), Chris's NEFL screener for founder-led network-effect stocks, local AI bootcamps with high-ticket upsells (Brandon has 27 sign-ups), shipping-container storage, luxury garage sales, buying estate-sale leftovers, and pop-up headshot booths. Chris also shows Backyard Fun House, a sport-court business that subs out every trade and gets leads from selfie-video Meta ads at $23-36 each, which he expects to turn $2,500 of ad spend into $25-45k net profit. Key takeaway: cheap AI-built apps and lead ads let you test ideas fast, and you should track ads through to closed deals.

video.title: The 4 Best Rural Side Hustles for 2026

summary: Chris Koerner throws a dart at a map of Texas, lands near Flatonia/Emory, and tries to start a business there with about $20, with the rule that he can't go home until he has doubled his money. After many door-to-door rejections he mows a lawn for $20 (tipped to $30), then sells $1 water outside a fair using price anchoring to reach $38. He also spots a brokerage-style opportunity: listing a rural man's old tractor and smoker online for a cut. Key takeaway: rural markets are hard, door-to-door is tough, and the most workable ideas are simple local services, selling-on-behalf for offline people, and arbitrage-style hustles. The title's '4 best rural side hustles' is not really delivered; it is an entertaining challenge video.

video.title: The Most Valuable Skill in Business

summary: Marcus explains how he uses Google Ads and YouTube Ads to help local service businesses generate leads, and Chris Koerner asks which niches and offers work best. Marcus describes researching competitors, improving landing pages, targeting YouTube audiences, remarketing, and letting campaigns mature. The examples include cleaning, roofing, solar, and a hypnosis practice, with results that vary by market and by the client’s ability to close leads. His advice for a new marketer is to get testimonials through free work, make the landing page clear, and be patient.

tactics.name: Choose niches with enough customer value
steps: Prioritize recurring or high-ticket local services whose customer lifetime value is in the thousands.
Check local competition because the same niche can perform differently between nearby markets.
Do not assume that a low one-off customer value will support paid acquisition.

quote.text: So, you want to have a a business where your the lifetime value of a client is in the thousands.
quote.speaker: Marcus

tactics.name: Research competitors before taking on a campaign
steps: Check whether the business category is allowed to advertise on Google.
Review where competitors send paid traffic and what their websites look like.
Look for pages that fail to explain how the business helps, how to contact it, and whether it has proof such as testimonials or case studies.
Use competitor weaknesses to find a practical advantage.

quote.text: The first thing to look at is can I even advertise like am I even allowed to advertise that on Google?
quote.speaker: Marcus

tactics.name: Make the landing page answer three questions quickly
steps: State how the business helps the visitor.
Show reviews or testimonials as proof.
Make contact or booking easy to find.
Put those answers where a visitor can see them in the first three to five seconds.

quote.text: If your website can answer those three things in the first 3 to 5 seconds, you have a good website.
quote.speaker: Marcus

tactics.name: Structure a YouTube lead generation ad to earn the click
steps: Use an in-stream ad.
Use the first five seconds to call out the intended customer and filter out others.
Describe the customer's problem, explain how the offer helps, and ask for the click.
Let the landing page generate the lead and the sales conversation generate the sale.

quote.text: Your ad generates a click. Your landing page generates the lead. And then when they talk to you, you generate the sale.
quote.speaker: Marcus

tactics.name: Use clear audio and a relevant script for YouTube placements
steps: Write a script that calls out the intended audience and problem.
Use a good phone and a microphone rather than assuming expensive equipment is required.
Check that audio and video quality are adequate so the campaign does not land in poor placements.

quote.text: You just need this like a good h a good phone, you know, with a nice DJI mic or whatever.
quote.speaker: Marcus

tactics.name: Build layered YouTube and remarketing campaigns
steps: Start with Google Ads and establish a regular flow of leads and an acceptable acquisition cost.
Add YouTube lead generation targeting in-market audiences, relevant search terms, and competitor websites.
Add broad brand awareness in the chosen service radius when lead generation is working.
Track website visitors and run remarketing through YouTube, display, and Facebook.
Use a special offer for remarketing visitors who did not convert.

quote.text: Once I got Google ads up and running and it's I'm getting regular leads, I know my target se I know what my target cost per acquisition is
quote.speaker: Marcus

tactics.name: Improve campaigns with small regular tests
steps: Test one part of the top of the landing page, such as the headline.
Review ad copy and click-through rate.
Make small changes regularly and compare results.

quote.text: Just all these little bits once a month makes a huge huge difference.
quote.speaker: Marcus

tactics.name: Create a lead follow-up sequence
steps: Measure call show rate rather than judging campaigns only by lead volume.
Use more than a single email reminder for booked calls.
Consider reminder messages, while ensuring that contact is permitted and compliant.

quote.text: what's your follow-up sequence do you have emails going out reminder emails going out do you have text messages
quote.speaker: Marcus

tactics.name: Get testimonials before scaling a new business
steps: Reach out to people in your network and explain the service.
Offer to do initial work for free in exchange for a testimonial.
Use the testimonials on the landing page as proof.
Ask satisfied clients for introductions to relevant contacts.

quote.text: I will help you with this. All I want is a testimonial. You have to pay me nothing. All I want is a testimonial.

tactics.name: Give campaigns time to mature
steps: Do not stop a campaign after a small number of disappointing calls.
Review the landing page, follow-up, show rate, and closing process before deciding that ads do not work.
Allow at least the stated three-month period for the system to get established.

quote.text: So, you need to be patient. This is like a threemonth process minimum to really get this humming.

video.title: I Asked AI to Help Me Beat the Stock Market

summary: Chris Koerner shows how he vibe-coded a stock portfolio backtesting app in Replit (Agent 3) to test his thesis that founder-led S&P 500 companies with strong network effects beat the market. He used ChatGPT deep research to find candidates, then built a live Google Sheet using the GOOGLEFINANCE formula, and used GPT for Sheets to score every S&P 500 company 1-10 on network effects and founder leadership for about $15 in credits. Replit then turned the sheet into a filterable dashboard. On his 8-10/8-10 filter over 10 years he reports 22.4% vs the S&P's 9% weighted and 12% unweighted. He shares about a dozen ChatGPT prompts for generating stock-picking theses and says he put the free tool ("Nel Stocks") behind an email form on a domain he bought. The business angle is small: a free, email-gated vibe-coded tool used as a lead magnet. Most of the video is personal investing, not a business.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Romain (Roma) Torres, founder of Arcads, an AI tool for generating talking AI actors for video ads and AI influencers. He shows examples (an AI influencer reportedly making $10M/year, a language app that reached $12-20M ARR on AI ads, disability-benefit lead gen) and explains which audiences tolerate AI ads. His fastest path to $10-15k/month is an AI UGC agency: find advertisers in the Facebook Ads Library, send the CEO a free AI recreation of one of their ads, and sell $2k/20-ad packages or $3-5k monthly retainers, later automating production via API. Key takeaway: AI video makes creative volume cheap; money is in selling it to companies already spending on ads, or building niche AI personas with consistent creative.

They describe additional services such as construction-site inventory checks and social media footage, plus separate examples including aerial photo sales and storm debris removal. Their central recommendation is to start part-time, build on existing industry relationships, and expand services after earning a customer's trust. Most operating figures come from the hosts' research or stories about other people rather than a directly interviewed operator.
