video.title: If People Pay for This, Your Idea Will Work Too

summary: Chris Koerner and a co-host brainstorm business ideas built around the theme that people will pay for almost anything, and that ego stops people from doing weird, attention-getting things. Ideas include novelty competition events (horse haircut show, Excel esports, vibe-coding competitions, survival challenges), a plaque-selling service triggered by magazine features, a YouTube-to-print-magazine service, and quirky marketing stunts such as a realtor 'ghost free guarantee'. Evidence is mostly brainstorming and second-hand anecdotes, with few verified numbers. Key takeaway: memorable, talk-worthy content or events can create demand and customers in otherwise boring niches.

video.title: Google Veo 3 Just Changed the Game: Here’s Your Money-Making Tutorial

summary: Chris Koerner gives a tutorial-style roundup of ways to make money with Google's Veo 3 video model ($250/month, half off for the first 3 months). Ideas include white-label AI video for production agencies, AI UGC for small ecom brands, realtor promos, stock footage, productized monthly reel packages for niche local businesses, upselling into $1k/month content retainers, prompt packs ($29), micro-courses ($49), a paid newsletter or community, and licensing your voice on ElevenLabs. He gives specific cold-DM scripts (an opt-in ask to agency owners on personal Instagram) and a 5-step 'start with $250' plan: 3 demos, 30 DMs, a $100 test video, reinvest, then a $500/month offer. He also cites a viral Reddit post where a creator now quotes $10-15k for Veo commercials. Most figures are hypothetical pricing suggestions rather than results the host has achieved. Much of the outreach relies on cold DMs, which would hit UK PECR limits when the targets are individuals or sole traders.

warnings.warning: UK PECR (extractor note): the cold DM and text tactics aimed at individuals, sole-trader trades and agency owners' personal Instagram are unsolicited electronic marketing without consent. Use company email for limited companies, or in-person or phone outreach screened against TPS/CTPS.
AI 'UGC' that looks like real customers may be misleading advertising (ASA/CMA); disclose AI-generated content (extractor note).

lessons.lesson: The AI tool isn't the product; the packaged offer is.

evidence_quality.rationale: Hype-driven roundup recorded days after launch. Nearly all pricing and income figures are hypothetical suggestions or hearsay (a Reddit post, voice-licensing earnings). The host reports no Veo revenue of his own; only the newsletter subscriber count is first-hand.

video.title: How to Start a Business? Don’t Wait for Permission.

summary: Chris Koerner speaks to a homeschool class of about 20 high schoolers, telling his story from selling washed golf balls at age 10 to iPhone repair stores, an LCD screen recycling business and a failed mobile home park venture. He answers Q&A on starting with no money, validating demand by selling before building (Facebook Marketplace, a tree trimming ad test), business partnerships, and his marketing-heavy, operations-light approach. The key takeaway is to sell something before doing 'procrastination' tasks like LLCs and websites, and to use constraints as a source of creativity.

summary: The Niche Pursuits host unboxes his second $700 Amazon return 'monster' pallet, identifying and pricing each item (ice makers, scooters, vanity desks, an automatic litter box, treadmill, shelving). video.title: AI Is Replacing Content Creators (Here’s How to Profit)

summary: Chris Koerner chats with Sam (an agency operator, Service Scalers) about AI-generated content. Topics: licensing your cloned voice on ElevenLabs for passive income, AI-generated 'boomer bait' animal videos on Facebook monetised by impressions, and Sam's stack for AI-cloned spokesperson video ads (ChatGPT, Photoshop, face swap, ElevenLabs voice-to-voice, HeyGen Avatar 4) that he says already book calls at about $10. Chris also shares a Houston billboard test for his podcast versus Facebook ads. Key takeaway: AI video is good enough to run as ad creative, and unconventional channels can be tested if you track the maths (CAC/LTV, hit rate).

summary: Chris Koerner presents ways to use ChatGPT and other AI tools for research, writing, business brainstorming, and repeatable workflows. He recommends giving AI specific context, refining prompts, and testing ideas with real audience feedback. Business examples include a local market research app, a review-fixing service, and several physical product or service concepts. The video focuses on prompting techniques rather than operating any of those businesses, and it promotes the host’s community, newsletter, and podcast.

acquisition.how: The transcript gives no way to find paying customers. If sold as software, agents could support inbound marketing and lead qualification, with a human checking demand and positioning.

onboarding.how: A web app could collect a location and industry automatically; a human may need to resolve data or setup issues.

delivery.how: Review collection, analysis, and city comparisons could run automatically, with occasional human checks for data quality and relevance.

tactics.name: Prompt for strategies and angles
steps: Ask for angles, tactics, and strategy instead of a broad request for facts.
Specify the type of opportunity, audience, or outcome you want the model to explore.
Use the response as a starting point and follow up on promising directions.

quote.text: don't just ask it for facts ask it for angles tactics leverage instead of saying things like What are some good business ideas?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Give the model reference material
steps: State the audience and desired reading level or style.
Provide examples, images, video, or text that show what you want.
Ask the model what makes a set of examples effective, then reuse those findings in a project.

quote.text: feed it as much reference data as you can whether that's an image a video or just text
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Turn prompts into reusable workflows
steps: Write a prompt that can produce the same kind of result repeatedly.
Save it in a custom GPT or project.
Upload strong examples and ask the model to identify the qualities to reproduce.

quote.text: you're not asking for answers you're asking for systems because the quality of your questions is the ceiling of your output
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Test content angles with audience polls
steps: Ask ChatGPT for eight marketing angles.
Run polls with four options at a time, asking which YouTube title people would click.
Let each poll run for about 30 minutes, then take one or two winners into a final bracket-style poll.
Use the winning angle to write the title, thumbnail, newsletter, or post.

quote.text: i will take four of the eight marketing angles post them as a poll and say Which YouTube title would you click on?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use customer reviews as research and content
steps: Collect customer reviews for a business or niche.
Use the review language to identify customer problems and search terms.
Turn suitable review themes into keyword-focused content or a specific service offer.
Check the facts and obtain any needed permissions before publishing customer material.

tactics.name: Compare local markets before choosing a business
steps: Identify industries with poor reviews in a local area.
Choose comparable cities and compare business density and average review ratings.
Treat differences as leads for further validation, not proof that a new business will succeed.

tactics.name: Refine answers across models
steps: Ask the same question in several language models.
Compare the responses and choose the one with the most useful answer.

video.title: How to Get a Yes From Anyone (and Change Your Life)

summary: Stu Heinik discusses contact marketing: researching a small number of influential people and approaching them with a distinctive, personal campaign. Examples include a targeted Facebook ad that reportedly led a tongue-scraper startup to a Walmart order, a custom sword sent to struggling-company CEOs, and personalized cartoons and mail. Host Chris Koerner adds examples from his own businesses and pitches AI-assisted research and creative outreach. The central takeaway is to make a relevant approach memorable, then stay flexible about what the recipient needs.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office.

speakers.name: Stu Heinik
speakers.description: Author of How to Get a Meeting with Anyone and practitioner of contact marketing.

ideas.name: Personalized contact marketing campaigns
ideas.one_liner: Create highly tailored campaigns to get a meeting with a small number of influential prospects.
ideas.business_model: Not stated; the guest describes creating campaigns for clients.
ideas.customer: Businesses or people seeking meetings with prospective clients, mentors, partners, or other influential decision-makers.
ideas.problem: Usual outreach channels can fail to attract attention from important prospects.
ideas.offer: Research a prospect and create a distinctive, personalized contact campaign, including cartoon mailings.

pricing.notes: The guest does not state what he charges clients.

acquisition_channels.details: Personalized cartoons were used in mailings. How the guest acquired paying clients is not stated.

quote.text: I wanted to use cartoons in those mailings. That's where it started.
quote.speaker: Stu Heinik

ideas.delivery: The guest describes personalized cartoon mailings and a group of skilled cartoonists. The cartoon is tailored to the recipient; a window in a FedEx envelope can reveal part of it and prompt the recipient to open the mailpiece. Human research and creative work are central.
unit_economics_claims: The guest says his first contact campaign achieved a 100% response rate.
The video introduction describes a campaign reaching about two dozen people, all of whom responded, met, and became clients.

acquisition.how: Software could help research prospects and prepare mailing lists, but selecting a small, high-value audience and creating relevant approaches requires human judgment. Physical mail is a possible UK-compliant channel, subject to data-protection rules.

onboarding.how: A form could collect target names and campaign goals, but a person would need to clarify the relationship, context, and appropriate tone.

delivery.how: Cartoon selection, personal research, and humor require substantial human creative work. Software could assist with research or production, but the guest stresses the distinctive work of practiced cartoonists.

billing.how: Invoicing and payment collection could be automated once a service and fee are agreed.

support.how: Routine status updates could be automated, but campaign changes and client feedback require human judgment.

uk_applicability.notes: Personalized mail and prospect research can work in the UK. The operator would need to handle personal data lawfully and respect direct-marketing rules.

risks: Personalization can take substantial time and skilled creative work.
Humor that disparages the recipient or gets details wrong can damage the approach; the guest advises keeping the recipient out of frame and making them come out well.
A memorable approach can earn a response without producing a sale or engagement.

quotes.speaker: Stu Heinik

acquisition.how: Ad targeting, campaign delivery, and inbound lead capture can be automated. Creative development, compliance review, and retail-buyer relationship management still need human oversight.

onboarding.how: Online orders can be processed automatically. Retail onboarding, buyer negotiations, and product approval would need human involvement.

delivery.how: The product must be manufactured, packed, and physically shipped, so software cannot perform most delivery work.

billing.how: Online payments and invoices can be processed by ecommerce and accounting software; retailer terms may need human review.

support.how: Automated answers could handle routine order questions, with escalation for product and retailer issues.

uk_applicability.notes: The product and online-sales model could work in the UK, but the specific Walmart route and Bentonville targeting are US-specific. UK product, labelling, and retail requirements would need to be addressed.

risks: The reported order and valuation are second-hand claims from an interview, not independently verified figures.
The ad drew a response from Walmart's legal department; creative targeting and claims about a retailer's employees can create legal or reputational concerns.
A physical product requires manufacturing, stock, fulfilment, and retailer acceptance.

video.title: You’re Not Ready for What’s Coming: Robert Scoble on AI + Future Tech

summary: Koerner Office host Chris Koerner interviews futurist Robert Scoble about AI, wearables (smart glasses, Vision Pro), autonomous cars (Waymo vs Tesla), Neuralink, humanoid robots and the US-China race. Scoble argues AI is still underhyped, that people resist new technology until they try it, and that this boom is far bigger than the dot-com era. Almost no concrete business ideas or numbers are given; the only practical advice is to ask AI to do market research and to find niches the big labs will not serve. The video is mostly trend commentary and speculation.

summary: Niche Pursuits host buys two mixed pallets of Amazon/Temu-style liquidation returns for about $700 (the transcript mentions $700 for a pallet) and unboxes one pallet on camera, researching each item's retail price. video.title: How to Build a Thriving Business in the Middle of Nowhere

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Alan Doan of the Missouri Star Quilt Company about turning Hamilton, Missouri (pop. 1,500) into a quilting destination with 16 quilt shops, restaurants, a retreat hotel, an e-commerce site and YouTube tutorials. Growth came from free YouTube content, a newsletter, a daily-deal site and a bi-monthly magazine that repurposes tutorials. He then pitches how others could build niche 'destination towns' (sourdough, fish, cheese), and riffs on side ideas: a home-services membership, a home-maintenance subscription, unstaffed small-town bodegas, small-town micro apartment roll-ups, and a tiny-town Airbnb network. Key takeaway: build an audience and a company first, then add physical experiences in undervalued small-town real estate.

video.title: 17 Years, 75 Businesses, 1 Marriage: How We Make It Work

summary: Chris Koerner talks with his wife about the strains and rewards of building businesses as a couple, including a phone repair shop, LCD work, car buying, and a home bakery. They discuss financial uncertainty, trust, backup plans, communication, and making time for family. The conversation also recalls several business concepts and possible future careers, but gives few operating or financial details for most of them. The main practical lessons are to test demand, agree on risks together, and set boundaries around work.

video.title: I've Started 75+ Businesses: Here’s What Actually Matters

summary: Chris Koerner looks back on businesses he started over 15 years and uses them to explain how a small-business CEO should handle operations, people, capital, focus, and risk. The examples include iPhone repair, LCD Cycle, online bread sales, e-commerce food fulfilment, Bitcoin mining, RV and mobile-home parks, and tree trimming. He emphasizes learning how the work is done before delegating, protecting employees and company culture, and checking partners and deals carefully. His cautionary examples show that fast growth and attractive spreadsheets can hide weak margins, concentration risk, or poor partner fit.

ideas.name: Phone Restore iPhone repair stores
ideas.one_liner: A walk-in iPhone repair business that grew from a college storefront to multiple locations and tested a mall kiosk.
ideas.business_model: Repair services; the specific pricing model was not stated.
ideas.customer: People with broken iPhones, including college students.
ideas.problem: Customers needed broken iPhones repaired.
ideas.offer: In-person iPhone repairs from storefronts and a mall kiosk. The founder learned repairs as customers arrived.

pricing.notes: No repair price was stated. The $600 figure refers to a customer's phone, not the repair charge.

acquisition_channels.details: He put an advertisement on wristbands and distributed them to college bars. Students who broke their phones returned with the advertised wristband.

quote.text: I ordered a few boxes of them. I distributed them to bars. College students would go to the bar, break their iPhone, get drunk, wake up, broke an iPhone and a wristband with an ad on it.

quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

quote.text: So, we went to Home Depot, put this sign up. People felt bad for us. We got some sales.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: After the tornadoes, he listed phones bought back from customers that had not yet been listed on eBay. This generated cash from inventory rather than repair bookings.

quote.text: And we had a bunch of iPhones that we had bought back from customers that we had never listed on eBay. So, we thought, "Okay, let's list those on eBay."
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Repairs were performed in person. The founder initially learned how to repair each customer's phone using YouTube, then later ran stores and a kiosk. A repair mistake damaged a customer's phone and caused data loss.
unit_economics_claims: The business grew to four locations before it was sold.
The founder says two-cent wristbands were used for local advertising.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The founder signed a lease with a personal guarantee; wristbands cost two cents each.

acquisition.how: Store foot traffic, local bar wristband distribution, and a physical sign require local presence and coordination. A website or paid advertising could supplement these channels, but neither was described.

onboarding.how: A customer brings in a device and staff assess it. The transcript describes a walk-in interaction, not automated intake.

delivery.how: A person must physically diagnose and repair each phone.

billing.how: The transcript does not explain payment or invoicing; an online point-of-sale system could handle routine charges, with staff resolving exceptions.

support.how: Questions and device problems require human judgement, especially where a repair damages a device or data.

uk_applicability.notes: The local repair-store model and venue-based advertising can work in the UK. The described inbound walk-in strategy does not rely on unsolicited electronic marketing.

risks: A personal lease guarantee created personal exposure.
The founder initially accepted repair jobs before knowing how to do them, creating stressful customer experiences.
A punctured battery produced smoke, and the customer lost data and had to receive a replacement phone.
A tornado destroyed part of the store and overnight revenue fell to zero.
A trusted employee stole phones and cash, according to the founder.
The mall kiosk test involved physical battery repairs and customer property, so an error could be costly.

video.title: 5 TYPES of Websites That Can Make $5k/Month in 12 Months

summary: Spencer Haws of Niche Pursuits lists the five types of websites he would build to reach $5,000 a month within 12 months: SaaS tools, e-commerce with your own product, free tool websites monetised by ads, paid membership communities, and newsletters grown with paid ads against known revenue per subscriber. He backs each with examples (his Link Whisper and Long Tail Pro, his pillow brand sold for $425k, youtubethumbnaildownloader.com, ZeroGPT, Creator Science Lab, MarketBeat). He also says to avoid search-dependent blogs, affiliate sites and social-traffic sites because of AI, Google and platform algorithm risk. Key takeaway: build websites with utility or owned audiences rather than search-dependent content.

video.title: Secrets to Making BIG Profits from Small Email Lists

summary: Koerner Office host Chris Koerner interviews Tyler Deng, co-founder of Beehive (newsletter platform, ex-Morning Brew growth lead), about monetising small email lists and growing newsletters. Topics include niche audiences monetised through cohorts, recruiting fees and events, paid acquisition and co-registration (Boost), local newsletters, content-led brand building, a referral-program 80/20 and turning a company's customer email list into a daily ad-supported newsletter. Key takeaway: niche, high-intent audiences can out-earn larger lists, and quality content plus cheap, trackable acquisition matters more than growth hacks. Both speakers have affiliate or product interests in Beehive.

lessons.lesson: Treat an audience as an asset with many possible monetisation routes; start with one and expand.
Measure acquisition quality, not just cost per signup.
Leaders should be open to testing unconventional channels, provided you can track results.
Early adoption of new ad placements gives low CPMs before the window closes.
Content-led brand building wins purchase decisions later even if it cannot be attributed directly.
Founders should have expertise or real interest in the niche they build an audience around.
Make the first referral the easiest and most rewarding step; low barriers beat large far-away rewards.
Existing business assets such as customer email lists can be repurposed into separate revenue streams.

evidence_quality.rationale: Mostly second-hand examples and back-of-envelope math; Tyler's first-hand Morning Brew experience is credible but figures are sparse and unverified. Many revenue claims are hypothetical.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Tyler Deng co-founded Beehive and Chris Koerner promotes a Beehive affiliate link and his own newsletter and podcast.

video.title: what I wish I knew at age 20

summary: Chris Koerner uses personal stories to argue that durable business results come from building a sound foundation, doing difficult sales work, testing assumptions, and focusing on what works. He briefly describes Voltera, his medical-billing software business, and shares examples from his newsletter, videos, and marketing experiments. The recurring lesson is to balance persistence and small improvements with avoiding shortcuts and over-optimization. He closes by urging gratitude and helping others without expecting recognition.

tactics.name: Make sales the foundation
steps: Start with direct conversations with potential customers.
Expect discomfort and awkward situations as part of selling.
Follow up persistently, even when it feels uncomfortable.

quote.text: You got to go talk to people. You got to be uncomfortable. You got to put yourself in awkward situations. You have to follow up to the point of annoyance.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Prefer labor-intensive outreach to an untested shortcut
steps: Compare the results of software-sent cold emails with messages written by hand.
Track deliverability and response outcomes before scaling the automated approach.
Treat the speaker's preference for manual email as an anecdote, not a measured result.

quote.text: it's not as effective as literally just typing out cold emails to people by hand.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Run small tests and revisit old winners
steps: Test one change at a time, such as a subject line or offer.
Keep a stable, effective version while testing alternatives.
Revisit old tests when the audience or conditions have changed.

quote.text: And so to this day, I do that, but I haven't tested it in over a year.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Look for high-leverage customers
steps: Compare the work needed to sign a small account with the work needed for a larger account.
When a larger customer is within reach, estimate the added locations and overhead before prioritizing it.
Do not assume large customers can be sourced on demand; Chris says there are power laws at play.

quote.text: And it's taking just as much work, if not less, to sign that customer than it's taken to sign our customers with single locations.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Review content performance and focus on outliers
steps: Track which videos drive followers rather than judging only by total publishing volume.
Identify the small group of videos responsible for most audience growth.
Study the outliers for repeatable themes while recognizing that results may not generalize.

quote.text: I've put out about 600 short form videos over the last year, and 90% of my followers have come from 2% of those.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Balance optimization with preserving a working baseline
steps: Record the settings and results of a stable campaign before changing it.
Test changes in a controlled way instead of changing multiple variables at once.
Stop testing when the cost of further experimentation outweighs likely improvement.

quote.text: You can, it is very easy to overoptimize anything.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

video.title: You Don’t Need to Be a Genius! Just Do This.

summary: Chris Koerner and regular guest Sam (Grow Faster community, Unlimited Content SEO agency) trade ideas and lessons. Sam explains selling his AI cooking app for $1,000 plus 20% of revenue, and they critique Chris's AI business-partner app idea, concluding monthly churn would be high for make-money-online products. They discuss letting customers define offers (Sam's $500/month backlinks-only SEO offer), copying competitors' iterated offers via the Wayback Machine and Facebook Ads Library, and AI-generated niche training programmes like $150-$250 rucking plans. Sam demos a custom task manager he built in Lovable in two hours. Key takeaway: get sales, follow momentum, and let the market tell you what to sell.

video.title: The Most Overlooked Way to Make Money On the Internet

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Freychu, a solo operator who builds SEO-driven niche directory websites. He owns six directories (three fully built) that draw roughly 70-90k organic monthly visitors and earn about $2,300-$3,000/month passively. The episode walks through finding niches via Ahrefs 'near me' keyword research (low keyword difficulty, decent volume), analysing example directories (dry ice, movie locations, towing capacity), tooling, monetisation and a cheap backlink-swap tactic. Key takeaway: directories are slow-burn SEO assets; pick low-competition niches, build ugly-but-useful mobile-friendly sites, enrich the data, and buy a few high-quality swapped backlinks.

tactics.name: Find directory niches with the 'near me' keyword method
steps: Open Ahrefs Keywords Explorer and search 'near me'
Skip branded keywords (Target, McDonald's)
Scroll deep, sorting by keyword difficulty; look for low KD (green) with decent volume
Aim for KD at or below about 20 generally, 0-5 for beginners; volume of 15k-60k worked best
Reject product-led or fad queries where e-commerce dominates (e.g. Dubai chocolate)
Check search intent and narrow broad terms (e.g. 'emergency towing')

quote.text: I find a lot of promise in keywords that hover around like 15,000 monthly search volume to like 60,000
quote.speaker: Freychu

tactics.name: Use a 'bounty' competitor as validation
steps: Find a mom-and-pop-looking site already getting traffic in the niche
Check its traffic in Ahrefs Site Explorer
Judge whether you can beat it; being 2nd-5th can still pay
Snipe its keywords and backlinks

quote.text: finding a website that already succeeded that looks like kind of a mom and pop publisher
quote.speaker: Freychu

tactics.name: Backlink swap outreach
steps: Pull the competitor's backlinks in Ahrefs
Contact the sites linking to them
Offer about $50 to swap their link to yours (not just add)
Prefer pages with high domain rating, real traffic, and few outbound links
Avoid bulk Fiverr or low-quality link services; if buying, route through an intermediate article

quote.text: Can I pay you 50 bucks to swap out the link for ours
quote.speaker: Freychu

tactics.name: Validate demand with Reddit, TikTok and Google Maps reviews
steps: Search Reddit for the question; many threads signal unmet need
Use TikTok comments for unfiltered social listening
Read Google Maps review tags
Spend a couple of hours reading threads to find nuance for the directory's value

tactics.name: Programmatic build with data enrichment
steps: Collect location data in a database
Bulk import with WP Import and publish with GeoDirectory
Add filters with JetEngine (e.g. fenced area for small dogs)
Use AI to enrich listings with answers visitors need
Make it mobile-friendly; design matters less

tactics.name: Stack low-effort sites and wait
steps: Launch a directory and build another while you wait
Expect months for SEO results

Check monetisation potential before choosing a niche: RPMs vary hugely (gaming low, finance high), so traffic alone doesn't indicate revenue.
Use AI mainly for data enrichment that saves visitors time, not just for ideas; user-generated content gives better ideation signal.
Mine your own life moments (moving, graduation, hobbies) for directory ideas, since your experience gives unique angles.
Sharing the domain publicly invites copycats; keep winning niches quiet.

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest is a first-hand operator with consistent, plausible figures (~$2.3-3k/month, 70-90k visitors) but unverified, with no screenshots of revenue shown. Estimates for third-party sites (movie-locations, Penguin) are guesses from Ahrefs. The guest withholds domains, limiting verification. Tactics are specific and credible.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Freychu runs a free community and sells enrich.directory; the host promotes his own newsletter/podcast (tkopod.com). The host says the guest has nothing to sell, but the enrichment tool is a product.

video.title: You're Overthinking It. Here’s the Simple Way to Start (ft. Nick Huber)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Nick Huber about choosing practical businesses, finding customers, managing teams, and staying involved in operations. Huber describes his storage, recruiting, insurance, construction consulting, marketing, and other businesses, along with the student storage company he grew through chalk ads. He argues that straightforward services can be easier to start than novel ideas, while emphasizing that business ownership is stressful and not right for everyone. The conversation also covers AI, delegation, family, and Huber’s book, The Sweaty Startup.

video.title: Fastest Way to Copy Winning Digital Products (Picsart)

summary: Chris Koerner shows how to find and copy winning digital products on Etsy. The old-school method sorts printables by top reviews and looks for sellers with many reviews but few products, cross-checked on Google Trends. The faster hack changes 'star' to 'best' in the Etsy filter URL to reveal hidden best-sellers. He then uses Picsart's AI enhance and image generation to create similar designs, tests them on Facebook Marketplace or $20 Facebook ads, and moves winners to Etsy. The key takeaway is to copy what already works and change nothing at first.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; presents solo screen-share tutorial

ideas.name: Copycat Etsy digital printables using AI image tools
ideas.one_liner: Reverse engineer Etsy best-selling printables, generate similar designs with Picsart AI, and sell them as instant downloads on Etsy.
ideas.business_model: One-off digital product sales (instant download printables) on Etsy, net of Etsy fees
ideas.customer: Etsy shoppers buying printables: wall art, junk journals, baby shower games, coloring pages, stickers, homework pages
ideas.problem: Digital product markets are crowded, so sellers waste months on products with too much supply and too little demand
ideas.offer: Printable designs closely modelled on proven best-sellers, with AI-generated variations (e.g. seasonal wall art such as an Easter bunny)

pricing.model: Per-download price set near the proven best-seller; not specified
pricing.notes: No specific price given; the baby shower game price is only a guessing game in the video

acquisition_channels.details: List on Etsy and use Etsy's own search; use Etsy Ads on printables since the only cost is time/ad spend against a near-zero marginal product cost; optionally buy an established Etsy account whose feedback the algorithm already favours.

quote.text: you can buy Etsy accounts that have established feedback you're not necessarily buying a full store or a business or anything
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Test designs on Facebook Marketplace: list five designs with the same title, price and description as a pure A/B test and compare views, clicks and messages.

quote.text: Facebook Marketplace is the best place to test concepts like this because you could take five rabbit designs like these
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Run Facebook ads at a $20 budget each with the same ad but a different design, then move the winning design to Etsy.

quote.text: use that to launch some Facebook ads $20 budget each same ad different design see what people are clicking on
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Digital instant download. Designs are created in Picsart using AI enhance and AI image generation, using a best-seller screenshot as the style reference, then listed with multiple mock-up pictures. Delivery to the buyer is automatic via Etsy.
unit_economics_claims: Top Etsy printable sellers show 175,000 to 462,000 sales
Etsy Ads cost to acquire a customer is bounded by product price less Etsy fees
Four to six hours of research suggested to find winning categories
ideas.startup_cost: Low: Etsy listing fees, a Picsart subscription, a $20 per design ad test; exact figures not stated

acquisition.how: Etsy search, Etsy Ads and Facebook ads are inbound and software-run, so agents can do most of it. Research scraping can be done by agents (Manus/Operator), but the Etsy URL hack may be fragile and Etsy's terms may restrict scraping.

onboarding.how: Buyers purchase and download instantly with no onboarding.

delivery.how: AI generates designs and listing images, and Etsy delivers the files. A human or vision-checked review is needed for quality, text errors and copyright similarity.

billing.how: Etsy handles payments and payouts.

support.how: Low volume of buyer messages and refund questions; an agent can handle most with occasional human approval.

uk_applicability.notes: Etsy operates in the UK and sellers can list digital goods. UK VAT on digital sales needs handling (Etsy collects VAT in many cases), and HMRC trading income must be declared. Seasonal holidays differ (e.g. Easter works, Thanksgiving does not).

risks: Copying designs closely risks copyright or IP infringement claims and Etsy takedowns
Buying Etsy accounts likely breaches Etsy terms and can lead to suspension
The URL trick to reveal best-sellers may stop working
Heavy competition and low differentiation
AI struggles with text in images
Review counts are a proxy for sales, not a guarantee

quotes.text: a lot of the trick to this is finding a seller that has a rare combination of thousands of reviews but not a lot of products those are the diamonds in the rough

evidence_quality.rationale: A short tutorial with no first-hand sales results. All sales and review figures belong to other Etsy sellers and are read from screens. The method is concrete and reproducible but unproven by the speaker, and IP and platform-rule risks are not covered.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Host says he has no course to sell. He promotes a Facebook ad guide linked in the notes and appears to feature Picsart, which may be a sponsor or affiliate relationship, though this is not stated.

video.title: This Video Will Change How You Think About Money

summary: Chris Koerner interviews veteran reseller Shannon Jean on liquidation and bulk reselling. Shannon covers buying Costco/B-Stock returns pallets, soft-selling in scam-prone industries, letting buyers make most of the margin (e.g. $15M of watches with one buyer), always getting a manifest, and his best deal (salvage phones bought for $2M, sold for $11M). They discuss niches like college-town couch flipping, scratch-and-dent appliances and Blackstone cleanups, and Chris's 10-minute Tesla Cyber Quad flip. Key takeaway: reselling profits are averages over time, built on relationships, credibility and systems.

video.title: I Just Bought 3 Amazon Return Pallets for $1,500...Here's What I Found

summary: The host buys three liquidation pallets for $1,500 to give his son and other teenagers a chance to learn business skills and earn money for college. He sorts, researches, tests, lists and ships returned products, with some items broken, expired or difficult to identify. After a couple of weeks, he reports $219.82 in sales and says the work is substantial; his initial goal is to break even after wages. The video presents pallet reselling as an enjoyable but labor-intensive experiment, not a proven profit opportunity.

ideas.one_liner: Buy mixed retail returns in bulk, identify and test saleable products, then list and ship them individually.
ideas.business_model: Buy return pallets at a fixed cost and resell individual items through marketplaces and direct sales.

ideas.problem: Buyers can obtain returned or surplus products at a discount; teenagers can earn money and learn business skills.

ideas.delivery: The host and teenagers unpack and sort the pallets, research items online, test products where needed, take inventory, list items, and ship orders. unit_economics_claims: Three pallets cost $1,500 in total; the host estimated that selling everything for $4,000 could leave no profit after $2,500 in wages.
The host estimated the first pallet might yield $500 or $600 after discounting, but said this was uncertain and the work was substantial.
He reported $219.82 in sales after listing about 30 items and selling six, before final wages and other costs were known.
Shipping was initially free and sometimes cost more than the host expected; he planned to charge customers for shipping.
ideas.startup_cost: The host spent $1,500 on three pallets: $400, $700 and $400. He said his detached garage provided storage at no cost. He expected to spend about $2,500 on wages for his son and other teenagers; the hourly rate was not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: About a couple of weeks: the host said six items had sold by then. The exact date of the first sale was not stated.

acquisition.how: Marketplace listings and opt-in email notices can be assisted by software, but sourcing, product identification, pricing and listing details require substantial human input.

onboarding.how: Marketplace checkout can collect buyer and order details automatically; direct family sales may be handled manually.

delivery.how: People must sort physical stock, inspect or test products, pack orders and hand parcels to a carrier. Software can help track inventory and labels, but cannot perform the physical work.

billing.how: Marketplace payments can be processed automatically, while direct sales may need manual recording.

support.how: Agents could draft answers to common questions, but a person would need to handle condition disputes, missing parts, returns and product-safety concerns.

uk_applicability.notes: The basic buy-in-bulk and resell model can work in the UK, and marketplace selling is not inherently US-specific. A UK operator would need UK suppliers, GBP pricing and shipping, and to check relevant product-safety, consumer-sale and expiry rules, especially for electrical goods, cosmetics and health products.

risks: Pallet contents are uncertain; products may be broken, damaged, expired, incomplete or difficult to identify.
Retail or marketplace asking prices are not equivalent to realized sales or profit.
The process requires substantial manual sorting, research, testing, listing, packing and shipping.
Shipping costs can erase the margin if they are underestimated or included in a free-shipping offer.
Wages, marketplace fees, shipping and unsold stock may consume the apparent spread between pallet cost and estimated resale value.
Storing bulky and unsold items takes space; the host's free garage storage is a personal advantage that may not transfer to another operator.
Products with expired dates or uncertain safety and condition may be unsuitable to resell; UK rules would need to be checked before operating locally.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jacob Posel, an Australian AI builder in San Francisco, on the day OpenAI released its image generation API. They brainstorm consumer wrapper apps (Ghibli-style portraits, future-baby images, weight-loss visualiser, ageing), vertical uses (virtual staging, Airbnb photos, tree-trimming lead images) and, most deeply, AI ad creative: white-labelling high-volume ad variants for agencies or selling a $200/month tool to agencies via permissionless remade ads. Jacob shares reference-image prompting tips and says reliable viable-ad systems are still unsolved. Key takeaway: be ready to ship the moment a new capability drops, and target outputs that make customers money.

summary: Chris Koerner and Sam Thompson brainstorm business ideas enabled by ChatGPT's new image generation. They argue standalone novelty products (custom coloring books, print-on-demand art) are real but short-lived, and that the bigger opportunity is selling AI-generated personalised before/after mockups to home-service businesses (landscaping, painting, tree trimming, pool, remodel) for direct-mail and sales use. The pitch is a ~$500/month mockup tool or service sold to local contractors, found via Valpak mailers, plus tracked-number revenue-share deals. Key takeaway: the best marketer and channel wins, and the B2B application is less obvious than consumer novelty products. All numbers are speculative and untested.

video.title: Build Your Next Business With This Viral AI Tool

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Max Brodeur, co-founder of Y Combinator-backed Gumloop, a drag-and-drop AI workflow automation platform described as an AI-first Zapier. Max demos internal workflows (lead enrichment on signup, support-chat digest, pre-meeting research, SEO keyword filtering, YouTube-to-blog, Meta ads competitor analysis). Chris pitches businesses built on top: Gumloop expert/freelance builder, Facebook ads reverse-engineering as a service, programmatic SEO as a service, white-labelled flows. The key takeaway is that niche workflow knowledge encoded into AI workflows can be sold as a service, but the video is partly promotional (affiliate link) and numbers are sparse.

video.title: Billy Quit his Job to Start an AI App Agency: Here's How

summary: Billy Howell, a self-taught vibe coder and former defense contractor, explains how he runs an AI app agency (Stupid Simple Apps) with a team of four, building small custom internal apps for business owners using Replit, v0, Cursor and similar tools. He describes landing his first app job on Upwork by building a demo and undercutting a no-code stack, and gives detailed Upwork tips (Looms, connects, client vetting). He advises against starting with consumer apps, shares side-project ideas (recipe generator, plant time-lapse), and discusses shiny-object syndrome and building in public for inbound. Key takeaway: sell niche B2B custom apps to paying clients first, using fast AI-built demos and relationship-based sales.

summary: Chris Koerner and Nick compare how entrepreneurs use AI tools and discuss lessons from 30 interviews. They describe ChatGPT as a thought partner, Claude as a coding partner, Perplexity for research, and Gemini for Google Workspace workflows, while also discussing Cursor and Replit. The business opportunities raised include AI-assisted mediation, a certification and rating service, an AI model selection quiz, and AI sales workflows. A recurring takeaway is to focus AI on sales and other work that can be tied directly to revenue.

video.title: Don’t Sleep on This Specific $0-to-Millions Reselling Strategy

summary: Host Chris Koerner interviews reseller and liquidator Shannon about buying discounted liquidation lots and finding buyers before bidding. Shannon describes his past handbag business, examples involving industrial goods, apparel and other categories, and the research and sales processes he uses. His central advice is to build a repeatable system, check what inventory can sell for before buying it, and make sure the deal leaves room for freight and resale work. The examples are hands-on, but the businesses depend on sourcing, handling and shipping physical inventory.

tactics.name: Validate buyers before bidding
steps: Find the likely resale market for a product before bidding.
Use eBay Product Research to check sold prices and the number of sales.
Call likely business buyers to ask what they need and what price they would pay.
Only bid once you have a credible route to recovering the purchase cost.

quote.text: the first law of auctions is never buy anything unless you know what you can already sell it for.
quote.speaker: Shannon

tactics.name: Calculate a conservative landed bid
steps: Discount the stated retail price because Shannon says it can be misleading.
Estimate a cautious resale value and subtract freight and other costs.
Use a spreadsheet or product equation to set a maximum bid.
Bid with math rather than emotion.

quote.text: I use math to bid, not emotion. I've studied. I've done my research.
quote.speaker: Shannon

tactics.name: Study a category before scaling
steps: Watch auctions and research the category before making large purchases.
Make small mistakes while the stakes are low.
Learn how listings, photos, authenticity, shipping and returns work.
Move into larger lots only after the market and process make sense.

quote.text: So studying that when you can make small mistakes is really powerful and that's what I was doing.
quote.speaker: Shannon

tactics.name: Build platform relationships before problems arise
steps: Find platform category managers and product managers on LinkedIn.
Interact with their public posts and congratulate them on relevant work.
Send a short introduction explaining the category and sales activity.
Offer to speak about the seller experience, then build the relationship over time.

quote.text: You don't want to ask him for anything, but you want to get in his conversation flow.
quote.speaker: Shannon

tactics.name: Differentiate listings with evidence
steps: Look at what other sellers include in their listings.
For used goods, record a short video showing the item working.
Use clear photography and explain condition accurately.
For high-value goods, package them carefully and include a thank-you card or coupon where economics allow.

quote.text: I've got video of me walking around or if it's used I have a video of it working all that kind of stuff.
quote.speaker: Shannon

tactics.name: Handle complaints with empathy
steps: Acknowledge the customer's disappointment instead of arguing about fault.
Offer a prepaid return label promptly.
Consider a future-purchase coupon when it is economically sensible.
Take responsibility for the overall transaction and delivery experience.

quote.text: So, you always choose the end of the world token and you say, Oh my gosh, I'm so sorry.
quote.speaker: Shannon

tactics.name: Sell bulk goods to the businesses that use them
steps: Identify businesses that consume or transform the product, such as screen printers for blank apparel.
Use the lot manifest to explain what is available.
Ask potential buyers what they would pay before buying the inventory.
Follow up when a suitable lot becomes available.

quote.text: The story just tell them the truth. Hey, I'm I'm in the resale business and I get all these opportunities
quote.speaker: Shannon

tactics.name: Look for an unfair advantage
steps: Identify what you can do better than other sellers: capital, storage, delivery, expertise or customer service.
Choose product categories where that advantage matters.
Use the advantage to make an otherwise difficult lot easier to buy or sell.

quote.text: I call it what is your unfair advantage? What do you have that other people don't?
quote.speaker: Shannon

tactics.name: Track product and category changes
steps: Watch how product design and repairability change over time.
Notice when a previously profitable category loses parts or margin.
Move research to another category rather than assuming the old opportunity will persist.

quote.text: Nothing stays the same. And if and if you don't continually invol evolve what you're working on, you'll be left behind.
quote.speaker: Shannon

summary: Niche Pursuits presents FormulaBot.com, an Excel add-on chatbot built by non-programmer David Brestler on Bubble.io, reportedly making about $26,000/month. The host then builds his own simple AI side-hustle idea generator live in about 45 minutes with Hostinger Horizons (the video's sponsor) and shows the iterative prompting. evidence_quality.rationale: The episode is a conversational idea session with several proposed businesses and anecdotal examples. It contains practical testing suggestions, but most ideas lack operating detail, verified customer data or consistent unit economics. Several scale claims about third-party apparel brands are second-hand. The speakers do not clearly identify every turn, so some speaker attributions are left null.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host briefly promotes a newsletter and audio podcast. No course or software sale is stated.

video.title: Is Rucking the Next Gold Rush?

summary: Chris Koerner and Nick discuss business opportunities around new AI image generation, including resume graphics and family portraits, then turn to rucking products and services. They brainstorm a low-cost backpack and weights kit, premium gear, a guide, affiliate products, and a rucking app. The conversation also uses home services and side hustles to discuss how founders can build experience, find an edge, and start before overthinking. Most opportunities are speculative; the speakers give a few first-hand examples but little operating evidence.

warnings.warning: Image generation may refuse prompts involving a named public figure, and the generated image may still depict that person despite the refusal wording.
Image editing is not fully reliable: the speakers show altered text, changed people, and image details that need review.
AI-generated family portraits involve personal photographs and require careful consent and privacy handling.
The speakers caution that free work and viral content do not guarantee a successful business; luck is not a strategy.
A builder says that the proposed free silt-fence repair pitch would not work for him; the tactic may not convert with every buyer.
Heavy weights can make shipping expensive, which may undermine the low-cost rucking kit idea.
Do not assume an operator can be hired to replace understanding the business; the speakers argue founders need to learn the work.
Chris promotes his newsletter and podcast during the video, creating a promotional conflict, though the discussion is not a direct software or course pitch.

evidence_quality.rationale: The video is a brainstorming conversation rather than a documented case study. The speakers describe a few first-hand experiments, but most business concepts are proposals, and the GoRuck sales and pricing figures are second-hand and not verified.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Chris promotes his newsletter and podcast during the episode; no course or sponsor product is pitched.

video.title: How to Make Money With Tariffs While Everyone Panics

summary: Chris Koerner discusses business opportunities arising from the April 2025 US 'Liberation Day' tariffs. He pitches a sourcing-intelligence play using ImportYeti and Jungle Scout (sourcing agent, newsletter, cold outreach to Shopify stores), offshore staffing/placement agencies, a last-mile agency finishing AI-built (vibe-coded) projects, tariff consulting, buying distressed small businesses with seller financing, and made-in-America ecommerce. He also urges not to panic and cites companies founded in downturns. Mostly speculative brainstorming, not first-hand operator proof.

video.title: This Little AI Device Will Print Millionaires

summary: Chris Koerner and Nick discuss ways to build AI implementation services around a voice-recording pendant, especially for physicians and sales teams. They brainstorm other uses in assisted living, therapy, retail, remote work and coaching, while noting that integrations, consent and privacy create real barriers. The conversation also explores AI-powered background research and a possible pay-per-use Deep Research website. Most of the business ideas are hypotheses rather than tested operations.

video.title: Stop Chasing Billion Dollar Ideas. Do This Instead.

summary: Chris Koerner and an unnamed guest discuss small, testable business ideas, including a cooking app, social media theme pages, digital guides and AI-generated business plans. Chris describes a programmatic workflow for repurposing viral cooking videos and says he tests offers with paid ads. The guest explains Unlimited Content’s SEO blog service and how it uses AI with human editing. Their shared theme is to make a clear offer, test it quickly and sell convenience while keeping delivery simple.

video.title: How to Start a $1M Online Business WITHOUT "Gimmicks"!

summary: The Niche Pursuits host contrasts fragile online loopholes with businesses built around real customer problems. He describes his past niche websites, his Long Tail Pro software business, and products including a thin pillow and Link Whisper, then lists seven models he considers risky. His five-step framework is to solve a real problem, work directly with customers, build an email audience, diversify beyond algorithms, and recruit affiliates. The central takeaway is that durable products and customer relationships offer more control than income dependent on platform rules or trends.

video.title: AI Agents Are Overhyped. Use THIS Instead

summary: The hosts compare AI agents with current research tools, arguing that deep research is more useful today for many tasks than agents that still need close supervision. They demonstrate using AI to explore a US banana-ketchup opportunity and pitch a business selling forward-looking industry reports. They also discuss an interactive floor-tile games business and retell Ethan Cohen’s stories about a sports book and campus vending machines. Most business figures are estimates or second-hand claims, and the transcript does not establish that any idea is already being run autonomously.

tactics.name: Use deep research for structured desk research
steps: Give the research tool a specific task and name the sources or websites to inspect.
Ask it to return findings in a defined format, such as a table.
For large datasets, state the number of rows and require the full dataset rather than a sample.
Ask for concise bullet points after receiving a long report.
Check key claims against an independent source such as Google Trends before treating them as evidence.

tactics.name: Give AI explicit research instructions
steps: Describe the input data, its size, and the fields in each row.
Specify the output fields, categories, and constraints.
Explain how to score or rank results.
Follow up to clarify gaps rather than assuming the first response is complete.

quote.text: if you want to get the right answer you've got to ask a longer question and even after asking that I there were other follow-up questions

tactics.name: Validate AI-generated market ideas with another data point
steps: Use deep research to generate a candidate product or trend.
Check a separate source such as Google Trends for evidence of search interest.
Return to the research tool with the candidate and ask for a feasibility or market analysis.
Treat the result as a lead to investigate, not proof of demand.

video.title: How This "NICHE DIRECTORY" Website Makes $10M/Year!

summary: Niche Pursuits host Spencer Haws reviews five niche directory websites: HappyCow (vegan restaurants, estimated $10M/yr by Growjo), SoakOregon (Oregon hot springs, ~30k visits/month), Sober Nation (rehab directory, ~$250k/yr across a small network, plus an SEO agency for rehab directories), Care.com (acquired for $500M) and MCP.so (MCP server directory, 3 months old, ~52k visits/month). Revenue figures are mostly estimates from Growjo, SimilarWeb traffic and an ad RPM calculator rather than verified numbers. The key takeaway is that niche directories monetise via display ads and sponsored placements, and that a directory can lead into an adjacent service business. A Hostinger sponsor segment is included.

video.title: How This "CALCULATOR" Website Makes $36,000/Month!

summary: The Niche Pursuits host reviews four free calculator websites and estimates their traffic and display-ad revenue using third-party traffic data and assumed RPMs. The examples range from a simple bedtime calculator to a large general-purpose calculator site, with a seasonal snow-day predictor and a gematria tool in between. The host suggests calculator tools can work in narrow niches or be added to an existing website. The central lesson is that traffic and monetization matter as much as building the calculator, but the revenue figures are estimates rather than operator-verified results.

tactics.name: Check the search terms bringing visitors to a calculator
steps: Use a search or traffic-research service to identify the organic visitor estimate.
Review related queries, including exact calculator terms and adjacent problem searches.
Check whether the site ranks across many related keywords rather than a single phrase.

quote.text: Overall, this website ranks for thousands of sleep calculator related keywords in Google.
quote.speaker: Niche Pursuits host (name not stated)

tactics.name: Account for seasonal traffic before estimating revenue
steps: Compare traffic peaks and valleys across the year.
Identify the months that drive the high season.
Estimate revenue for the high season separately instead of treating it as a year-round monthly run rate.

quote.text: But for a solid three or four months out of the year, this website is likely getting slammed with traffic.

tactics.name: Consider a narrow calculator or a calculator feature on an existing site
steps: Look for a simple, specific calculation that people already search for.
Consider whether a calculator could improve an existing website's offer.
For a new standalone idea, choose a niche or entertaining use case; validate demand before assuming traffic or revenue.
